A
HOUSEHOLD BOOK
OF
E N G L I S H P O E T R Y

lg.l: SELECTED AND ARRANGED
With Notes
BY
RICHARD CHENEVIX TRENCH, D.D.
ARCHBISHOP OF DUBLIN
LONDON
M A C M I L L A N A N D C O.
LONDON: PRINTED BY
SPOTTISWOODE AND CO., NEW-STREET SQUARE
AND PARLIAMENT STREET

div.head: PREFACE.
div.p: The first question which I asked myself, when I resumed a purpose long ago entertained, and then for a long while laid aside, of publishing such a selection of English Poetry as the present, was this, namely, whether Mr. Palgrave’s Golden Treasury had not so occupied the ground that there was no room for one who should come after. The selection is one made with so exact an acquaintance with the sources from which his Treasury was to be replenished, with so fine a taste in regard of what was worthy to be admitted there, that this was the conclusion to which at the first I was disposed to arrive. Presently, however, I saw reason to change my mind. The volume which I meditated was on so different a scheme and plan from his, that, while no doubt I should sometimes go over ground which he had gone over before, it was evident that for the most part our paths would be different, and my choice not identical with his. This to so great an extent has proved the case, that of more than three hundred pieces which compose this volume, less than seventy have appeared in his. And it is easy to perceive how this should be. His is a Treasury of the best songs and lyrical poems in the English Language, and of these exclusively; but within this circle he proposes to include all which is of first-rate excellence in our language by authors not living. My scheme is at once broader and narrower; broader, in that I limit myself to no one particular class of poetry, and embrace the living and the dead alike; narrower, in that I make no attempt to be exhaustive, or to give more than a very few samples even of the best and greatest of our poets.

But if Mr. Palgrave had not forestalled me, I certainly did not feel that any other had so done. Most of the collections which have fallen under my eye have failed to give me the impression of being the result of direct and immediate investigation on the part of the collector into the treasures of our English Poetry. There is so much there which invites citation, and which has never been cited yet in any of our popular anthologies, that it is difficult to think that any one who had himself wandered in this garden of riches would not have carried off some flowers and fruits of his own gathering; instead of offering to us again, as most do, though it may be in somewhat different combinations, what already has been offered by others. When I see, for example, ‘Queen and huntress chaste and fair,’ doubtless a very graceful lyric, with one or two other familiar poems, doing duty in one collection after another as the specimens of Ben Jonson’s verse, it is hard to suppose that his rich and pleasant Underwood has been wandered through; since in that case something which others have not brought already would surely have been brought away from thence; while the specimens from other poets provoke a similar misgiving. Whatever merit or demerit this may imply, the volume here presented lays claim to a certain originality—or, if that word cannot in this matter be allowed,—to a certain independence of judgment. There has not, indeed, been any attempt, as certainly there has been no desire, to reverse the general judgment and decision about the great poems of the language. He who should offer to do this would merely betray his own presumption, and his unfitness for even so humble a task as that here attempted. But in poems of a very high merit, which yet do not attain to the highest rank of all, there is ample space for the play of such an independent judgment, and I have not hesitated to exercise this. Many, which almost all collections have hitherto contained, will be looked for in vain in this; not a few which, so far as I know, none have included, have found room in it. It is not always that I have considered what I bring forward better than what to make place for it I set aside; but where I have only considered it as good, it has seemed a real gain to put new treasures within the reach of those who are little able, or, if able, are little likely, to go and discover such for themselves. But in very many instances I feel sure that what I have made room for is not merely as good, but better than that which to make room for it I have dismissed; nor has it been a little pleasure to draw from obscure retreats, or from retreats only familiar to those who have made English poetry more or less of a special study, and acquainted themselves with its bye ways no less than its high ways, poems which little merit the oblivion into which they had fallen.

I have called this volume a Household Book of English Poetry, by this name implying that it is a book for all, that there is nothing in it to prevent it from being confidently placed in the hands of every member of the household. I wish I could have kept it within a moderate size by no more than the excluding from it everything of inferior value; but it will be evident to all who are at all acquainted with the inexhaustible opulence of English Poetry that I could only do this by continual acts of self-denial, having, at every step of my progress, to set my seal to the truth of that Eastern proverb which says, ‘You may bring a nosegay to the city, but you cannot bring the garden.’ This is indeed all which in this anthology I have attempted. To have allowed it to grow to a larger bulk would have defeated my hopes that it might be a volume which the emigrant, finding room for little not absolutely necessary, might yet find room for it in his trunk, and the traveller in his knapsack, and that on some narrow shelves where there are few books this might be one. But indeed the actual amount which such a volume contains, whether it be much or little, will be of less consequence in our eyes, when once we have apprehended that Horace was only under the mark when he affirmed of good poetry that ten times repeated it will please. It would be truer to say of a poem which in motive, in form, in diction, in melody, in unity of plan, satisfies all conditions, that it is ‘a joy for ever.’ It is impossible so to draw out the sweetness of it that it shall not still have as much to yield us, or it maybe more than it had at the beginning. How many another book, once read, can yield no more pleasure or profit to us—but poems of the highest order are in their very essence sources of a delight which is inexhaustible. However much of this has been drawn from them, as much or more remains behind.

There is another reflection which may console us in leaving so much untouched, namely, that almost every considerable poet has written something, in which all that he has of highest and most characteristic has come to a head. Thus I remember that Wordsworth used to speak of Shelley’s Ode to a Skylark as the expression of the highest to which his genius had attained. Wordsworth’s own Lines on revisiting the banks of the Wye, or, higher perhaps even than these, his Lines suggested by a picture of Peele Castle in a Storm, I should regard as fulfilling for him the same conditions; and what is true of these two, is no less true of other poets out of number.

I have nowhere given extracts from larger poems, but only poems which may be regarded as complete in themselves. It is true that I have sometimes made room for such as, through their length, or through some other cause, must otherwise have been shut out, by omissions; but only where I believed these omissions to be real gains; and I do not think I have anywhere done this without giving warning to the reader. There are, no doubt, certain inconveniences which attend a resolution only to give entire poems and not extracts; and this the chief one—that the space allotted to different poets cannot in all or nearly all instances represent or correspond to their several importance. Some poets have thrown all or well nigh all their poetic faculty into the composition of one or two great poems; and have very seldom indeed allowed themselves in briefer excursions into the land of song. Others on the contrary, of not higher, or it may be not nearly so high, a gift, have put a large part of their strength into these occasional poems, and will therefore yield for a volume like the present infinitely more than their more illustrious compeers. Under the action of this rule, and dramatic poetry being of necessity excluded, there is nothing of Shakespeare’s to choose from but his Sonnets and his Songs—these certainly being in themselves much, but still little when compared with what is passed by. Again, one who does not believe in Alexander’s Feast, and still less in the Ode on the Death of Mrs. Killigrew, finds it hard, indeed impossible, to deal anything approaching to justice to Dryden, or by specimens which are at his command to afford any true representation of the range of his powers or the eminence of his place in English literature. It is the same and nearly to the same extent with Pope; while others, like Gray and Campbell, get justice and more than justice; though, yielding what they do, one does not grudge this to them in the least. The inconvenience would certainly be a grave one, if the volume presented itself as primarily a Manual of English Poetry, or an assistance to the study of the history of this; but having quite another as its primary object, it is one which may very well be borne, while the advantages of such a rule of selection are undoubted.

I have attached a few notes to this volume. I had intended to add many more, but under the pressure of events which now claim, and for a long time to come are likely to claim, nearly all one’s thoughts and leisure, have been obliged to renounce the carrying of this intention out, and only to print those which were ready. If in them there is little or nothing with which professed students of English literature are not already familiar, I can only urge that this volume was not designed, and still less were the notes designed, for such; but for readers who, capable of an intelligent interest in the subject, have yet had neither time nor opportunity for special studies of their own in it, and who must therefore rely more or less on the hand-leading of others; nor I trust shall I be found fault with that I have sometimes taken upon me in these notes to indicate what seemed worthy of special admiration; or sought in other ways to plant the reader at that point of view from which the merits of some poem might be most deeply felt and best understood. If I am, I must plead in excuse that for myself in other regions of art, as in music or painting, where I have comparatively little or no confidence in my own judgment, I have been and often am most thankful to those, being persons whom I could trust, who have told me what to admire, and given me the reasons for so doing. If we set aside a few intuitive geniuses, it is only thus that any of us can ever hope to be educated into independence of judgment; and I am sure that some, acknowledging this, will be grateful for notes of admiration, by which I have sometimes called their attention to that which otherwise might not obtain it, or might not obtain it to the full of its deserts.
London: May 8th, 1868.

div.head:
A
HOUSEHOLD BOOK
OF
E N G L I S H P O E T R Y

head.label: I
head.hi: A MEDITATION UPON THE FRAILTY OF THIS LIFE.

lg.l: O trifling toys that toss the brains,
While loathsome life doth last;
O wishèd wealth, O sugared joys,
O life when death is past;

div.p: Who loaths exchange of loss with gain? 5
Yet loath we death as hell.
What woeful wight would wish his woe?
Yet wish we here to dwell.
O Fancy frail, that feeds on earth,
And stays on slippery joys; 10

lg.l: O noble mind, O happy man,
That can contemn such toys!
Such toys as neither perfect are,
And cannot long endure;

div.p: Our greatest skill, our sweetest joy, 15

lg.l: Uncertain and unsure.
For life is short, and learning long,
All pleasure mixt with woe;
Sickness and sleep steal time unseen,

div.p: And joys do come and go. 20

lg.l: Thus learning is but learned by halves,
And joy enjoyed no while;
That serves to show thee what thou want’st,
This helps thee to beguile.

div.p: But after death is perfect skill, 25

lg.l: And joy without decay;
When sin is gone, that blinds our eyes,
And steals our joys away;
No crowing cock shall raise us up,

div.p: To spend the day in vain; 30

lg.l: No weary labour shall us drive
To go to bed again.
But for we feel not what we want,
Nor know not what we have;

div.p: We love to keep the body’s life, 35
We loath the soul to save.

head.label: II
head.hi: LOVE THE ONLY PRICE OF LOVE.

lg.l: The fairest pearls that northern seas do breed,
For precious stones from eastern coasts are sold;
Nought yields the earth that from exchange is freed;
Gold values all, and all things value gold.

div.p: Where goodness wants an equal change to make, 5

lg.l: There greatness serves, or number place doth take.
No mortal thing can bear so high a price,
But that with mortal thing it may be bought;
The corn of Sicil buys the western spice;

div.p: French wine of us, of them our cloth is sought. 10
No pearls, no gold, no stones, no corn, no spice,
No cloth, no wine, of Love can pay the price.
What thing is Love, which nought can countervail?
Nought save itself, ev’n such a thing is Love.
All worldly wealth in worth as far doth fail, 15
As lowest earth doth yield to heaven above.
Divine is Love, and scorneth worldly pelf,
And can be bought with nothing but with self.

head.label: III
head.hi: A POESY TO PROVE AFFECTION IS NOT LOVE

lg.l: Conceit, begotten by the eyes,
Is quickly born, and quickly dies;
For while it seeks our hearts to have,
Meanwhile there reason makes his grave:

div.p: For many things the eyes approve, 5

lg.l: Which yet the heart doth seldom love.
For as the seeds, in springtime sown,
Die in the ground ere they be grown;
Such is conceit, whose rooting fails,

div.p: As child that in the cradle quails; 10

lg.l: Or else within the mother’s womb
Hath his beginning, and his tomb.
Affection follows Fortune’s wheels,
And soon is shaken from her heels;

div.p: For following beauty or estate, 15

lg.l: Her liking still is turned to hate;
For all affections have their change,
And Fancy only loves to range.
Desire himself runs out of breath,

div.p: And, getting, doth but gain his death; 20

lg.l: Desire nor reason hath, nor rest,
And, blind, doth seldom choose the best:
Desire attained is not desire,
But as the cinders of the fire.

div.p: As ships in ports desired are drowned; 25

lg.l: As fruit, once ripe, then falls to ground;
As flies, that seek for flames, are brought
To cinders by the flames they sought:
So fond Desire, when it attains,

div.p: The life expires, the woe remains. 30

lg.l: And yet some poets fain would prove
Affection to be perfect love;
And that Desire is of that kind,
No less a passion of the mind,

div.p: As if wild beasts and men did seek 35
To like, to love, to choose alike.

lg.l: The World’s a bubble, and the Life of Man
Less than a span;
In his conception wretched; from the womb
So to the tomb;

div.p: Curst from his cradle, and brought up to years 5

lg.l: With cares and fears.
Who then to frail mortality shall trust,
But limns on water, or but writes in dust.
Yet whilst with sorrow here we live opprest,

div.p: What life is best? 10

lg.l: Courts are but only superficial schools
To dandle fools:
The rural parts are turned into a den
Of savage men:

div.p: And where’s a city from foul vice so free, 15

lg.l: But may be termed the worst of all the three?
Domestic cares afflict the husband’s bed,
Or pains his head:
Those that live single, take it for a curse,

div.p: Or do things worse: 20

lg.l: Some would have children; those that have them, moan,
Or wish them gone:
What is it, then, to have, or have no wife,
But single thraldom, or a double strife?

div.p: Our own affections still at home to please 25

lg.l: Is a disease:
To cross the seas to any foreign soil,
Peril and toil:
Wars with their noise affright us; when they cease,

div.p: We’ are worse in peace:— 30
What then remains, but that we still should cry
For being born, or, being born, to die?

lg.l: The lowest trees have tops; the ant her gall;
The fly her spleen; the little sparks their heat:
The slender hairs cast shadows, though but small;
And bees have stings, although they be not great.

div.p: Seas have their surges, so have shallow springs; 5

lg.l: And love is love, in beggars as in kings.
Where rivers smoothest run, deep are the fords;
The dial stirs, yet none perceives it move;
The firmest faith is in the fewest words;

div.p: The turtles cannot sing, and yet they love. 10
True hearts have eyes, and ears, no tongues to speak;
They hear, and see, and sigh; and then they break.

lg.l: Go, Soul, the body’s guest,
Upon a thankless errand;
Fear not to touch the best;
The truth shall be thy warrant.

div.p: Go, since I needs must die, 5

lg.l: And give the world the lie.
Say to the Court it glows
And shines like rotten wood;
Say to the Church it shows

div.p: What’s good, and doth no good. 10

lg.l: If Church and Court reply,
Then give them both the lie.
Tell Potentates they live
Acting by others’ action;

div.p: Not loved unless they give, 15

lg.l: Not strong but by affection.
If Potentates reply,
Give Potentates the lie.
Tell men of high condition,

div.p: That manage the Estate, 20

lg.l: Their purpose is ambition,
Their practice only hate.
And if they once reply,
Then give them all the lie.

div.p: Tell them that brave it most, 25

lg.l: They beg for more by spending,
Who in their greatest cost
Like nothing but commending:
And if they make reply,

div.p: Then tell them all they lie. 30

lg.l: Tell Zeal it wants devotion;
Tell Love it is but lust;
Tell Time it is but motion;
Tell Flesh it is but dust.

div.p: And wish them not reply, 35

lg.l: For thou must give the lie.
Tell Age it daily wasteth;
Tell Honour how it alters;
Tell Beauty how she blasteth;

div.p: Tell Favour how it falters. 40

lg.l: And as they shall reply,
Give every one the lie.
Tell Wit how much it wrangles
In tickle points of niceness;

div.p: Tell Wisdom she entangles 45

lg.l: Herself in over-wiseness.
And when they do reply,
Straight give them both the lie.
Tell Physic of her boldness;

div.p: Tell Skill it is pretension; 50

lg.l: Tell Charity of coldness;
Tell Law it is contention.
And as they do reply,
So give them all the lie.

div.p: Tell Fortune of her blindness; 55

lg.l: Tell Nature of decay;
Tell Friendship of unkindness;
Tell Justice of delay.
And if they will reply,

div.p: Then give them all the lie. 60

lg.l: Tell Arts they have no soundness,
But vary by esteeming;
Tell Schools they want profoundness,
And stand so much on seeming.

div.p: If Arts and Schools reply, 65

lg.l: Give Arts and Schools the lie.
Tell Faith it’s fled the city;
Tell how the country erreth;
Tell Manhood shakes off pity;

div.p: Tell Virtue least preferreth. 70

lg.l: And if they do reply,
Spare not to give the lie.
So when thou hast, as I
Commanded thee, done blabbing,

div.p: Because to give the lie 75

lg.l: Deserves no less than stabbing,
Stab at thee who that will,
No stab the soul can kill.
Anon..

div.p: What is the world? tell, worldling, if thou know it.
If it be good, why do all ills o’erflow it?
If it be bad, why dost thou like it so?
If it be sweet, how comes it bitter then?
If it be bitter, what bewitcheth men? 5
If it be friend, why kills it, as a foe,
Vain-minded men that over-love and lust it?
If it be foe, fondling, how dar’st thou trust it?

lg.l: Friend faber, cast me a round hollow ball,
Blown full of wind, for emblem of this All;
Adorn it fair, and flourish every part
With flowers and fruits, with brooks, beasts, fish, and fowl,

div.p: With rarest cunning of thy curious art: 5
And grave in gold, about my silver bowl,

p.hi: Thus rolls the world, the idol of mankind,

div.p: Whose fruit is fiction; whose foundation wind.

lg.l: Where, where are now the great reports
Of those huge haughty earthborn giants?
Where are the lofty towers and forts
Of those proud kings bade Heaven defiance?

div.p: When these I to my mind revoke, 5
Methinks I see a mighty smoke
Thick mounting from quick-burning matter,
Which in an instant winds do scatter.

lg.l: Go, silly worm, drudge, trudge, and travel,
Despising pain, so thou may’st gain
Some honour or some golden gravel;
But death the while, to fill his number,

div.p: With sudden call takes thee from all, 5
To prove thy days but dream and slumber.

lg.l: The World and Death one day them cross-disguisèd,
To cozen man, when sin had once beguiled him.
Both called him forth, and questioning advisèd
To say whose servant he would fairly yield him.

div.p: Man, weening then but to the World to’ have given him, 5

lg.l: By the false World became the slave of Death;
But from their fraud he did appeal by faith
To Him whose death killed Death, and from the world has driven him.

head.label: VIII
head.hi: THE STORY OF A SUMMER DAY.

lg.l: O perfect Light, which shaid away
The darkness from the light,
And set a ruler o’er the day,
Another o’er the night;

div.p: Thy glory, when the day forth flies, 5

lg.l: More vively does appear,
Than at midday unto our eyes
The shining sun is clear.
The shadow of the earth anon

div.p: Removes and drawis by, 10

lg.l: While in the east, when it is gone,
Appears a clearer sky.
Which soon perceive the little larks,
The lapwing and the snipe,

div.p: And tune their songs, like Nature’s clerks, 15

lg.l: O’er meadow, muir, and stripe.
Our hemisphere is polished clean,
And lightened more and more;
While everything is clearly seen,

div.p: Which seemèd dim before: 20

lg.l: Except the glistering astres bright,
Which all the night were clear,
Offuskèd with a greater light
No longer do appear.

div.p: The golden globe incontinent 25

lg.l: Sets up his shining head,
And o’er the earth and firmament
Displays his beams abread.
For joy, the birds with boulden throats

div.p: Against his visage sheen 30

lg.l: Take up their kindly music notes
In woods and gardens green.
The dew upon the tender crops,
Like pearles white and round,

div.p: Or like to melted silver drops, 35

lg.l: Refreshes all the ground.
The misty reek, the clouds of rain
From tops of mountains skails,
Clear are the highest hills and plain,

div.p: The vapours take the vales. 40

lg.l: The ample heaven, of fabric sure,
In cleanness does surpass
The crystal and the silver pure,
Or clearest polished glass.

div.p: The time so tranquil is and still, 45

lg.l: That no where shall ye find,
Save on a high and barren hill,
The air of peeping wind.
All trees and simples, great and small,

div.p: That balmy leaf do bear, 50

lg.l: Than they were painted on a wall,
No more they move or steir.
Calm is the deep and purple sea,
Yea, smoother than the sand;

div.p: The waves, that weltering wont to be, 55

lg.l: Are stable like the land.
So silent is the cessile air,
That every cry and call,
The hills and dales and forest fair

div.p: Again repeats them all. 60

lg.l: The flourishes and fragrant flowers,
Through Phœbus’ fostering heat,
Refreshed with dew and silver showers,
Cast up an odour sweet.

div.p: The cloggèd busy humming bees, 65

lg.l: That never think to drone,
On flowers and flourishes of trees,
Collect their liquor brown.
The sun, most like a speedy post,

div.p: With ardent course ascends; 70

lg.l: The beauty of the heavenly host
Up to our zenith tends;
Not guided by a Phaëthon,
Not trainèd in a chair,

div.p: But by the high and holy One, 75

lg.l: Who does all where empíre.
The burning beams down from his face
So fervently can beat,
That man and beast now seek a place

div.p: To save them from the heat. 80

lg.l: The herds beneath some leafy tree,
Amidst the flowers they lie;
The stable ships upon the sea
Tend up their sails to dry.

div.p: With gilded eyes and open wings, 85

lg.l: The cock his courage shows;
With claps of joy his breast he dings,
And twenty times he crows.
The dove with whistling wings so blue,

div.p: The winds can fast collect, 90

lg.l: Her purple pens turn many a hue
Against the sun direct.
Now noon is went; gone is midday,
The heat does slake at last,

div.p: The sun descends down west away, 95

lg.l: For three o’clock is past.
The rayons of the sun we see
Diminish in their strength,
The shade of every tower and tree

div.p: Extended is in length. 100

lg.l: Great is the calm, for everywhere
The wind is setting down,
The reek throws right up in the air
From every tower and town.

div.p: The gloming comes, the day is spent, 105

lg.l: The sun goes out of sight,
And painted is the occident
With purple sanguine bright.
The scarlet nor the golden thread,

div.p: Who would their beauty try, 110

lg.l: Are nothing like the colour red
And beauty of the sky.
Our west horizon circular,
From time the sun be set,

div.p: Is all with rubies, as it were, 115

lg.l: Or roses red o’erfret.
What pleasure were to walk and see,
Endlong a river clear,
The perfect form of every tree

div.p: Within the deep appear. 120

lg.l: Oh then it were a seemly thing,
While all is still and calm,
The praise of God to play and sing
With cornet and with shalm!

div.p: All labourers draw home at even, 125

lg.l: And can to other say,
Thanks to the gracious God of heaven,
Which sent this summer day.

head.label: IX
head.hi: A VOW TO LOVE FAITHFULLY, HOWSOEVER HE BE REWARDED.

lg.l: Set me whereas the sun doth parch the green,
Or where his beams do not dissolve the ice;
In temperate heat where he is felt and seen;
In presence prest of people, mad or wise;

div.p: Set me in high, or yet in low degree; 5

lg.l: In longest night, or in the shortest day;
In clearest sky, or where clouds thickest be;
In lusty youth, or when my hairs are gray:
Set me in heaven, in earth, or else in hell,

div.p: In hill or dale, or in the foaming flood; 10

lg.l: Thrall, or at large, alive whereso I dwell,
Sick or in health, in evil fame or good,
Hers will I be; and only with this thought
Content myself, although my chance be nought.
Forget not yet the tried intent
Of such a truth as I have meant;
My great travail so gladly spent
Forget not yet!

div.p: Forget not yet when first began 5

lg.l: The weary life ye know, since whan
The suit, the service none tell can;
Forget not yet!
Forget not yet the great assays,

div.p: The cruel wrong, the scornful ways; 10

lg.l: The painful patience in delays,
Forget not yet!
Forget not! oh! forget not this,
How long ago hath been, and is

div.p: The mind that never meant amiss— 15

lg.l: Forget not yet!
Forget not then thine own approved,
The which so long hath thee so loved,
Whose steadfast faith yet never moved—

div.p: Forget not this! 20

lg.l: If women could be fair, and yet not fond,
Or that their love were firm, not fickle still,
I would not marvel that they make men bond
By service long to purchase their good will;

div.p: But when I see how frail those creatures are, 5

lg.l: I muse that men forget themselves so far.
To mark the choice they make, and how they change,
How oft from Phœbus they do flee to Pan;
Unsettled still, like haggards wild they range,

div.p: These gentle birds that fly from man to man; 10

lg.l: Who would not scorn and shake them from the fist,
And let them fly, fair fools, which way they list?
Yet for disport we fawn and flatter both,
To pass the time when nothing else can please,

div.p: And train them to our lure with subtle oath, 15

lg.l: Till, weary of their wiles, ourselves we ease;
And then we say when we their fancy try,
To play with fools, oh what a fool was I!
Give place, ye lovers, here before
That spent your boasts and brags in vain:
My lady’s beauty passeth more
The best of yours, I dare well say’n,

div.p: Than doth the sun the candle light, 5

lg.l: Or brightest day the darkest night.
And thereto hath a troth as just
As had Penelope the fair;
For what she saith, ye may it trust,

div.p: As it by writing sealèd were; 10

lg.l: And virtues hath she many mo,
Than I with pen have skill to show.
I could rehearse, if that I would,
The whole effect of Nature’s plaint,

div.p: When she had lost the perfect mould, 15

lg.l: The like to whom she could not paint:
With wringing hands how she did cry,
And what she said, I know it, I.
I know she swore with raging mind,

div.p: Her kingdom only set apart, 20

lg.l: There was no loss by law of kind
That could have gone so near her heart;
And this was chiefly all her pain:
‘She could not make the like again.’

div.p: Sith Nature thus gave her the praise 25

lg.l: To be the chiefest work she wrought;
In faith, methink! some better ways
On your behalf might well be sought,
Than to compare, as ye have done,

div.p: To match the candle with the sun. 30

lg.l: When first mine eyes did view and mark
Thy beauty fair for to behold,
And when mine ears ’gan first to hark
The pleasant words that thou me told,

div.p: I would as then I had been free 5

lg.l: From ears to hear, and eyes to see.
And when in mind I did consent
To follow thus my fancy’s will,
And when my heart did first relent

div.p: To taste such bait, myself to spill, 10

lg.l: I would my heart had been as thine,
Or else thy heart as soft as mine.
O flatterer false! thou traitor born,
What mischief more might thou devise

div.p: Than thy dear friend to have in scorn, 15
And him to wound in sundry wise;
Which still a friend pretends to be,
And art not so by proof I see?
Fie, fie upon such treachery!

lg.l: I do confess thou’rt smooth and fair,
And I might have gone near to love thee,
Had I not found the slightest prayer
That lips could speak, had power to move thee;

div.p: But I can let thee now alone, 5

lg.l: As worthy to be loved by none.
I do confess thou’rt sweet, but find
Thee such an unthrift of thy sweets,
Thy favours are but like the wind,

div.p: That kisses everything it meets: 10

lg.l: And since thou can with more than one,
Thou’rt worthy to be kissed by none.
The morning rose that untouched stands,
Armed with her briars, how sweetly smells

div.p: But, plucked and strained through ruder hands, 15

lg.l: Her scent no longer with her dwells.
But scent and beauty both are gone,
And leaves fall from her, one by one.
Such fate ere long will thee betide,

div.p: When thou hast handled been a while; 20

lg.l: Like sere flowers to be thrown aside;—
And I will sigh, while some will smile,
To see thy love for more than one
Hath brought thee to be loved by none.
While that the sun with his beams hot
Scorchèd the fruits in vale and mountain,
Philon the shepherd, late forgot,
Sitting beside a crystal fountain,

div.p: In shadow of a green oak tree 5

lg.l: Upon his pipe this song playèd he:
Adieu Love, adieu Love, untrue Love,
Untrue Love, untrue Love, adieu Love;
Your mind is light, soon lost for new love.

div.p: So long as I was in your sight, 10

lg.l: I was your heart, your soul, and treasure;
And evermore you sobbed and sighed,
Burning in flames beyond all measure:
Three days endured your love to me,

div.p: And it was lost in other three! 15

lg.l: Adieu Love, adieu Love, untrue Love,
Untrue Love, untrue Love, adieu Love;
Your mind is light, soon lost for new love.
Another shepherd you did see,

div.p: To whom your heart was soon enchainèd; 20

lg.l: Full soon your love was leapt from me,
Full soon my place he had obtainèd.
Soon came a third, your love to win,
And we were out, and he was in.

div.p: Adieu Love, adieu Love, untrue Love, 25

lg.l: Untrue Love, untrue Love, adieu Love;
Your mind is light, soon lost for new love.
Sure you have made me passing glad
That you your mind so soon removèd,

div.p: Before that I the leisure had 30

lg.l: To choose you for my best belovèd:
For all your love was past and done
Two days before it was begun:—
Adieu Love, adieu Love, untrue Love,

div.p: Untrue Love, untrue Love, adieu Love; 35
Your mind is light, soon lost for new love.

lg.l: Rudely thou wrongest my dear hearts desire,
In finding fault with her too portly pride:
The thing which I do most in her admire,
Is of the world unworthy most envíed;

div.p: For in those lofty looks is close implied 5

lg.l: Scorn of base things and sdeign of foul dishonour,
Threatening rash eyes which gaze on her so wide,
That loosely they ne dare to look upon her.
Such pride is praise, such portliness is honour;

div.p: That boldness innocence bears in her eyes; 10
And her fair countenance, like a goodly banner,
Spreads in defiance of all enemies.
Was never in this world ought worthy tried,
Without some spark of such self-pleasing pride.

lg.l: Like as a huntsman after weary chace,
Seeing the game from him escaped away,
Sits down to rest him in some shady place,
With panting hounds beguilèd of their prey;

div.p: So after long pursuit and vain assay, 5

lg.l: When I all weary had the chace forsook,
The gentle deer returned the self-same way,
Thinking to quench her thirst at the next brook;
There she beholding me with milder look,

div.p: Sought not to fly, but fearless still did bide, 10

lg.l: Till I in hand her yet half trembling took,
And with her own good-will her firmly tied;
Strange thing meseemed to see a beast so wild
So goodly won, with her own will beguiled.

head.label: XVIII
head.hi: A VISION UPON THE FAIRY QUEEN.

lg.l: Methought I saw the grave where Laura lay,
Within that temple where the vestal flame
Was wont to burn; and passing by that way
To see that buried dust of living fame,

div.p: Whose tomb fair Love and fairer Virtue kept, 5

lg.l: All suddenly I saw The Fairy Queen:
At whose approach the soul of Petrarch wept;
And from thenceforth those Graces were not seen,
For they this Queen attended; in whose stead

div.p: Oblivion laid him down on Laura’s hearse. 10

lg.l: Hereat the hardest stones were seen to bleed,
And groans of buried ghosts the heavens did pierce,
Where Homer’s spright did tremble all for grief,
And cursed the access of that celestial thief.

head.label: XIX
head.hi: THE PASSIONATE SHEPHERD TO HIS LOVE.

lg.l: Come live with me, and be my love,
And we will all the pleasures prove,
That valleys, groves, [or] hills and fields,
Woods or steepy mountains yields.

div.p: And we will sit upon the rocks, 5

lg.l: Seeing the shepherds feed their flocks
By shallow rivers, to whose falls
Melodious birds sing madrigals.
And I will make thee beds of roses,

div.p: And a thousand fragrant posies, 10

lg.l: A cap of flowers, and a kirtle,
Embroidered all with leaves of myrtle;
A gown made of the finest wool,
Which from our pretty lambs we pull;

div.p: Fair-linèd slippers for the cold, 15

lg.l: With buckles of the purest gold;
A belt of straw and ivy-buds,
With coral clasps and amber studs:
And if these pleasures may thee move,

div.p: Come live with me, and be my love. 20

lg.l: Thy silver dishes for thy meat,
As precious as the gods do eat,
Shall, on an ivory table, be
Prepared each day for thee and me.

div.p: The shepherd swains shall dance and sing 25
For thy delight each May-morning.
If these delights thy mind may move,
Come live with me, and be my love.

lg.l: If all the world and Love were young,
And truth in every shepherd’s tongue,
These pretty pleasures might me move
To live with thee, and be thy love,

div.p: Time drives the flocks from field to fold, 5

lg.l: When rivers rage, and rocks grow cold;
Then Philomel becometh dumb,
The rest complains of cares to come.
The flowers do fade, and wanton fields

div.p: To wayward winter reckoning yields; 10

lg.l: A honey tongue, a heart of gall,
Is fancy’s spring, but sorrow’s fall.
Thy gowns, thy shoes, thy bed of roses,
Thy cap, thy kirtle, and thy posies,

div.p: Soon break, soon wither, soon forgotten; 15

lg.l: In folly ripe, in reason rotten.
Thy belt of straw and ivy-buds,
Thy coral clasps and amber studs,
All these in me no means can move,

div.p: To come to thee, and be thy love. 20

lg.l: What should we talk of dainties then,
Of better meat than’s fit for men?
These are but vain: that’s only good
Which God hath blessed and sent for food.

div.p: But could youth last, and love still breed, 25

lg.l: Had joys no date, nor age no need;
Then those delights my mind might move,
To live with thee, and be thy love.
Like to Diana in her summer weed,
Girt with a crimson robe of brightest dye,
Goes fair Samela;
Whiter than be the flocks that straggling feed,

div.p: When washed by Arethusa faint they lie, 5

lg.l: Is fair Samela;
As fair Aurora in her morning grey,
Decked with the ruddy glister of her love,
Is fair Samela;

div.p: Like lovely Thetis on a calmèd day, 10

lg.l: Whenas her brightness Neptune’s fancy move,
Shines fair Samela;
Her tresses gold, her eyes like glassy streams,
Her teeth are pearl, the breasts are ivory

div.p: Of fair Samela; 15

lg.l: Her cheeks like rose and lily yield forth gleams,
Her brows’ bright arches framed of ebony;
Thus fair Samela
Passeth fair Venus in her bravest hue,

div.p: And Juno in the show of majesty, 20

lg.l: For she’s Samela:
Pallas in wit, all three, if you will view,
For beauty, wit, and matchless dignity
Yield to Samela.
Rose-cheeked Laura, come!
Sing thou smoothly with thy beauty’s
Silent music, either other
Sweetly gracing.

div.p: Lovely forms do flow 5

lg.l: From concent divinely framed,
Heaven is music, and thy beauty’s
Birth is heavenly.
These dull notes we sing

div.p: Discords need for helps to grace them; 10

lg.l: Only beauty purely loving
Knows no discord;
But still moves delight,
Like clear springs renewed by flowing,

div.p: Ever perfect, ever in them-selves eternal. 15

lg.l: See the chariot at hand here of Love,
Wherein my lady rideth!
Each that draws is a swan or a dove,
And well the car Love guideth.

div.p: As she goes, all hearts do duty 5

lg.l: Unto her beauty,
And enamoured do wish, so they might
But enjoy such a sight,
That they still were to run by her side,

div.p: Through swords, through seas, whither she would ride. 10

lg.l: Do but look on her eyes, they do light
All that Love’s world compriseth!
Do but look on her hair, it is bright
As Love’s star when it riseth!

div.p: Do but mark, her forehead’s smoother 15

lg.l: Than words that soothe her!
And from her arched brows, such a grace
Sheds itself through the face,
As alone there triumphs to the life

div.p: All the gain, all the good of the elements’ strife. 20

lg.l: Have you seen but a bright lily grow,
Before rude hands have touched it?
Have you marked but the fall o’ the snow,
Before the soil hath smutched it?

div.p: Have you felt the wool of the beaver? 25
Or swan’s down ever?
Or have smelt o’ the bud of the briar?
Or the nard in the fire?
Or have tasted the bag o’ the bee?
O so white! O so soft! O so sweet is she! 30

lg.l: Roses, their sharp spines being gone,
Not royal in their smells alone,
But in their hue;
Maiden-pinks, of odour faint;

div.p: Daisies smell-less, yet most quaint, 5

lg.l: And sweet thyme true;
Primrose, first-born child of Ver,
Merry spring-time’s harbinger,
With her bells dim;

div.p: Oxlips in their cradles growing, 10

lg.l: Marigolds on death-beds blowing,
Lark-heels trim;
All, dear Nature’s children sweet,
Lie ’fore bride and bridegroom’s feet,

div.p: Blessing their sense! 15

lg.l: Not an angel of the air,
Bird melodious, or bird fair,
Be absent hence!
The crow, the slanderous cuckoo, nor

div.p: The boding raven, nor chough hoar, 20

lg.l: Nor chattering pie,
May on our bride-house perch or sing,
Or with them any discord bring,
But from it fly!
You that do search for every purling spring,
Which from the ribs of old Parnassus flows,
And every flower, not sweet perhaps, which grows
Near thereabouts, into your posy wring;

div.p: You that do dictionaries’ method bring 5

lg.l: Into your rhymes, running in rattling rows;
You that poor Petrarch’s long deceasèd woes
With new-born sighs and wit disguisèd sing;
You take wrong ways: those far-fetched helps be such

div.p: As do bewray a want of inward touch: 10
And sure at length stoln goods do come to light.

lg.l: But if (both for your love and skill) your name
You seek to nurse at fullest breasts of fame,
Stella behold, and then begin to’ endite.
Come Sleep, O Sleep, the certain knot of peace,
The baiting place of wit, the balm of woe,
The poor man’s wealth, the prisoner’s release,
The indifferent Judge between the high and low;

div.p: With shield of proof shield me from out the prease 5

lg.l: Of those fierce darts Despair at me doth throw.
Oh! make in me those civil wars to cease;
I will good tribute pay, if thou do so.
Take thou of me smooth pillows, sweetest bed,

div.p: A chamber deaf to noise, and blind of light, 10

lg.l: A rosy garland, and a weary head:
And if these things, as being thine by right,
Move not thy heavy grace, thou shalt in me
Livelier than elsewhere Stella’s image see.
To yield to those I cannot but disdain,
Whose face doth but entangle foolish hearts;
It is the beauty of the better parts,
With which I mind my fancies for to chain.

div.p: Those that have nought wherewith men’s minds to gain, 5

lg.l: But only curlèd locks and wanton looks,
Are but like fleeting baits that have no hooks,
Which may well take, but cannot well retain.
He that began to yield to the outward grace,

div.p: And then the treasures of the mind doth prove, 10
He who as ’twere was with the mask in love,
What doth he think whenas he sees the face?
No doubt being limed by the outward colours so,
That inward worth would never let him go.

lg.l: When to the sessions of sweet silent thought
I summon up remembrance of things past,
I sigh the lack of many a thing I sought,
And with old woes new wail my dear time’s waste;

div.p: Then can I drown an eye, unused to flow, 5

lg.l: For precious friends hid in death’s dateless night,
And weep afresh love’s long-since-cancelled woe,
And moan the expense of many a vanished sight.
Then can I grieve at grievances foregone,

div.p: And heavily from woe to woe tell o’er 10

lg.l: The sad account of fore-bemoanèd moan,
Which I new pay as if not paid before:—
But if the while I think on thee, dear friend,
All losses are restored, and sorrows end.
From you have I been absent in the spring,
When proud-pied April, dressed in all his trim,
Hath put a spirit of youth in every thing,
That heavy Saturn laughed and leaped with him.

div.p: Yet nor the lays of birds, nor the sweet smell 5

lg.l: Of different flowers in odour and in hue,
Could make me any summer’s story tell,
Or from their proud lap pluck them where they grew:
Nor did I wonder at the lily’s white,

div.p: Nor praise the deep vermilion in the rose; 10
They were but sweet, but figures of delight,
Drawn after you—you pattern of all those.
Yet seemed it winter still, and, you away,
As with your shadow I with these did play.

lg.l: Oh how much more doth beauty beauteous seem,
By that sweet ornament which truth doth give!
The rose looks fair, but fairer we it deem
For that sweet odour which doth in it live.

div.p: The canker-blooms have full as deep a dye 5

lg.l: As the perfumèd tincture of the roses,
Hang on such thorns, and play as wantonly
When summer’s breath their maskèd buds discloses;
But, for their virtue only is their show,

div.p: They live unwooed, and unrespected fade; 10

lg.l: Die to themselves. Sweet roses do not so;
Of their sweet deaths are sweetest odours made:
And so of you, beauteous and lovely youth,
When that shall vade, by verse distils your truth.
A good that never satisfies the mind,
A beauty fading like the April flowers,
A sweet with floods of gall that runs combined,
A pleasure passing ere in thought made ours,

div.p: A honour that more fickle is than wind, 5

lg.l: A glory at opinion’s frown that lowers,
A treasury which bankrupt time devours,
A knowledge than grave ignorance more blind,
A vain delight our equals to command,

div.p: A style of greatness, in effect a dream, 10

lg.l: A swelling thought of holding sea and land,
A servile lot, decked with a pompous name;
Are the strange ends we toil for here below,
Till wisest death make us our errors know.
Look how the flower which lingeringly doth fade,
The morning’s darling late, the summer’s queen,
Spoiled of that juice which kept it fresh and green,
As high as it did raise, bows low the head:

div.p: Right so my life, contentments being dead, 5

lg.l: Or in their contraries but only seen,
With swifter speed declines than erst it spread,
And, blasted, scarce now shows what it hath been.
As doth the pilgrim therefore, whom the night

div.p: Hastes darkly to imprison on his way, 10

lg.l: Think on thy home, my soul, and think aright
Of what yet rests thee of life’s wasting day;
Thy sun posts westward, passèd is thy morn,
And twice it is not given thee to be born.
Alexis, here she stayed; among these pines,
Sweet hermitress, she did alone repair;
Here did she spread the treasure of her hair,
More rich than that brought from the Colchian mines.

div.p: She sat her by these muskèd eglantines, 5

lg.l: The happy place the print seems yet to bear;
Her voice did sweeten here thy sugared lines,
To which winds, trees, beasts, birds did lend an ear.
Me here she first perceived, and here a morn

div.p: Of bright carnations did o’erspread her face: 10
Here did she sigh, here first my hopes were born,
Here first I got a pledge of promised grace:
But ah! what served it to be happy so?
Sith passèd pleasures double but new woe?

lg.l: Sweet spring, thou turn’st with all thy goodly train,
Thy head with flames, thy mantle bright with flowers;
The zephyrs curl the green locks of the plain,
The clouds for joy in pearls weep down their showers,

div.p: Thou turn’st, sweet youth; but ah! my pleasant hours 5

lg.l: And happy days with thee come not again;
The sad memorials only of my pain
Do with thee come, which turn my sweets to sours.
Thou art the same which still thou wast before,

div.p: Delicious, lusty, amiable, fair; 10
But she, whose breath embalmed thy wholesome air,
Is gone; nor gold nor gems her can restore.
Neglected Virtue! seasons go and come,
When thine, forgot, lie closèd in a tomb.

lg.l: Since there’s no help, come let us kiss and part—
Nay, I have done, you get no more of me;
And I am glad, yea, glad with all my heart,
That thus so cleanly I myself can free;

div.p: Shake hands for ever, cancel all our vows, 5

lg.l: And when we meet at any time again,
Be it not seen in either of our brows
That we one jot of former love retain.
Now at the last gasp of love’s latest breath,

div.p: When, his pulse failing, passion speechless lies, 10

lg.l: When faith is kneeling by his bed of death,
And innocence is closing up his eyes,—
Now if thou would’st, when all have given him over,
From death to life thou might’st him yet recover!
Weep no more, nor sigh, nor groan,
Sorrow calls no time that’s gone:
Violets plucked, the sweetest rain
Makes not fresh nor grow again;

div.p: Trim thy locks, look cheerfully; 5

lg.l: Fate’s hidden ends eyes cannot see:
Joys as wingèd dreams fly fast,
Why should sadness longer last?
Grief is but a wound to woe;

div.p: Gentlest fair, mourn, mourn no mo. 10
Come, Sleep, and with thy sweet deceiving
Lock me in delight awhile;
Let some pleasing dreams beguile
All my fancies; that from thence
I may feel an influence, 5

lg.l: All my powers of care bereaving!
Though but a shadow, but a sliding,
Let me know some little joy!
We that suffer long annoy

div.p: Are contented with a thought, 10
Through an idle fancy wrought:
Oh, let my joys have some abiding!

lg.l: Lay a garland on my hearse
Of the dismal yew;
Maidens, willow branches bear;
Say, I died true.

div.p: My love was false, but I was firm 5
From my hour of birth.
Upon my buried body lie
Lightly, gentle earth!

head.label: XXXIX
head.hi: THE SHEPHERD’S PRAISE OF HIS SACRED DIANA.

lg.l: Praised be Diana’s fair and harmless light,
Praised be the dews, wherewith she moists the ground:
Praised be her beams, the glory of the night,
Praised be her power, by which all powers abound.
Praised be her nymphs, with whom she decks the woods,

div.p: Praised be her knights, in whom true honour lives: 6
Praised be that force by which she moves the floods,
Let that Diana shine which all these gives.
In heaven Queen she is among the spheres,
She, mistress-like, makes all things to be pure; 10

lg.l: Eternity in her oft change she bears,
She beauty is, by her the fair endure.
Time wears her not, she doth his chariot guide,
Mortality below her orb is placed;

div.p: By her the virtue of the stars down slide, 15
In her is Virtue’s perfect image cast.
A knowledge pure it is her worth to know:
With Circe let them dwell that think not so.

lg.l: It is not growing like a tree
In bulk, doth make men better be;
Or standing long an oak, three hundred year,
To fall a log at last, dry, bald, and sere.

div.p: A lily of a day 5

lg.l: Is fairer far in May,
Although it fall and die that night;
It was the plant and flower of light.
In small proportions we just beauties see,

div.p: And in short measures life may perfect be. 10

lg.l: Fair stood the wind for France
When we our sails advance,
Nor now to prove our chance
Longer will tarry;

div.p: But putting to the main, 5

lg.l: At Kaux, the mouth of Seine,
With all his martial train,
Landed King Harry.
And taking many a fort,

div.p: Furnished in warlike sort, 10

lg.l: Marched towards Agincourt
In happy hour;
Skirmishing day by day
With those that stopped his way,

div.p: Where the French general lay 15

lg.l: With all his power.
Which in his height of pride,
King Henry to deride,
His ransom to provide

div.p: To the King sending; 20

lg.l: Which he neglects the while,
As from a nation vile,
Yet with an angry smile,
Their fall portending.

div.p: And turning to his men, 25

lg.l: Quoth our brave Henry then,
‘Though they to one be ten,
Be not amazèd.
Yet have we well begun,

div.p: Battles so bravely won 30
Have ever to the sun
By fame been raisèd.
‘And for myself,’ quoth he,
‘This my full rest shall be;
England ne’er mourn for me, 35

lg.l: Nor more esteem me.
Victor I will remain,
Or on this earth lie slain,
Never shall she sustain

div.p: Loss to redeem me. 40

lg.l: ‘Poictiers and Cressy tell,
When most their pride did swell,
Under our swords they fell:
No less our skill is,

div.p: Than when our grandsire great, 45

lg.l: Claiming the regal seat
By many a warlike feat,
Lopped the French lilies.’
The Duke of York so dread,

div.p: The eager vaward led; 50

lg.l: With the main Henry sped,
Amongst his henchmen.
Exeter had the rear,
A braver man not there,

div.p: O Lord! how hot they were 55

lg.l: On the false Frenchmen!
They now to fight are gone,
Armour on armour shone,
Drum now to drum did groan,

div.p: To hear was wonder; 60

lg.l: That with the cries they make,
The very earth did shake,
Trumpet to trumpet spake,
Thunder to thunder.

div.p: Well it thine age became, 65

lg.l: O noble Erpingham
Which did the signal aim
To our hid forces;
When from a meadow by,

div.p: Like a storm suddenly, 70

lg.l: The English archery
Stuck the French horses.
With Spanish yew so strong,
Arrows a cloth-yard long,

div.p: That like to serpents stung, 75

lg.l: Piercing the weather;
None from his fellow starts,
But playing manly parts,
And like true English hearts,

div.p: Stuck close together. 80

lg.l: When down their bows they threw,
And forth their bilbows drew,
And on the French they flew;
Not one was tardy;

div.p: Arms were from shoulders sent; 85

lg.l: Scalps to the teeth were rent,
Down the French peasants went,
Our men were hardy.
This while our noble king,

div.p: His broad sword brandishing, 90

lg.l: Down the French host did ding,
As to o’erwhelm it;
And many a deep wound lent,
His arms with blood besprent,

div.p: And many a cruel dent 95

lg.l: Bruisèd his helmet.
Gloucester, that duke so good,
Next of the royal blood,
For famous England stood,

div.p: With his brave brother; 100

lg.l: Clarence, in steel so bright,
Though but a maiden knight,
Yet in that furious fight
Scarce such another.

div.p: Warwick in blood did wade, 105

lg.l: Oxford the foe invade,
And cruel slaughter made,
Still as they ran up;
Suffolk his axe did ply,

div.p: Beaumont and Willoughby 110

lg.l: Bare them right doughtily,
Ferrers and Fanhope.
Upon Saint Crispin’s day
Fought was this noble fray,

div.p: Which fame did not delay 115

lg.l: To England to carry.
Oh, when shall Englishmen
With such acts fill a pen,
Or England breed again

div.p: Such a King Harry! 120

lg.l: Where dost thou careless lie,
Buried in ease and sloth?
Knowledge, that sleeps, doth die;
And this security,

div.p: It is the common moth 5

lg.l: That eats on wits and arts, and [so] destroys them both.
Are all the Aonian springs
Dried up? lies Thespia waste?
Doth Clarius’ harp want strings,

div.p: That not a nymph now sings! 10

lg.l: Or droop they as disgraced,
To see their seats and bowers by chattering pies defaced?
If hence thy silence be,
As ’tis too just a cause,

div.p: Let this thought quicken thee: 15
Minds that are great and free,
Should not on Fortune pause;
’Tis crown enough to Virtue still, her own applause.
What though the greedy fry
Be taken with false baits 20

lg.l: Of worded balladry,
And think it poesy?
They die with their conceits,
And only piteous scorn upon their folly waits.

div.p: Then take in hand thy lyre, 25

lg.l: Strike in thy proper strain,
With Japhet’s line, aspire
Sol’s chariot for new fire,
To give the world again:
Who aided him, will thee, the issue of Jove’s brain.

div.p: And since our dainty age 31
Cannot endure reproof,
Make not thyself a page
To that strumpet the stage,
But sing high and aloof, 35
Safe from the wolf’s black jaw, and the dull ass’s hoof.

lg.l: Hence, all you vain delights,
As short as are the nights
Wherein you spend your folly!
There’s nought in this life sweet,

div.p: If man were wise to see’t, 5

lg.l: But only melancholy,
Oh, sweetest melancholy!
Welcome, folded arms, and fixèd eyes,
A sigh that piercing mortifies,

div.p: A look that’s fastened to the ground, 10

lg.l: A tongue chained up without a sound!
Fountain-heads, and pathless groves,
Places which pale passion loves!
Moonlight walks, when all the fowls

div.p: Are warmly housed, save bats and owls! 15
A midnight bell, a parting groan!

lg.l: These are the sounds we feed upon;
Then stretch our bones in a still gloomy valley;
Nothing’s so dainty sweet as lovely melancholy.
Misdeeming eye! that stoopeth to the lure
Of mortal worths, not worth so worthy love;
All beauty’s base, all graces are impure,
That do thy erring thoughts from God remove.

div.p: Sparks to the fire, the beams yield to the sun, 5

lg.l: All grace to God, from whom all graces run.
If picture move, more should the pattern please;
No shadow can with shadowed thing compare,
And fairest shapes, whereon our loves do seize,

div.p: But silly signs of God’s high beauty are. 10

lg.l: Go, starving sense, feed thou on earthly mast;
True love, in heaven seek thou thy sweet repast.
Glean not in barren soil these offal ears,
Sith reap thou may’st whole harvests of delight;

div.p: Base joys with griefs, bad hopes do end with fears, 15

lg.l: Lewd love with loss, evil peace with deadly fight:
God’s love alone doth end with endless ease,
Whose joys in hope, whose hope concludes in peace.
Let not the luring train of fancies trap,

div.p: Or gracious features, proofs of Nature’s skill, 20

lg.l: Lull Reason’s force asleep in Error’s lap,
Or draw thy wit to bent of wanton will.
The fairest flowers have not the sweetest smell;
A seeming heaven proves oft a damning hell.

div.p: Self-pleasing souls, that play with beauty’s bait, 25

lg.l: In shining shroud may swallow fatal hook;
Where eager sight on semblant fair doth wait,
A lock it proves, that first was but a look:
The fish with ease into the net doth glide,

div.p: But to get out the way is not so wide. 30

lg.l: So long the fly doth dally with the flame,
Until his singèd wings do force his fall;
So long the eye doth follow fancy’s game,
Till love hath left the heart in heavy thrall.

div.p: Soon may the mind be cast in Cupid’s jail, 35

lg.l: But hard it is imprisoned thoughts to bail.
Oh! loathe that love whose final aim is lust,
Moth of the mind, eclipse of reason’s light;
The grave of grace, the mole of Nature’s rust,

div.p: The wrack of wit, the wrong of every right; 40
In sum, an ill whose harms no tongue can tell;
In which to live is death, to die is hell.

head.label: XLV
head.hi: TO THE WORLD. A FAREWELL FOR A GENTLEWOMAN, VIRTUOUS AND NOBLE.

lg.l: False world, good night, since thou hast brought
That hour upon my morn of age,
Henceforth I quit thee from my thought,
My part is ended on thy stage.

div.p: Do not once hope, that thou canst tempt 5

lg.l: A spirit so resolved to tread
Upon thy throat, and live exempt
From all the nets that thou canst spread.
I know thy forms are studied arts,

div.p: Thy subtil ways be narrow straits; 10

lg.l: Thy courtesy but sudden starts,
And what thou call’st thy gifts, are baits.
I know too, though thou strut and paint,
Yet art thou both shrunk up and old;

div.p: That only fools make thee a saint, 15

lg.l: And all thy good is to be sold.
I know thou whole art but a shop
Of toys and trifles, traps and snares,
To take the weak, or make them stop:

div.p: Yet art thou falser than thy wares. 20

lg.l: And, knowing this, should I yet stay,
Like such as blow away their lives,
And never will redeem a day,
Enamoured of their golden gyves?

div.p: Or having ’scaped, shall I return, 25

lg.l: And thrust my neck into the noose,
From whence so lately I did burn
With all my powers myself to loose?
What bird or beast is known so dull,

div.p: That fled his cage, or broke his chain, 30

lg.l: And tasting air and freedom, wull
Render his head in there again?
If these who have but sense, can shun
The engines that have them annoyed;

div.p: Little for me had reason done, 35

lg.l: If I could not thy gins avoid.
Yes, threaten, do. Alas, I fear
As little, as I hope from thee:
I know thou canst nor show, nor bear

div.p: More hatred than thou hast to me. 40

lg.l: My tender, first, and simple years
Thou didst abuse, and then betray;
Since stirr’dst up jealousies and fears,
When all the causes were away.

div.p: Then in a soil hast planted me, 45

lg.l: Where breathe the basest of thy fools;
Where envious arts professèd be,
And pride and ignorance the schools:
Where nothing is examined, weighed;

div.p: But as ’tis rumoured, so believed; 50

lg.l: Where every freedom is betrayed,
And every goodness taxed or grieved.
But what we’re born for, we must bear:
Our frail condition it is such,

div.p: That what to all may happen here, 55

lg.l: If’t chance to me, I must not grutch,
Else I my state should much mistake,
To harbour a divided thought
From all my kind: that for my sake

div.p: There should a miracle be wrought. 60

lg.l: No! I do know that I was born
To age, misfortune, sickness, grief:
But I will bear these with that scorn,
As shall not need thy false relief.

div.p: Nor for my peace will I go far, 65

lg.l: As wanderers do, that still do roam;
But make my strengths, such as they are,
Here in my bosom, and at home.

head.label: XLVI
head.hi: TO THE MEMORY OF BEN JONSON.

lg.l: The Muses’ fairest light in no dark time,
The wonder of a learnèd age; the line
Which none can pass; the most proportioned wit
To nature, the best judge of what was fit;

div.p: The deepest, plainest, highest, clearest pen; 5

lg.l: The voice most echoed by consenting men;
The soul which answered best to all well said
By others, and which most requital made;
Tuned to the highest key of ancient Rome,

div.p: Returning all her music with his own; 10

lg.l: In whom with nature study claimed a part,
And yet who to himself owed all his art:
Here lies Ben Jonson! every age will look
With sorrow here, with wonder on his book.
I weigh not fortune’s frown or smile;
I joy not much in earthly joys;
I seek not state, I seek not style;
I am not fond of fancy’s toys;

div.p: I rest so pleased with what I have, 5

lg.l: I wish no more, no more I crave.
I quake not at the thunder’s crack;
I tremble not at noise of war;
I swound not at the news of wrack;

div.p: I shrink not at a blazing star; 10

lg.l: I fear not loss, I hope not gain,
I envy none, I none disdain.
I see ambition never pleased;
I see some Tantals starved in store;

div.p: I see gold’s dropsy seldom eased; 15

lg.l: I see e’en Midas gape for more:
I neither want, nor yet abound—
Enough’s a feast, content is crowned.
I feign not friendship, where I hate;

div.p: I fawn not on the great in show; 20

lg.l: I prize, I praise a mean estate—
Neither too lofty nor too low:
This, this is all my choice, my cheer—
A mind content, a conscience clear.
Poor Soul, the centre of my sinful earth,
Fooled by these rebel powers that thee array,
Why dost thou pine within, and suffer dearth,
Painting thy outward walls so costly gay?

div.p: Why so large cost, having so short a lease, 5
Dost thou upon thy fading mansion spend?
Shall worms, inheritors of this excess.
Eat up thy charge? is this thy body’s end?
Then, Soul, live thou upon thy servant’s loss,
And let that pine to aggravate thy store; 10

lg.l: Buy terms divine in selling hours of dross;
Within be fed, without be rich no more:—
So shalt thou feed on Death, that feeds on men;
And Death once dead, there’s no more dying then.
The expense of spirit in a waste of shame
Is lust in action; and till action, lust
Is perjured, murderous, bloody, full of blame,
Savage, extreme, rude, cruel, not to trust;

div.p: Enjoyed no sooner than despisèd straight; 5

lg.l: Past reason hunted; and no sooner had,
Past reason hated, as a swallowed bait,
On purpose laid to make the taker mad:
Mad in pursuit, and in possession so;

div.p: Had, having, and in quest to have, extreme; 10

lg.l: A bliss in proof—and proved, a very woe;
Before, a joy proposed; behind, a dream:
All this the world well knows; yet none knows well
To shun the heaven that leads men to this hell.
The loppèd tree in time may grow again;
Most naked plants renew both fruit and flower;
The sorriest wight may find release of pain,
The driest soil suck in some moistening shower;

div.p: Times go by turns, and chances change by course, 5

lg.l: From foul to fair, from better hap to worse.
The sea of Fortune doth not ever flow,
She draws her favours to the lowest ebb;
Her tides have equal times to come and go;

div.p: Her loom doth weave the fine and coarsest web; 10

lg.l: No joy so great but runneth to an end,
No hap so hard but may in fine amend.
Not always fall of leaf, nor ever spring;
No endless night, yet not eternal day;

div.p: The saddest birds a season find to sing; 15

lg.l: The roughest storm a calm may soon allay;
Thus with succeeding turns God tempereth all,
That man may hope to rise, yet fear to fall.
A chance may win that by mischance was lost;

div.p: That net that holds no great, takes little fish; 20

lg.l: In some things all, in all things none are crossed;
Few all they need, but none have all they wish;
Unmeddled joys here to no man befall,
Who least hath some, who most hath never all.
This Life, which seems so fair,
Is like a bubble blown up in the air,
By sporting children’s breath,
Who chase it everywhere,

div.p: And strive who can most motion it bequeath; 5

lg.l: And though it sometimes seem of its own might
Like to an eye of gold to be fixed there,
And firm to hover in that empty height,
That only is because it is so light.

div.p: But in that pomp it doth not long appear; 10
For when ’tis most admirèd, in a thought,
Because it erst was nought, it turns to nought.

lg.l: Like as the damask rose you see,
Or like the blossom on the tree,
Or like the dainty flower in May,
Or like the morning of the day,

div.p: Or like the sun, or like the shade, 5

lg.l: Or like the gourd which Jonas had—
E’en such is man; whose thread is spun,
Drawn out, and cut, and so is done.
The rose withers; the blossom blasteth;

div.p: The flower fades; the morning hasteth; 10

lg.l: The sun sets, the shadow flies;
The gourd consumes; and man he dies!
Like to the grass that’s newly sprung,
Or like a tale that’s new begun,

div.p: Or like the bird that’s here to day, 15

lg.l: Or like the pearlèd dew of May,
Or like an hour, or like a span,
Or like the singing of a swan—
E’en such is man; who lives by breath,

div.p: Is here, now there, in life, and death. 20

lg.l: The grass withers, the tale is ended;
The bird is flown, the dew’s ascended;
The hour is short, the span is long;
The swan’s near death; man’s life is done!

head.label: LIII
head.hi: OF MY DEAR SON GERVASE BEAUMONT.

lg.l: Can I, who have for others oft compiled
The songs of death, forget my sweetest child,
Which, like the flower crusht, with a blast is dead,
And ere full time hangs down his smiling head,

div.p: Expecting with clear hope to live anew, 5

lg.l: Among the angels fed with heavenly dew?
We have this sign of joy, that many days,
While on the earth his struggling spirit stays,
The name of Jesus in his mouth contains

div.p: His only food, his sleep, his ease from pains. 10

lg.l: Oh! may that sound be rooted in my mind,
Of which in him such strong effect I find.
Dear Lord, receive my son, whose winning love
To me was like a friendship, far above

div.p: The course of nature, or his tender age; 15

lg.l: Whose looks could all my bitter griefs assuage;
Let his pure soul, ordained seven years to be
In that frail body, which was part of me,
Remain my pledge in heaven, as sent to show,

div.p: How to this port at every step I go. 20

lg.l: Fear no more the heat o’ the sun,
Nor the furious winter’s rages;
Thou thy worldly task hast done,
Home art gone, and ta’en thy wages:

div.p: Golden lads and girls all must, 5

lg.l: As chimney-sweepers, come to dust.
Fear no more the frown o’ the great,
Thou art past the tyrant’s stroke;
Care no more to clothe and eat;

div.p: To thee the reed is as the oak: 10

lg.l: The sceptre, learning, physic, must
All follow this, and come to dust.
Fear no more the lightning-flash,
Nor the all-dreaded thunder-stone;

div.p: Fear not slander, censure rash; 15
Thou hast finished joy and moan:
All lovers young, all lovers must
Consign to thee, and come to dust.
No exorciser harm thee!
Nor no witchcraft charm thee!
Ghost unlaid forbear thee! 20
Nothing ill come near thee!
Quiet consummation have;
And renownèd be thy grave!

head.label: LV
head.hi: ON THE TOMBS IN WESTMINSTER ABBEY.

lg.l: Mortality, behold and fear!
What a change of flesh is here!
Think how many royal bones
Sleep within these heaps of stones;

div.p: Here they lie, had realms and lands, 5

lg.l: Who now want strength to stir their hands,
Where from their pulpits sealed with dust
They preach, ‘In greatness is no trust.’
Here’s an acre sown indeed

div.p: With the richest royallest seed 10

lg.l: That the earth did e’er suck in,
Since the first man died for sin:
Here the bones of birth have cried,
‘Though gods they were, as men they died!’

div.p: Here are sands, ignoble things, 15

lg.l: Dropt from the ruined sides of kings:
Here’s a world of pomp and state
Buried in dust, once dead by fate.

div.p: Victorious men of earth, no more
Proclaim how wide your empires are;
Though you bind-in every shore
And your triumphs reach as far
As night or day, 5

lg.l: Yet you, proud monarchs, must obey,
And mingle with forgotten ashes, when
Death calls ye to the crowd of common men.
Devouring Famine, Plague, and War,

div.p: Each able to undo mankind, 10

lg.l: Death’s servile emissaries are;
Nor to these alone confined,
He hath at will
More quaint and subtle ways to kill;

div.p: A smile or kiss, as he will use the art, 15
Shall have the cunning skill to break a heart.

lg.l: The glories of our blood and state
Are shadows, not substantial things;
There is no armour against fate;
Death lays his icy hand on kings:

div.p: Sceptre and crown 5

lg.l: Must tumble down,
And in the dust be equal made
With the poor crookèd scythe and spade.
Some men with swords may reap the field,

div.p: And plant fresh laurels where they kill: 10

lg.l: But their strong nerves at last must yield;
They tame but one another still:
Early or late
They stoop to fate,

div.p: And must give up their murmuring breath 15

lg.l: When they, pale captives, creep to death.
The garlands wither on your brow;
Then boast no more your mighty deeds;
Upon Death’s purple altar now

div.p: See where the victor-victim bleeds: 20

lg.l: Your heads must come
To the cold tomb;
Only the actions of the just
Smell sweet, and blossom in their dust.

head.label: LVIII
head.hi: LINES WRITTEN BY ONE IN THE TOWER, BEING YOUNG AND CONDEMNED TO DIE.

lg.l: My prime of youth is but a frost of cares;
My feast of joy is but a dish of pain;
My crop of corn is but a field of tares;
And all my good is but vain hope of gain:

div.p: The day is [fled], and yet I saw no sun; 5

lg.l: And now I live, and now my life is done!
The spring is past, and yet it hath not sprung;
The fruit is dead, and yet the leaves are green;
My youth is gone, and yet I am but young;

div.p: I saw the world, and yet I was not seen: 10

lg.l: My thread is cut, and yet it is not spun;
And now I live, and now my life is done!
I sought my death, and found it in my womb;
I looked for life, and saw it was a shade;

div.p: I trod the earth, and knew it was my tomb; 15

lg.l: And now I die, and now I am but made:
The glass is full, and now my glass is run;
And now I live, and now my life is done!

head.label: LIX
head.hi: LINES WRITTEN THE NIGHT BEFORE HIS EXECUTION.

lg.l: E’en such is time; which takes on trust
Our youth, our joys, our all we have,
And pays us but with earth and dust;
Which in the dark and silent grave,

div.p: When we have wandered all our ways, 5

lg.l: Shuts up the story of our days:
But from this earth, this grave, this dust,
My God shall raise me up, I trust.
Most glorious Lord of life, that on this day
Didst make thy triumph over death and sin,
And, having harrowed hell, didst bring away
Captivity thence captive, us to win;

div.p: This joyous day, dear Lord, with joy begin, 5

lg.l: And grant that we, for whom Thou diddest die,
Being with thy dear blood clean washed from sin,
May live for ever in felicity:
And that thy love we weighing worthily,

div.p: May likewise love Thee for the same again; 10
And for thy sake, that alllike dear didst buy,
With love may one another entertain.
So let us love, dear Love, like as we ought;
Love is the lesson which the Lord us taught.

lg.l: Jerusalem, my happy home,
When shall I come to thee?
When shall my sorrows have an end,
Thy joys when shall I see?

div.p: O happy harbour of the saints! 5

lg.l: O sweet and pleasant soil!
In thee no sorrow may be found,
No grief, no care, no toil.
In thee no sickness may be seen,

div.p: Nor hurt, nor ache, nor sore; 10

lg.l: There is no death, nor ugly dole,
But Life for evermore.
There lust and lucre cannot dwell,
There envy bears no sway;

div.p: There is no hunger, heat, nor cold, 15

lg.l: But pleasure every way.
Thy walls are made of precious stones,
Thy bulwarks diamonds square;
Thy gates are of right orient pearl,

div.p: Exceeding rich and rare. 20

lg.l: Thy turrets and thy pinnacles
With carbuncles do shine;
Thy very streets are paved with gold,
Surpassing clear and fine.

div.p: Thy houses are of ivory, 25

lg.l: Thy windows crystal clear;
Thy tiles are made of beaten gold;—
O God, that I were there!
Ah, my sweet home, Jerusalem,

div.p: Would God I were in thee! 30

lg.l: Would God my woes were at an end,
Thy joys that I might see!
Thy saints are crowned with glory great;
They see God face to face;

div.p: They triumph still, they still rejoice, 35

lg.l: Most happy is their case.
We that are here in banishment
Continually do moan,
We sigh, and sob, we weep and wail,

div.p: Perpetually we groan. 40

lg.l: Our sweet is mixed with bitter gall,
Our pleasure is but pain,
Our joys scarce last the looking on,
Our sorrows still remain.

div.p: But there they live in such delight, 45

lg.l: Such pleasure and such play,
As that to them a thousand years
Doth seem as yesterday.
Thy gardens and thy gallant walks

div.p: Continually are green; 50

lg.l: There grow such sweet and pleasant flowers
As nowhere else are seen.
Quite through the streets, with silver sound,
The flood of Life doth flow;

div.p: Upon whose banks on every side 55

lg.l: The wood of Life doth grow.
There trees for evermore bear fruit,
And evermore do spring;
There evermore the angels sit,

div.p: And evermore do sing. 60
Jerusalem, my happy home,
Would God I were in thee!
Would God my woes were at an end,
Thy joys that I might see!

lg.l: How happy is he born and taught,
That serveth not another’s will;
Whose armour is his honest thought,
And simple truth his utmost skill!

div.p: Whose passions not his masters are, 5

lg.l: Whose soul is still prepared for death;
Not tied unto the world with care
Of public fame, or private breath;
Who envies none that chance doth raise,

div.p: Or vice; who never understood 10

lg.l: How deepest wounds are given by praise;
Nor rules of state, but rules of good:
Who hath his life from rumours freed,
Whose conscience is his strong retreat;

div.p: Whose state can neither flatterers feed, 15

lg.l: Nor ruin make accusers great;
Who God doth late and early pray
More of his grace than gifts to lend;
And entertains the harmless day

div.p: With a religious book or friend; 20

lg.l: —This man is freed from servile bands
Of hope to rise, or fear to fall;
Lord of himself, though not of lands;
And having nothing, yet hath all.
Away, let nought to love displeasing,
My Winifreda, move your care,
Let nought delay the heavenly blessing,
Nor squeamish pride nor gloomy fear.

div.p: What though no grants of royal donors 5

lg.l: With pompous titles grace our blood?
We’ll shine in more substantial honours,
And to be noble we’ll be good.
Our name, while virtue thus we tender,

div.p: Will sweetly sound where’er ’tis spoke; 10

lg.l: And all the great ones, they shall wonder
How they respect such little folk.
What though from fortune’s lavish bounty
No mighty treasures we possess,

div.p: We’ll find within our pittance plenty, 15

lg.l: And be content without excess.
Still shall each returning season
Sufficient for our wishes give;
For we will live a life of reason,

div.p: And that’s the only life to live. 20

lg.l: Through youth and age in love excelling,
We’ll hand in hand together tread;
Sweet smiling peace shall crown our dwelling,
And babes, sweet smiling babes, our bed.

div.p: How should I love the pretty creatures, 25

lg.l: While round my knees they fondly clung;
To see them look their mother’s features,
To hear them lisp their mother’s tongue.
And when with envy time transported,

div.p: Shall think to rob us of our joys, 30
You’ll in your girls again be courted,
And I’ll go wooing in my boys.
Stand still, and I will read to thee
A lecture, Love, in love’s philosophy.
These three hours that we have spent
Walking here, two shadows went
Along with us, which we ourselves produced: 5

lg.l: But, now the sun is just above our head,
We do those shadows tread,
And to brave clearness all things are reduced.
So whilst our infant loves did grow,

div.p: Disguises did and shadows flow 10

lg.l: From us and from our cares; but now it is not so.
That love hath not attained the highest degree,
Which is still diligent lest others see;
Except our loves at this noon stay,

div.p: We shall new shadows make the other way. 15

lg.l: As the first were made to blind
Others, these which come behind
Will work upon ourselves, and blind our eyes,
If our loves faint, and westwardly decline,

div.p: To me thou falsely thine, 20

lg.l: And I to thee mine actions shall disguise.
The morning shadows wear away,
But these grow longer all the day;
But, oh! love’s day is short, if love decay.

div.p: Love is a growing or full constant light, 25
And his short minute, after noon, is night.

lg.l: Ask me no more where Jove bestows,
When June is past, the fading rose;
For in your beauties, orient deep.
These flowers, as in their causes, sleep.

div.p: Ask me no more, whither do stray 5

lg.l: The golden atoms of the day;
For, in pure love, heaven did prepare
Those powders to enrich your hair.
Ask me no more, whither doth haste

div.p: The nightingale, when May is past; 10

lg.l: For in your sweet dividing throat
She winters, and keeps warm her note.
Ask me no more, where those stars light,
That downwards fall in dead of night;

div.p: For in your eyes they sit, and there 15

lg.l: Fixèd become, as in their sphere.
Ask me no more, if east or west,
The phœnix builds her spicy nest;
For unto you at last she flies,

div.p: And in your fragrant bosom dies. 20

div.head:
LXVI
THE PRIMROSE.

lg.l: Ask me why I send you here
This sweet Infanta of the year?
Ask me why I send to you
This primrose, thus bepearled with dew?

div.p: I will whisper to your ears, 5

lg.l: The sweets of love are mixt with tears.
Ask me why this flower does show
So yellow-green, and sickly too?
Ask me why the stalk is weak,

div.p: And bending, yet it doth not break? 10
I will answer, these discover
What fainting hopes are in a lover.

lg.l: It is not beauty I demand,
A crystal brow, the moon’s despair,
Nor the snow’s daughter, a white hand,
Nor mermaid’s yellow pride of hair:

div.p: Tell me not of your starry eyes, 5

lg.l: Your lips that seem on roses fed,
Your breasts, where Cupid tumbling lies,
Nor sleeps for kissing of his bed:—
A bloomy pair of vermeil cheeks,

div.p: Like Hebe’s in her ruddiest hours, 10

lg.l: A breath that softer music speaks
Than summer winds a-wooing flowers,
These are but gauds: nay, what are lips?
Coral beneath the ocean-stream,

div.p: Whose brink when your adventurer slips, 15

lg.l: Full oft he perisheth on them.
And what are cheeks, but ensigns oft
That wave hot youth to fields of blood?
Did Helen’s breast, though ne’er so soft,

div.p: Do Greece or Ilium any good? 20

lg.l: Eyes can with baleful ardour burn;
Poison can breathe, that erst perfumed;
There’s many a white hand holds an urn
With lovers’ hearts to dust consumed.

div.p: For crystal brows there’s nought within, 25

lg.l: They are but empty cells for pride;
He who the Siren’s hair would win
Is mostly strangled in the tide.
Give me, instead of beauty’s bust,

div.p: A tender heart, a loyal mind, 30

lg.l: Which with temptation I would trust,
Yet never linked with error find,—
One in whose gentle bosom I
Could pour my secret heart of woes,

div.p: Like the care-burthened honey-fly 35

lg.l: That hides his murmurs in the rose,—
My earthly comforter! whose love
So indefeasible might be
That, when my spirit wonned above,

div.p: Hers could not stay, for sympathy. 40

lg.l: Go, lovely Rose!
Tell her, that wastes her time and me,
That now she knows,
When I resemble her to thee,

div.p: How sweet and fair she seems to be. 5

lg.l: Tell her that’s young,
And shuns to have her graces spied,
That had’st thou sprung
In deserts where no men abide,

div.p: Thou must have uncommended died. 10

lg.l: Small is the worth
Of beauty from the light retired:
Bid her come forth,
Suffer herself to be desired,

div.p: And not blush so to be admired. 15

lg.l: Then die! that she
The common fate of all things rare
May read in thee:
How small a part of time they share,

div.p: That are so wondrous sweet and fair! 20

lg.l: Thou blushing rose, within whose virgin leaves
The wanton wind to sport himself presumes,
Whilst from their rifled wardrobe he receives
For his wings purple, for his breath perfumes!

div.p: Blown in the morning, thou shalt fade ere noon; 5
What boots a life which in such haste forsakes thee?
Thou’ art wondrous frolic, being to die so soon,
And passing proud a little colour makes thee.

head.label: LXX
