head.hi: TO CASTARA. THE REWARD OF INNOCENT LOVE.

lg.l: We saw and wooed each other’s eyes,
My soul contracted then with thine,
And both burnt in one sacrifice,
By which our marriage grew divine.

div.p: Let wilder youth, whose soul is sense, 5

lg.l: Profane the temple of delight,
And purchase endless penitence
With the stol’n pleasure of one night.
Time’s ever ours, while we despise

div.p: The sensual idol of our clay, 10

lg.l: For though the suns do set and rise,
We joy one everlasting day;
Whose light no jealous clouds obscure,
While each of us shine innocent;

div.p: The troubled stream is still impure; 15

lg.l: With virtue flies away content.
And though opinions often err,
We’ll court the modest smile of fame,
For sin’s black danger circles her

div.p: Who hath infection in her name. 20

lg.l: Thus when to one dark silent room
Death shall our loving coffins thrust,
Fame will build columns on our tomb,
And add a perfume to our dust.

div.head:
LXXI
LOVE’S ANNIVERSARY.
TO THE SUN.

lg.l: Thou art returned, great light, to that blest hour
In which I first by marriage, sacred power,
Joined with Castara hearts: and as the same
Thy lustre is, as then, so is our flame;

div.p: Which had increased, but that by love’s decree 5
’Twas such at first, it ne’er could greater be.
But tell me, glorious lamp, in thy survey
Of things below thee, what did not decay
By age to weakness? I since that have seen
The rose bud forth and fade, the tree grow green 10

lg.l: And wither, and the beauty of the field
With winter wrinkled. Even thyself dost yield
Something to time, and to thy grave fall nigher;
But virtuous love is one sweet endless fire.
My once dear Love! hapless that I no more
Must call thee so—the rich affection’s store
That fed our hopes, lies now exhaust and spent,
Like sums of treasure unto bankrupts lent.

div.p: We, that did nothing study but the way 5

lg.l: To love each other, with which thoughts the day
Rose with delight to us, and with them set,
Must learn the hateful art, how to forget.
We, that did nothing wish that Heaven could give,

div.p: Beyond ourselves, nor did desire to live 10

lg.l: Beyond that wish, all these now cancel must,
As if not writ in faith, but words and dust.
Yet witness those clear vows which lovers make,
Witness the chaste desires that never brake

div.p: Into unruly heats; witness that breast, 15
Which in thy bosom anchored his whole rest,
’Tis no default in us, I dare acquit
Thy maiden faith, thy purpose fair and white
As thy pure self. Cross planets did envy
Us to each other, and Heaven did untie 20

lg.l: Faster than vows could bind. Oh that the stars,
When lovers meet, should stand opposed in wars!
Since then some higher destinies command,
Let us not strive, nor labour to withstand

div.p: What is past help. The longest date of grief 25

lg.l: Can never yield a hope of our relief;
And though we waste ourselves in moist laments,
Tears may drown us, but not our discontents.
Fold back our arms; take home our fruitless loves,

div.p: That must new fortunes try, like turtle doves 30

lg.l: Dislodgèd from their haunts. We must in tears
Unwind a love knit up in many years.
In this last kiss I here surrender thee
Back to thyself,—so thou again art free;

div.p: Thou in another, sad as that, resend 35
The truest heart that lover e’er did lend.
Now turn from each. So fare our severed hearts,
As the divorced soul from her body parts.

lg.l: O waly, waly up the bank,
And waly, waly down the brae,
And waly, waly yon burn-side,
Where I and my Love wont to gae.

div.p: I leaned my back unto an aik, 5

lg.l: I thought it was a trusty tree;
But first it bowed, and syne it brak’,
Sae my true Love did lichtly me.
O waly, waly, but love be bonnie,

div.p: A little time while it is new, 10

lg.l: But when ’tis auld, it waxeth cauld,
And fades away like morning dew.
Oh! wherefore should I busk my head,
Or wherefore should I kame my hair?

div.p: For my true Love has me forsook, 15

lg.l: And says he’ll never love me mair.
Now Arthur-Seat shall be my bed,
The sheets shall ne’er be prest by me,
Saint Anton’s well shall be my drink,

div.p: Since my true Love’s forsaken me. 20
Martinmas wind, when wilt thou blaw,
And shake the green leaves off the tree?
O gentle Death! when wilt thou come?
For of my life I am wearie.
’Tis not the frost that freezes fell, 25
Nor blawing snaw’s inclemency;
’Tis not sic cauld that makes me cry,
But my Love’s heart grown cauld to me.
When we came in by Glasgow town,
We were a comely sight to see; 30

lg.l: My Love was clad in the black velvet,
And I mysel’ in cramasie.
But had I wist, before I kissed,
That love had been sae ill to win,

div.p: I’d locked my heart in a case of gowd, 35

lg.l: And pinned it with a siller pin.
And oh! if my young babe were born,
And set upon the nurse’s knee,
And I mysel’ were dead and gane,

div.p: With the green grass growing over me! 40

lg.l: I wish I were where Helen lies;
Night and day on me she cries;
Oh that I were where Helen lies
On fair Kirconnell lea!

div.p: Curst be the heart that thought the thought, 5

lg.l: And curst the hand that fired the shot,
When in my arms burd Helen dropt,
And died to succour me!
Oh think na but my heart was sair,

div.p: When my Love dropt down and spak nae mair! 10

lg.l: I laid her down wi’ meikle care
On fair Kirconnell lea.
As I went down the water-side,
None but my foe to be my guide,

div.p: None but my foe to be my guide, 15

lg.l: On fair Kirconnell lea;
I lighted down my sword to draw,
I hackèd him in pieces sma’,
I hackèd him in pieces sma’,

div.p: For her sake that died for me. 20

lg.l: O Helen fair, beyond compare!
I’ll make a garland of thy hair
Shall bind my heart for evermair
Until the day I die.

div.p: Oh that I were where Helen lies! 25

lg.l: Night and day on me she cries;
Out of my bed she bids me rise,
Says, ‘Haste and come to me!’
O Helen fair! O Helen chaste!

div.p: If I were with thee, I were blest, 30

lg.l: Where thou lies low and takes thy rest
On fair Kirconnell lea.
I wish my grave were growing green,
A winding-sheet drawn ower my een,

div.p: And I in Helen’s arms lying, 35

lg.l: On fair Kirconnell lea.
I wish I were where Helen lies:
Night and day on me she cries;
And I am weary of the skies,

div.p: Since my Love died for me. 40
Over the mountains
And over the waves,
Under the fountains
And under the graves;
Under floods that are deepest, 5

lg.l: Which Neptune obey,
Over rocks that are steepest
Love will find out the way.
Where there is no place

div.p: For the glowworm to lie; 10

lg.l: Where there is no space
For receipt of a fly;
Where the midge dares not venture,
Lest herself fast she lay;

div.p: If Love come, he will enter 15

lg.l: And find out the way.
You may esteem him
A child for his might;
Or you may deem him

div.p: A coward from his flight; 20

lg.l: But if she whom Love doth honour
Be concealed from the day,
Set a thousand guards upon her,
Love will find out the way.

div.p: Some think to lose him 25

lg.l: By having him confined;
And some do suppose him,
Poor heart! to be blind;
But if ne’er so close you wall him,

div.p: Do the best that you may, 30

lg.l: Blind Love, if so you call him,
Will find out his way.
You may train the eagle
To stoop to your fist;

div.p: Or you may inveigle 35

lg.l: The phœnix of the east;
The lioness, you may move her
To give o’er her prey;
But you’ll ne’er Stop a lover:

div.p: He will find out the way. 40

lg.l: If the earth should part him,
He would gallop it o’er;
If the seas should o’erthwart him,
He would swim to the shore.

div.p: Should his Love become a swallow, 45

lg.l: Through the air to stray,
Love will lend wings to follow,
And will find out the way.
There is no striving

div.p: To cross his intent, 50

lg.l: There is no contriving
His plots to prevent;
But if once the message greet him,
That his true-love doth stay,

div.p: If death should come and meet him, 55
Love will find out the way.

lg.l: There were twa brothers at the scule,
And when they got awa’—
‘Its will ye play at the stane-chucking,
Or will ye play at the ba’,

div.p: Or will ye gae up to yon hill head, 5

lg.l: And there we’ll warsell a fa’.’
‘I winna play at the stane-chucking,
Nor will I play at the ba’,
But I’ll gae up to yon bonnie green hill,

div.p: And there we’ll warsel a fa’.’ 10

lg.l: They warsled up, they warsled down,
Till John fell to the ground;
A dirk fell out of Willie’s pouch,
And gave him a deadly wound.

div.p: ‘Oh, Billie, lift me on your back, 15

lg.l: Take me to yon well fair,
And wash the bluid frae aff my wound,
And it will bleed nae mair.’
He’s lifted his brother upon his back,

div.p: Ta’en him to yon well fair; 20

lg.l: He’s washed the bluid frae aff his wound,
But ay it bled mair and mair.
‘Tak ye aff my Holland sark,
And rive it gair by gair,

div.p: And stap it in my bluidy wound, 25

lg.l: And syne ’twill bleed nae mair.’
He’s taken aff his Holland sark,
And torn it gair by gair;
He’s stappit it in his bluidy wound,

div.p: But ay it bled mair and mair. 30

lg.l: ‘Tak now aff my green sleiding,
And row me saftly in;
And tak me up to yon kirk style,
Where the grass grows fair and green.’

div.p: He’s taken aff the green sleiding, 35

lg.l: And rowed him saftly in;
He’s laid him down by yon kirk style,
Where the grass grows fair and green.
‘What will ye say to your father dear

div.p: When ye gae hame at e’en?’ 40
‘I’ll say ye’re lying at yon kirk style,
Where the grass grows fair and green.
‘O no, O no, my brother dear,
O you must not say so;
But say that I’m gane to a foreign land, 45
Where nae man does me know.
When he sat in his father’s chair
He grew baith pale and wan.
‘O what blude’s that upon your brow?
O dear son, tell to me.’ 50
‘It is the blude o’ my gude gray steed,
He wadna ride wi’ me.’
‘O thy steed’s blude was ne’er sae red,
Nor e’er sae dear to me: 55
O what blude’s this upon your cheek?
O dear son, tell to me.’
‘It is the blude of my greyhound,
He wadna hunt for me.’
‘O thy hound’s blude was ne’er sae red, 60

lg.l: Nor e’er sae dear to me:
O what blude’s this upon your hand?
O dear son, tell to me.’
‘It is the blude of my gay gosshawk,

div.p: He wadna flee for me.’ 65

lg.l: ‘O thy hawk’s blude was ne’er sae red,
Nor e’er sae dear to me:
O what blude’s this upon your dirk?
Dear Willie, tell to me.’

div.p: ‘It is the blude of my ae brother, 70
O dule and wae is me!’
‘O what will ye say to your father,
Dear Willie, tell to me?’
‘I’ll saddle my steed, and awa’ I’ll ride
To dwell in some far countrie.’ 75
‘O when will ye come hame again,
Dear Willie, tell to me?’
‘When the sun and mune dance on yon green,
And that will never be.’
She turned hersel’ right round about, 80

lg.l: And her heart burst into three:
‘My ae best son is deid and gane,
And my tother ane I’ll ne’er see.’
There were twa sisters lived in a bouir;
Binnorie, O Binnorie;
The youngest o’ them, oh, she was a flouir!

l.hi: By the bonnie mill-dams o’ Binnorie.

div.p: There came a squire frae the west; 5

lg.l: He lo’ed them baith, but the youngest best;
He gied the eldest a gay gowd ring;
But he lo’ed the youngest abune a’ thing.
He courted the eldest wi’ broach and knife;

div.p: But he lo’ed the youngest as his life. 10

lg.l: The eldest she was vexèd sair,
And sore envied her sister fair.
And it fell once upon a day,
The eldest to the youngest did say:

div.p: ‘Oh, sister, come to the sea-strand, 15

lg.l: And see our father’s ships come to land.
She’s ta’en her by the milk-white hand,
And led her down to the sea-strand.
The youngest sat upon a stane;

div.p: The eldest came and pushed her in. 20
‘Oh, sister, sister, lend me your hand,
And you shall be heir of half my land.’
‘Oh, sister, I’ll not reach my hand,
And I’ll be heir of all your land.
‘Shame fa’ the hand that I should take! 25
It twinned me and my world’s maik.’
‘Oh, sister, reach me but your glove,
And you shall be sweet William’s love.’
‘Sink on, nor hope for hand or glove,
And sweet William shall better be my love. 30

lg.l: ‘Your cherry cheeks and yellow hair
Had gar’d me gang maiden evermair.’
First she sank, and syne she swam,
Until she cam to Tweed mill-dam.

div.p: The miller’s dauchter was baking breid, 35

lg.l: And gaed for water as she had need.
‘Oh, father, father, in our mill-dam
There’s either a mermaid or a milk-white swan.’
The miller quickly drew his dam;

div.p: And there he fand a drowned woman. 40

lg.l: You couldna see her yellow hair,
For gowd and pearls that were sae rare.
You couldna see her middle sma’,
Her gowden girdle was sae braw.

div.p: You couldna see her lilie feet, 45

lg.l: Her gowden fringes were sae deep.
You couldna see her fingers sma’,
Wi’ diamond rings they were covered a’.
‘Sair will they be, whae’er they be,

div.p: The hearts that live to weep for thee!’ 50

lg.l: Then by there cam a harper fine,
That harpèd to the king at dine.
And, when he looked that lady on,
He sighed, and made a heavy moan.

div.p: He has ta’en three locks o’ her yellow hair, 55

lg.l: And wi’ them strung his harp sae fair.
And he brought the harp to her father’s hall,
And there the court was assembled all.
He laid his harp upon a stone,

div.p: And straight it began to play alone. 60
‘O yonder sits my father, the king!
And yonder sits my mother, the queen!
‘And yonder stands my brother Hugh,
And by him my William sweet and true!’
But the last tune that the harp played then, 65
Binnorie, O Binnorie,
Was, ‘Woe to my sister, false Helen!’

p.hi: By the bonny mill-dams o’ Binnorie.

lg.l: Lady, that in the prime of earliest youth
Wisely hast shunned the broad way and the green,
And with those few art eminently seen,
That labour up the hill of heavenly truth;

div.p: The better part with Mary and with Ruth 5

lg.l: Chosen thou hast; and they that overween,
And at thy growing virtues fret their spleen,
No anger find in thee, but pity’ and ruth.
Thy care is fixed, and zealously attends

div.p: To fill thy odorous lamp with deeds of light, 10

lg.l: And hope that reaps not shame. Therefore be sure
Thou, when the Bridegroom with his feastful friends
Passes to bliss at the mid hour of night,
Hast gained thy entrance, Virgin wise and pure.
How wisely Nature did decree,
With the same eyes to weep and see!
That, having viewed the object vain,
They might be ready to complain.

div.p: And, since the self-deluding sight 5

lg.l: In a false angle takes each height,
These tears, which better measure all,
Like watery lines and plummets fall.
Two tears, which sorrow long did weigh

div.p: Within the scales of either eye, 10

lg.l: And then paid out in equal poise,
Are the true price of all my joys.
What in the world most fair appears,
Yea, even laughter, turns to tears:

div.p: And all the jewels which we prize, 15

lg.l: Melt in these pendants of the eyes.
I have through every garden been,
Amongst the red, the white, the green;
And yet from all those flowers I saw,

div.p: No honey but these tears could draw. 20

lg.l: So the all-seeing sun each day
Distils the world with chymic ray;
But finds the essence only showers,
Which straight in pity back he pours.

div.p: Yet happy they whom grief doth bless, 25

lg.l: That weep the more, and see the less;
And, to preserve their sight more true,
Bathe still their eyes in their own dew.
So Magdalen in tears more wise

div.p: Dissolved those captivating eyes, 30

lg.l: Whose liquid chains could flowing meet,
To fetter her Redeemer’s feet.
Nor full sails hasting laden home,
Nor the chaste lady’s pregnant womb,

div.p: Nor Cynthia teeming shows so fair 35

lg.l: As two eyes, swoln with weeping, are.
The sparkling glance that shoots desire,
Drenched in these waves, does lose its fire.
Yea, oft the Thunderer pity takes,

div.p: And here the hissing lightning slakes. 40

lg.l: The incense was to Heaven dear,
Not as a perfume, but a tear;
And stars show lovely in the night,
But as they seem the tears of light.

div.p: Ope then, mine eyes, your double sluice, 45

lg.l: And practise so your noblest use;
For others too can see, or sleep;
But only human eyes can weep.
Now, like two clouds dissolving, drop,

div.p: And at each tear in distance stop: 50

lg.l: Now, like two fountains, trickle down:
Now, like two floods o’er-run and drown:
Thus let your streams o’erflow your springs,
Till eyes and tears be the same things;

div.p: And each the other’s difference bears; 55
These weeping eyes, those seeing tears.

head.label: LXXX
head.hi: TO MY WORTHY FRIEND MASTER GEORGE SANDYS, ON HIS TRANSLATION OF THE PSALMS.

lg.l: I press not to the choir, nor dare I greet
The holy place with my unhallowed feet;
My unwashed Muse pollutes not things divine,
Nor mingles her profaner notes with thine;

div.p: Here, humbly waiting at the porch, she stays, 5

lg.l: And with glad ears sucks in thy sacred lays.
So, devout penitents of old were wont,
Some without door, and some beneath the font,
To stand and hear the Church’s liturgies,

div.p: Yet not assist the solemn exercise: 10

lg.l: Sufficeth her, that she a lay-place gain,
To trim thy vestments, or but bear thy train;
Though not in tune nor wing she reach thy lark,
Her lyric feet may dance before the ark.

div.p: Who knows, but that her wandering eyes that run, 15

lg.l: Now hunting glowworms, may adore the sun:
A pure flame may, shot by Almighty power
Into her breast, the earthly flame devour:
My eyes in penitential dew may steep

div.p: That brine, which they for sensual love did weep. 20
So (though ’gainst nature’s course) fire may be quenched
With fire, and water be with water drenched;
Perhaps my restless soul, tired with pursuit
Of mortal beauty, seeking without fruit
Contentment there, which hath not, when enjoyed, 25

lg.l: Quenched all her thirst, nor satisfied, though cloyed,
Weary of her vain search below, above
In the first Fair may find the immortal Love.
Prompted by thy example, then no more

div.p: In moulds of clay will I my God adore; 30

lg.l: But tear those idols from my heart, and write
What his blest Spirit, not fond love, shall indite;
Then I no more shall court the verdant bay,
But the dry leafless trunk on Golgotha;

div.p: And rather strive to gain from thence one thorn, 35
Than all the flourishing wreaths by laureats worn.

lg.l: How fresh, O Lord, how sweet and clean
Are thy returns! e’en as the flowers in spring;
To which, besides their own demean,
The late-past frosts tributes of pleasure bring.

div.p: Grief melts away, 5

lg.l: Like snow in May,
As if there were no such cold thing.
Who would have thought my shrivelled heart
Could have recovered greenness? It was gone

div.p: Quite under ground; as flowers depart 10

lg.l: To see their mother-root, when they have blown;
Where they together
All the hard weather,
Dead to the world, keep house unknown.

div.p: These are thy wonders, Lord of power, 15

lg.l: Killing and quickening, bringing down to hell
And up to heaven in an hour;
Making a chiming of a passing bell.
We say amiss,

div.p: This or that is: 20

lg.l: Thy word is all, if we could spell.
Oh, that I once past changing were,
Fast in thy Paradise, where no flower can wither!
Many a spring I shoot up fair,

div.p: Offering at heaven, growing and groaning thither: 25

lg.l: Nor doth my flower
Want a spring-shower,
My sins and I joining together.
But while I grow in a straight line,

div.p: Still upwards bent, as if heaven were mine own, 30

lg.l: Thy anger comes, and I decline:
What frost to that? what pole is not the zone
Where all things burn,
When Thou dost turn,

div.p: And the least frown of thine is shown? 35

lg.l: And now in age I bud again,
After so many deaths I live and write;
I once more smell the dew and rain,
And relish versing: O my only Light,

div.p: It cannot be 40

lg.l: That I am he,
On whom thy tempests fell at night.
These are thy wonders, Lord of love,
To make us see we are but flowers that glide:

div.p: Which when we once can find and prove, 45
Thou hast a garden for us, where to bide.
Who would be more,
Swelling through store,
Forfeit their Paradise by their pride.

lg.l: Weigh me the fire; or canst thou find
A way to measure out the wind;
Distinguish all those floods that are
Mixt in that watery theatre;

div.p: And taste thou them as saltless there 5

lg.l: As in their channel first they were;
Tell me the people that do keep
Within the kingdoms of the deep;
Or fetch me back that cloud again,

div.p: Beshivered into seeds of rain; 10

lg.l: Tell me the motes, dust, sands, and spears
Of corn when summer shakes his ears;
Show me that world of stars, and whence
They noiseless spill their influence:

div.p: This if thou canst, then show me Him 15
That rides the glorious Cherubim.

lg.l: Blest pair of Sirens, pledges of Heaven’s joy,
Sphere-born harmonious sisters, Voice and Verse,
Wed your divine sounds, and mixed power employ,
Dead things with inbreathed sense able to pierce;

div.p: And to our high-raised phantasy present 5

lg.l: That undisturbèd song of pure concent,
Aye sung before the sapphire-coloured throne
To Him that sits thereon,
With saintly shout, and solemn jubilee;

div.p: Where the bright Seraphim in burning row 10

lg.l: Their loud up-lifted angel-trumpets blow;
And the Cherubic host in thousand quires
Touch their immortal harps of golden wires,
With those just Spirits that wear victorious palms,

div.p: Hymns devout and holy psalms 15

lg.l: Singing everlastingly:
That we on earth, with undiscording voice,
May rightly answer that melodious noise;
As once we did, till disproportioned sin

div.p: Jarred against Nature’s chime, and with harsh din 20

lg.l: Broke the fair music that all creatures made
To their great Lord, whose love their motion swayed
In perfect diapason, whilst they stood,
In first obedience and their state of good.

div.p: Oh may we soon again renew that song, 25

lg.l: And keep in tune with Heaven, till God ere long
To his celestial consort us unite,
To live with Him, and sing in endless morn of light!
Still young and fine! but what is still in view
We slight as old and soiled, though fresh and new.
How bright wert thou, when Shem’s admiring eye
Thy burnished, flaming arch did first descry!

div.p: When Terah, Nahor, Haran, Abram, Lot, 5

lg.l: The youthful world’s gray fathers, in one knot
Did with intentive looks watch every hour
For thy new light, and trembled at each shower!
When thou dost shine, darkness looks white and fair,

div.p: Forms turn to music, clouds to smiles and air: 10

lg.l: Rain gently spends his honey-drops, and pours
Balm on the cleft earth, milk on grass and flowers.
Bright pledge of peace and sunshine! the sure tie
Of thy Lord’s hand, the object of his eye!

div.p: When I behold thee, though my light be dim, 15

lg.l: Distant and low, I can in thine see Him,
Who looks upon thee from his glorious throne,
And minds the covenant betwixt all and One.

div.p: Hence, loathèd Melancholy,
Of Cerberus and blackest Midnight born,
In Stygian cave forlorn,
’Mongst horrid shapes, and shrieks, and sights unholy!
Find out some uncouth cell, 5

lg.l: Where brooding Darkness spreads his jealous wings,
And the night-raven sings;
There under ebon shades, and low-browed rocks,
As ragged as thy locks,

div.p: In dark Cimmerian desert ever dwell. 10

lg.l: But come, thou Goddess fair and free,
In heaven yclept Euphrosyne,
And by men, heart-easing Mirth;
Whom lovely Venus, at a birth,

div.p: With two sister Graces more, 15

lg.l: To ivy-crownèd Bacchus bore:
Or whether (as some sager sing)
The frolic wind that breathes the spring,
Zephyr, with Aurora playing,

div.p: As he met her once a-maying, 20

lg.l: There on beds of violets blue,
And fresh-blown roses washed in dew,
Filled her with thee, a daughter fair,
So buxom, blithe, and debonair.

div.p: Haste thee, Nymph, and bring with thee 25

lg.l: Jest, and youthful Jollity,
Quips, and cranks, and wanton wiles,
Nods, and becks, and wreathèd smiles,
Such as hang on Hebe’s cheek,

div.p: And love to live in dimple sleek; 30

lg.l: Sport, that wrinkled Care derides,
And Laughter, holding both his sides.
Come, and trip it as you go
On the light fantastic toe;

div.p: And in thy right hand lead with thee 35

lg.l: The mountain-nymph, sweet Liberty;
And, if I give thee honour due,
Mirth, admit me of thy crew,
To live with her, and live with thee,

div.p: In unreprovèd pleasures free; 40

lg.l: To hear the lark begin his flight,
And singing startle the dull night
From his watch-tower in the skies,
Till the dappled dawn doth rise;

div.p: Then to come, in spite of sorrow, 45

lg.l: And at my window bid good morrow,
Through the sweet-briar, or the vine,
Or the twisted eglantine:
While the cock, with lively din,

div.p: Scatters the rear of darkness thin; 50

lg.l: And to the stack, or the barn-door,
Stoutly struts his dames before:
Oft listening how the hounds and horn
Cheerly rouse the slumbering Morn,

div.p: From the side of some hoar hill, 55

lg.l: Through the high wood echoing shrill:
Sometimes walking, not unseen,
By hedge-row elms, on hillocks green,
Right against the eastern gate

div.p: Where the great Sun begins his state, 60

lg.l: Robed in flames and amber light,
The clouds in thousand liveries dight;
While the ploughman, near at hand,
Whistles o’er the furrowed land,

div.p: And the milkmaid singeth blithe, 65

lg.l: And the mower whets his scythe,
And every shepherd tells his tale
Under the hawthorn in the dale.
Straight mine eye hath caught new pleasures,

div.p: Whilst the landscape round it measures; 70

lg.l: Russet lawns, and fallows gray,
Where the nibbling flocks do stray;
Mountains, on whose barren breast
The labouring clouds do often rest;

div.p: Meadows trim with daisies pied, 75

lg.l: Shallow brooks, and rivers wide:
Towers and battlements it sees
Bosomed high in tufted trees,
Where perhaps some Beauty lies,

div.p: The Cynosure of neighbouring eyes. 80

lg.l: Hard by, a cottage chimney smokes,
From betwixt two agèd oaks,
Where Corydon and Thyrsis, met,
Are at their savoury dinner set

div.p: Of herbs, and other country messes, 85

lg.l: Which the neat-handed Phillis dresses;
And then in haste her bower she leaves,
With Thestylis to bind the sheaves;
Or, if the earlier season lead,

div.p: To the tanned haycock in the mead. 90

lg.l: Sometimes with secure delight
The upland hamlets will invite,
When the merry bells ring round,
And the jocund rebecks sound

div.p: To many a youth, and many a maid, 95

lg.l: Dancing in the chequered shade;
And young and old come forth to play
On a sunshine holiday,
Till the livelong daylight fail:

div.p: Then to the spicy nut-brown ale, 100

lg.l: With stories told of many a feat,
How faery Mab the junkets eat;
She was pinched, and pulled, she said;
And he, by friar’s lantern led,

div.p: Tells how the drudging goblin sweat, 105

lg.l: To earn his cream-bowl duly set,
When in one night, ere glimpse of morn,
His shadowy flail hath threshed the corn,
That ten day-labourers could not end;

div.p: Then lies him down the lubbar-fiend, 110

lg.l: And, stretched out all the chimney’s length,
Basks at the fire his hairy strength;
And crop-full out of doors he flings,
Ere the first cock his matin rings.

div.p: Thus done the tales, to bed they creep, 115

lg.l: By whispering winds soon lulled asleep.
Towered cities please us then,
And the busy hum of men,
Where throngs of knights and barons bold,

div.p: In weeds of peace, high triumphs hold, 120
With store of ladies, whose bright eyes
Rain influence, and judge the prize
Of wit, or arms, while both contend
To win her grace, whom all commend.
There let Hymen oft appear 125

lg.l: In saffron robe, with taper clear,
And pomp and feast and revelry,
With mask and antique pageantry,
Such sights as youthful poets dream

div.p: On summer eves by haunted stream. 130

lg.l: Then to the well-trod stage anon,
If Jonson’s learnèd sock be on,
Or sweetest Shakespeare, Fancy’s child,
Warble his native wood-notes wild.

div.p: And ever against eating cares 135

lg.l: Lap me in soft Lydian airs,
Married to immortal verse;
Such as the meeting soul may pierce
In notes, with many a winding bout

div.p: Of linkèd sweetness long drawn out, 140

lg.l: With wanton heed and giddy cunning;
The melting voice through mazes running,
Untwisting all the chains that tie
The hidden soul of harmony;

div.p: That Orpheus’ self may heave his head 145
From golden slumber on a bed
Of heaped Elysian flowers, and hear
Such strains as would have won the ear
Of Pluto, to have quite set free
His half-regained Eurydice. 150
These delights if thou canst give,
Mirth, with thee I mean to live.

lg.l: Hence, vain deluding Joys,
The brood of Folly without father bred!
How little you bested,
Or fill the fixèd mind with all your toys!

div.p: Dwell in some idle brain, 5

lg.l: And fancies fond with gaudy shapes possess,
As thick and numberless
As the gay motes that people the sunbeams;
Or likest hovering dreams,

div.p: The fickle pensioners of Morpheus’ train. 10

lg.l: But hail, thou Goddess, sage and holy,
Hail, divinest Melancholy!
Whose saintly visage is too bright
To hit the sense of human sight,

div.p: And therefore to our weaker view 15

lg.l: O’erlaid with black, staid Wisdom’s hue;
Black, but such as in esteem
Prince Memnon’s sister might beseem,
Or that starred Ethiop queen that strove

div.p: To set her beauty’s praise above 20

lg.l: The sea-nymphs’, and their powers offended:
Yet thou art higher far descended:
Thee bright-haired Vesta long of yore
To solitary Saturn bore;

div.p: His daughter she; in Saturn’s reign 25

lg.l: Such mixture was not held a stain:
Oft in glimmering bowers and glades
He met her, and in secret shades
Of woody Ida’s inmost grove,

div.p: Whilst yet there was no fear of Jove. 30

lg.l: Come, pensive Nun, devout and pure,
Sober, steadfast, and demure,
All in a robe of darkest grain,
Flowing with majestic train,

div.p: And sable stole of cypres lawn, 35

lg.l: Over thy decent shoulders drawn.
Come, but keep thy wonted state,
With even step, and musing gait;
And looks commercing with the skies,

div.p: Thy rapt soul sitting in thine eyes: 40

lg.l: There, held in holy passion still,
Forget thyself to marble, till
With a sad leaden downward cast
Thou fix them on the earth as fast:

div.p: And join with thee calm Peace, and Quiet, 45

lg.l: Spare Fast, that oft with gods doth diet,
And hears the Muses in a ring
Aye round about Jove’s altar sing:
And add to these retired Leisure,

div.p: That in trim gardens takes his pleasure: 50

lg.l: But first and chiefest with thee bring,
Him that yon soars on golden wing,
Guiding the fiery-wheeled throne,
The cherub Contemplation;

div.p: And the mute Silence hist along, 55
’Less Philomel will deign a song,
In her sweetest saddest plight,
Smoothing the rugged brow of night,
While Cynthia checks her dragon-yoke
Gently o’er the accustomed oak: 60

lg.l: Sweet bird, that shunn’st the noise of folly,
Most musical, most melancholy!
Thee, chantress, oft, the woods among,
I woo, to hear thy even-song;

div.p: And, missing thee, I walk unseen 65

lg.l: On the dry smooth-shaven green,
To behold the wandering moon,
Riding near her highest noon,
Like one that had been led astray

div.p: Through the heaven’s wide pathless way; 70

lg.l: And oft, as if her head she bowed,
Stooping through a fleecy cloud.
Oft, on a plat of rising ground,
I hear the far-off curfew sound

div.p: Over some wide-watered shore, 75

lg.l: Swinging slow with sullen roar:
Or, if the air will not permit,
Some still removèd place will fit,
Where glowing embers through the room

div.p: Teach light to counterfeit a gloom; 80

lg.l: Far from all resort of mirth,
Save the cricket on the hearth,
Or the bellman’s drowsy charm,
To bless the doors from nightly harm.

div.p: Or let my lamp at midnight hour 85

lg.l: Be seen in some high lonely tower,
Where I may oft out-watch the Bear,
With thrice-great Hermes, or unsphere
The spirit of Plato, to unfold

div.p: What worlds or what vast regions hold 90

lg.l: The immortal mind, that hath forsook
Her mansion in this fleshly nook:
And of those demons that are found,
In fire, air, flood, or under ground,

div.p: Whose power hath a true consent 95

lg.l: With planet, or with element.
Sometime let gorgeous Tragedy
In sceptered pall come sweeping by,
Presenting Thebes, or Pelops’ line,

div.p: Or the tale of Troy divine; 100

lg.l: Or what, though rare, of later age
Ennobled hath the buskined stage.
But, O sad Virgin, that thy power
Might raise Musæus from his bower!

div.p: Or bid the soul of Orpheus sing 105

lg.l: Such notes as, warbled to the string,
Drew iron tears down Pluto’s cheek,
And made Hell grant what love did seek!
Or call up him that left half-told

div.p: The story of Cambuscan bold, 110

lg.l: Of Camball, and of Algarsife,
And who had Canace to wife,
That owned the virtuous ring and glass;
And of the wondrous horse of brass,

div.p: On which the Tartar king did ride: 115

lg.l: And if aught else great bards beside
In sage and solemn tunes have sung,
Of turneys, and of trophies hung,
Of forests and enchantments drear,

div.p: Where more is meant than meets the ear. 120

lg.l: Thus, Night, oft see me in thy pale career,
Till civil-suited Morn appear,
Not tricked and frounced as she was wont
With the Attic boy to hunt,

div.p: But kercheft in a comely cloud, 125

lg.l: While rocking winds are piping loud,
Or ushered with a shower still,
When the gust hath blown his fill,
Ending on the rustling leaves,

div.p: With minute drops from off the eaves. 130

lg.l: And, when the sun begins to fling
His flaring beams, me, Goddess, bring
To archèd walks of twilight groves,
And shadows brown, that Sylvan loves,

div.p: Of pine, or monumental oak, 135

lg.l: Where the rude axe with heavèd stroke
Was never heard the Nymphs to daunt,
Or fright them from their hallowed haunt.
There in close covert by some brook,

div.p: Where no profaner eye may look, 140

lg.l: Hide me from day’s garish eye,
While the bee with honied thigh,
That at her flowery work doth sing,
And the waters murmuring,

div.p: With such consort as they keep, 145

lg.l: Entice the dewy-feather’d Sleep;
And let some strange mysterious dream
Wave at his wings, in aery stream
Of lively portraiture displayed,

div.p: Softly on my eyelids laid. 150

lg.l: And, as I wake, sweet music breathe
Above, about, or underneath,
Sent by some Spirit to mortals good,
Or the unseen Genius of the wood.

div.p: But let my due feet never fail 155

lg.l: To walk the studious cloisters pale,
And love the high-embowèd roof
With antique pillars massy-proof,
And storied windows richly dight,

div.p: Casting a dim religious light: 160

lg.l: There let the pealing organ blow,
To the full-voiced quire below,
In service high, and anthems clear,
As may with sweetness through mine ear

div.p: Dissolve me into ecstasies, 165

lg.l: And bring all Heaven before mine eyes.
And may at last my weary age
Find out the peaceful hermitage,
The hairy gown and mossy cell,

div.p: Where I may sit, and rightly spell 170

lg.l: Of every star that heaven doth shew,
And every herb that sips the dew;
Till old experience do attain
To something like prophetic strain.

div.p: These pleasures, Melancholy, give, 175
And I with thee will choose to live.

DIRECTED TO MY DEAR FATHER, AND MOST WORTHY FRIEND,
MR. ISAAC WALTON.

lg.l: Heaven, what an age is this! what race
Of giants are sprung up, that dare
Thus fly in the Almighty’s face,
And with his Providence make war!

div.p: I can go nowhere but I meet 5

lg.l: With malcontents and mutineers,
As if in life was nothing sweet,
And we must blessings reap in tears.
O senseless man! that murmurs still

div.p: For happiness, and does not know, 10

lg.l: Even though he might enjoy his will,
What he would have to make him so.
Is it true happiness to be
By undiscerning Fortune placed

div.p: In the most eminent degree, 15

lg.l: Where few arrive, and none stand fast?
Titles and wealth are Fortune’s toils,
Wherewith the vain themselves ensnare:
The great are proud of borrowed spoils,

div.p: The miser’s plenty breeds his care. 20

lg.l: The one supinely yawns at rest,
The other eternally doth toil;
Each of them equally a beast,
A pampered horse, or labouring moil:

div.p: The titulados oft disgraced 25

lg.l: By public hate or private frown,
And he whose hand the creature raised,
Has yet a foot to kick him down.
The drudge who wold all get, all save,

div.p: Like a brute beast both feeds and lies; 30

lg.l: Prone to the earth, he digs his grave,
And in the very labour dies.
Excess of ill-got, ill-kept, pelf
Does only death and danger breed;

div.p: Whilst one rich worldling starves himself 35

lg.l: With what would thousand others feed.
By which we see that wealth and power,
Although they make men rich and great,
The sweets of life do often sour,

div.p: And gull ambition with a cheat. 40

lg.l: Nor is he happier than these,
Who in a moderate estate,
Where he might safely live at ease,
Has lusts that are immoderate.

div.p: For he, by those desires misled, 45

lg.l: Quits his own vine’s securing shade,
To’ expose his naked, empty head
To all the storms man’s peace invade.
Nor is he happy who is trim,

div.p: Tricked up in favours of the fair, 50

lg.l: Mirrors, with every breath made dim.
Birds, caught in every wanton snare.
Woman, man’s greatest woe or bliss,
Does ofter far, than serve, enslave,

div.p: And with the magic of a kiss 55

lg.l: Destroys whom she was made to save.
Oh! fruitful grief, the world’s disease!
And vainer man, to make it so,
Who gives his miseries increase

div.p: By cultivating his own woe. 60

lg.l: There are no ills but what we make
By giving shapes and names to things;
Which is the dangerous mistake
That causes all our sufferings.

div.p: We call that sickness, which is health; 65

lg.l: That persecution, which is grace;
That poverty, which is true wealth;
And that dishonour, which is praise.
Alas! our time is here so short,

div.p: That in what state soe’er ’tis spent, 70

lg.l: Of joy or woe, does not import,
Provided it be innocent.
But we may make it pleasant too,
If we will take our measures right,

div.p: And not what Heaven has done, undo 75

lg.l: By an unruly appetite.
The world is full of beaten roads,
But yet so slippery withal,
That where one walks secure, ’tis odds

div.p: A hundred and a hundred fall. 80

lg.l: Untrodden paths are then the best,
Where the frequented are unsure;
And he comes soonest to his rest,
Whose journey has been most secure.

div.p: It is content alone that makes 85

lg.l: Our pilgrimage a pleasure here;
And who buys sorrow cheapest, takes
An ill commodity too dear.

div.p: Hope, of all ills that men endure
The only cheap and universal cure!
Thou captive’s freedom, and thou sick man’s health!
Thou loser’s victory, and thou beggar’s wealth!
Thou manna, which from heaven we eat, 5

lg.l: To every taste a several meat!
Thou strong retreat, thou sure entailed estate,
Which nought has power to alienate!
Thou pleasant, honest flatterer, for none

div.p: Flatter unhappy men, but thou alone! 10

lg.l: Hope, thou first-fruits of happiness!
Thou gentle dawning of a bright success!
Thou good preparative, without which our joy
Does work too strong, and whilst it cures, destroy;

div.p: Who out of fortune’s reach dost stand, 15

lg.l: And art a blessing still in hand!
Whilst thee, her earnest-money, we retain,
We certain are to gain,
Whether she her bargain break, or else fulfil;

div.p: Thou only good, not worse for ending ill! 20

lg.l: Brother of Faith, ’twixt whom and thee
The joys of Heaven and earth divided be!
Though Faith be heir, and have the fixed estate,
Thy portion yet in moveables is great.

div.p: Happiness itself’s all one 25

lg.l: In thee, or in possession!
Only the future’s thine, the present his!
Thine’s the more hard and noble bliss;
Best apprehender of our joys, which hast

div.p: So long a reach, and yet canst hold so fast! 30
Hope, thou sad lover’s only friend!
Thou way, that may’st dispute it with the end!
For love, I fear, ’s a fruit that does delight
The taste itself less than the smell and sight.
Fruition more deceitful is 35

lg.l: Than thou canst be, when thou dost miss;
Men leave thee by obtaining, and straight flee
Some other way again to thee:
And that’s a pleasant country, without doubt,

div.p: To which all soon return that travel out. 40
TO THE UNIVERSITY OF OXFORD. SPOKEN BY MR. HART, AT THE ACTING OF ‘THE SILENT WOMAN.’

lg.l: What Greece, when learning flourished, only knew,
Athenian judges, you this day renew.
Here too are annual rites to Pallas done,
And here poetic prizes lost or won.

div.p: Methinks I see you, crowned with olives, sit, 5

lg.l: And strike a sacred horror from the pit.
A day of doom is this of your decree,
Where even the best are but by mercy free:
A day, which none but Jonson durst have wished to see,

div.p: Here they, who long have known the useful stage, 10

lg.l: Come to be taught themselves to teach the age.
As your commissioners our poets go,
To cultivate the virtue which you sow;
In your Lycæum first themselves refined,

div.p: And delegated thence to human-kind. 15

lg.l: But as ambassadors, when long from home,
For new instructions to their princes come,
So poets, who your precepts have forgot,
Return, and beg they may be better taught:

div.p: Follies and faults elsewhere by them are shown, 20

lg.l: But by your manners they correct their own.
The illiterate writer, empiric-like, applies
To minds diseased, unsafe, chance remedies:
The learned in schools, where knowledge first began,

div.p: Studies with care the anatomy of man; 25

lg.l: Sees virtue, vice, and passions, in their cause,
And fame from science, not from fortune, draws.
So poetry, which is in Oxford made
An art, in London only is a trade.

div.p: There haughty dunces, whose unlearnèd pen 30

lg.l: Could ne’er spell grammar, would be reading men.
Such build their poems the Lucretian way;
So many huddled atoms make a play;
And if they hit in order by some chance,

div.p: They call that nature which is ignorance. 35

lg.l: To such a fame let mere town-wits aspire,
And their gay nonsense their own cits admire.
Our poet, could he find forgiveness here,
Would wish it rather than a plaudit there.

div.p: He owns no crown from those Prætorian bands, 40
But knows that right is in the senate’s hands,
Not impudent enough to hope your praise,
Low at the Muses’ feet his wreath he lays,
And, where he took it up, resigns his bays. 45
Kings make their poets whom themselves think fit,
But ’tis your suffrage makes authentic wit.
TO THE UNIVERSITY OF OXFORD.

lg.l: Though actors cannot much of learning boast,
Of all who want it, we admire it most:
We love the praises of a learnèd pit,
As we remotely are allied to wit.

div.p: We speak our poet’s wit; and trade in ore, 5

lg.l: Like those who touch upon the golden shore;
Betwixt our judges can distinction make,
Discern how much, and why, our poems take:
Mark if the fools, or men of sense, rejoice;

div.p: Whether the applause be only sound or voice. 10

lg.l: When our fop-gallants, or our city-folly,
Clap over-loud, it makes us melancholy:
We doubt that scene which does their wonder raise,
And, for their ignorance, contemn their praise.

div.p: Judge then, if we who act, and they who write, 15

lg.l: Should not be proud of giving you delight.
London likes grossly; but this nicer pit
Examines, fathoms all the depths of wit;
The ready finger lays on every blot;

div.p: Knows what should justly please, and what should not. 20

lg.l: Nature herself lies open to your view;
You judge by her, what draught of her is true,
Where outlines false, and colours seem too faint,
Where bunglers daub, and where true poets paint.

div.p: But, by the sacred genius of this place, 25

lg.l: By every Muse, by each domestic grace,
Be kind to wit, which but endeavours well,
And, where you judge, presumes not to excel.
Our poets hither for adoption come,

div.p: As nations sued to be made free of Rome: 30

lg.l: Not in the suffragating tribes to stand,
But in your utmost, last, provincial band.
If his ambition may those hopes pursue,
Who with religion loves your arts and you,

div.p: Oxford to him a dearer name shall be 35
Than his own mother University.
Thebes did his green unknowing youth engage;
He chooses Athens in his riper age.

lg.l: River is time in water; as it came,
Still so it flows; yet never is the same.
I wake, and so new live; a night’s protection
Is a new wonder, whiles a resurrection.

div.p: The sun’s up; yet myself and God most bright 5

lg.l: I can’t see; I’m too dark, and He’s too light.
Let devout prayér cast me to the ground,
So shall I yet to heaven be nearer found.
Clay, sand, and rock seem of a different birth;

div.p: So men; some stiff, some loose, some firm; all earth! 10

lg.l: By red, green, blue, which sometimes paint the air,
Guilt, pardon, Heaven, the rainbow does declare.
The world’s a prison; no man can get out;
Let the atheist storm then; Heaven is round about.

div.p: The rose is but the flower of a briar; 15

lg.l: The good man has an Adam to his sire.
The dying mole, some say, opens his eyes;
The rich, till ’tis too late, will not be wise.
The sick hart eats a snake, and so grows well;

div.p: Repentance digests sin, and man ’scapes hell. 20

lg.l: Flies, oft removed, return. Do they want fear,
Or shame, or memory? Flies are everywhere.
Pride cannot see itself by mid-day light;
The peacock’s tail is farthest from his sight.

div.p: The swallow’s a quick arrow, that may show 25

lg.l: With what an instant swiftness life doth flow.
The nightingale’s a quire, no single note;
O various power of God in one small throat!
The silkworm’s its own wonder; without loom

div.p: It does provide itself a silken room. 30

lg.l: The moon is the world’s glass; in which ’twere strange
If we saw her’s and saw not our own change.
Herodotus is history’s fresh youth;
Thucydides is judgment, age, and truth.

div.p: In sadness, Machiavel, thou didst not well, 35

lg.l: To help the world to run faster to hell.
The Italian’s the world’s gentleman, the Court
To which thrift, wit, lust, and revenge resort.
Bogs, purgatory, wolves, and ease, by fame

div.p: Are counted Ireland’s earth, mistake, curse, shame. 40

lg.l: The Indies, Philip, spread not like thy robe;
Art thou the new horizon to the globe?
Down, pickaxe; to the depths for gold let’s go;
We’ll undermine Peru. Is’nt heaven below?

div.p: Who gripes too much casts all upon the ground; 45
Too great a greatness greatness doth confound.
All things are wonder since the world began;
The world’s a riddle, and the meaning’s man.

lg.l: There’s none should places have in Fame’s high court
But those that first do win Invention’s fort;
Not messengers, that only make report.
To messengers rewards of thanks are due

div.p: For their great pains, telling their message true, 5

lg.l: But not the honour to invention new.
Many there are that suits will make to wear
Of several patches, stoln both here and there,
That to the world they gallants may appear:

div.p: And the poor vulgar, who but little know, 10

lg.l: And reverence all that makes a glistering show,
Examine not the same how they came to.
Then do they call their friends and all their kin;
They factions make the ignorant to win,

div.p: And with their help into Fame’s court get in. 15

head.label: XCIII
head.hi: ON THE DEATH OF PRINCE HENRY, SON OF JAMES THE FIRST.

lg.l: Methought his royal person did foretell
A kingly stateliness, from all pride clear;
His look majestic seemèd to compel
All men to love him, rather than to fear.

div.p: And yet though he were every good man’s joy, 5

lg.l: And the alonely comfort of his own,
His very name with terror did annoy
His foreign foes so far as he was known.
Hell drooped for fear; the Turkey moon looked pale;
Spain trembled; and the most tempestuous sea,

div.p: (Where Behemoth, the Babylonish whale, 10

lg.l: Keeps all his bloody and imperious plea)
Was swoln with rage, for fear he’d stop the tide
Of her o’er-daring and insulting pride.

head.label: XCIV
head.hi: ON HIS MISTRESS, THE QUEEN OF BOHEMIA.

lg.l: You meaner beauties of the night,
Which poorly satisfy our eyes,
More by your number than your light,—
You common people of the skies,

div.p: What are you, when the Moon shall rise? 5

lg.l: You violets that first appear,
By your pure purple mantles known,
Like the proud virgins of the year,
As if the spring were all your own,—

div.p: What are you, when the Rose is blown? 10

lg.l: You curious chanters of the wood,
That warble forth dame Nature’s lays,
Thinking your passions understood
By your weak accents,—what’s your praise,

div.p: When Philomel her voice doth raise? 15

lg.l: So when my Mistress shall be seen
In form and beauty of her mind,
By virtue first, then choice, a Queen,
Tell me, if she were not designed

div.p: The eclipse and glory of her kind? 20

head.label: XCV
head.hi: LORD STRAFFORD’S MEDITATIONS IN THE TOWER.

lg.l: Go, empty joys,
With all your noise,
And leave me here alone,
In sweet sad silence to bemoan

div.p: The fickle worldly height, 5

lg.l: Whose danger none can see aright,
Whilst your false splendours dim his sight.
Go, and ensnare
With your trim ware

div.p: Some other easy wight, 10

lg.l: And cheat him with your flattering light;
Rain on his head a shower
Of honours, favour, wealth, and power;
Then snatch it from him in an hour.

div.p: Fill his big mind 15

lg.l: With gallant wind
Of insolent applause;
Let him not fear all-curbing laws,
Nor king, nor people’s frown;

div.p: But dream of something like a crown, 20

lg.l: Then, climbing towards it, tumble down.
Let him appear
In his bright sphere
Like Cynthia in her pride,

div.p: With starlike troops on every side; 25

lg.l: For number and clear light
Such as may soon o’erwhelm him quite,
And blend them both in one dead night.
Welcome, sad night,

div.p: Grief’s sole delight, 30

lg.l: Thy mourning best agrees
With honour’s funeral obsequies!
In Thetis’ lap he lies,
Mantled with soft securities,

div.p: Whose too much sunshine dims his eyes. 35

lg.l: Was he too bold,
Who needs would hold
With curbing reins the Day,
And make Sol’s fiery steeds obey?

div.p: Then, sure, as rash was I, 40
Who with ambitious wings did fly
In Charles’s Wain too loftily.
I fall, I fall!
Whom shall I call?
Alas can he be heard, 45

lg.l: Who now is neither loved nor feared?
You who have vowed the ground
To kiss, where my blest steps were found,
Come, catch me at my last rebound.

div.p: How each admires 50

lg.l: Heaven’s twinkling fires,
Whilst from their glorious seat
Their influence gives light and heat;
But oh! how few there are,

div.p: Though danger from the act be far, 55
Will run to catch a falling star.
Now ’tis too late
To imitate
Those lights whose pallidness
Argues no inward guiltiness; 60

lg.l: Their course one way is bent;
Which is the cause there’s no dissent
In Heaven’s High Court of Parliament.

div.p: My dear and only Love, I pray
That little world of thee
Be governed by no other sway
But purest monarchy:
For if confusion have a part, 5

lg.l: Which virtuous souls abhor,
And hold a Synod in thy heart,
I’ll never love thee more.
As Alexander I will reign,

div.p: And I will reign alone; 10

lg.l: My thoughts did evermore disdain
A rival on my throne.
He either fears his fate too much,
Or his deserts are small,

div.p: Who dares not put it to the touch, 15

lg.l: To gain or lose it all.
But I will reign and govern still,
And always give the law,
And have each subject at my will,

div.p: And all to stand in awe: 20

lg.l: But ’gainst my batteries if I find
Thou storm, or vex me sore,
As if thou set me as a blind,
I’ll never love thee more.

div.p: And in the empire of thy heart, 25

lg.l: Where I should solely be,
If others do pretend a part,
Or dare to share with me:
Or committees if thou erect,

div.p: Or go on such a score, 30

lg.l: I’ll smiling mock at thy neglect,
And never love thee more.
But if no faithless action stain
Thy love and constant word,

div.p: I’ll make thee famous by my pen, 35

lg.l: And glorious by my sword.
I’ll serve thee in such noble ways
As ne’er was known before;
I’ll deck and crown thy head with bays,

div.p: And love thee more and more. 40

lg.l: When Love with unconfinèd wings
Hovers within my gates,
And my divine Althea brings
To whisper at the grates;

div.p: When I lie tangled in her hair, 5

lg.l: And fettered to her eye,
The birds, that wanton in the air,
Know no such liberty.
When flowing cups run swiftly round

div.p: With no allaying Thames, 10

lg.l: Our careless heads with roses crowned,
Our hearts with loyal flames;
When thirsty grief in wine we steep,
When healths and draughts go free,

div.p: Fishes, that tipple in the deep, 15
Know no such liberty.
When, like committed linnets, I
With shriller throat shall sing
The sweetness, mercy, majesty
And glories of my King; 20

lg.l: When I shall voice aloud how good
He is, how great should be,
Enlargèd winds, that curl the flood,
Know no such liberty.

div.p: Stone walls do not a prison make, 25

lg.l: Nor iron bars a cage;
Minds innocent and quiet take
That for an hermitage:
If I have freedom in my love,

div.p: And in my soul am free, 30
Angels alone, that soar above,
Enjoy such liberty.

head.label: XCVIII
head.hi: TO LUCASTA, ON GOING BEYOND THE SEAS.

lg.l: If to be absent were to be
Away from thee;
Or that when I am gone
You or I were alone;

div.p: Then, my Lucasta, might I crave 5

lg.l: Pity from blustering wind, or swallowing wave.
Though seas and land betwixt us both,
Our faith and troth,
Like separated souls,

div.p: All time and space controls: 10

lg.l: Above the highest sphere we meet
Unseen, unknown, and greet as angels greet.
So then we do anticipate
Our after-fate,

div.p: And are alive i’ the skies, 15

lg.l: If thus our lips and eyes
Can speak like spirits unconfined
In Heaven, their earthy bodies left behind.
A steed, a steed, of matchless speed,
A sword of metal keen;
All else to noble hearts is dross,
All else on earth is mean.

div.p: The neighing of the war-horse proud, 5

lg.l: The rolling of the drum,
The clangour of the trumpet loud,
Be sounds from heaven that come.
And oh! the thundering press of knights,

div.p: Whenas their war-cries swell, 10

lg.l: May toll from heaven an angel bright,
And rouse a fiend from hell.
Then mount, then mount, brave gallants all,
And don your helms amain;

div.p: Death’s couriers, Fame and Honour, call 15

lg.l: Us to the field again.
No shrewish tears shall fill our eye,
When the sword-hilt’s in our hand;
Heart-whole we’ll part, and no whit sigh

div.p: For the fairest in the land. 20

lg.l: Let piping swain and craven wight
Thus weep and puling cry;
Our business is like men to fight,
And, like to heroes, die!

head.label: C
head.hi: THE SOLDIER GOING TO THE FIELD.

lg.l: Preserve thy sighs, unthrifty girl,
To purify the air;
Thy tears to thread, instead of pearl,
On bracelets of thy hair.

div.p: The trumpet makes the echo hoarse, 5

lg.l: And wakes the louder drum;
Expense of grief gains no remorse,
When sorrow should be dumb:
For I must go, where lazy peace

div.p: Will hide her drowsy head; 10

lg.l: And, for the sport of kings, increase
The number of the dead.
But first I’ll chide thy cruel theft;
Can I in war delight,
Who, being of my heart bereft,

div.p: Can have no heart to fight? 15

lg.l: Thou know’st the sacred laws of old
Ordained a thief should pay,
To quit him of his theft, sevenfold
What he had stol’n away.

div.p: Thy payment shall but double be; 20

lg.l: Oh then with speed resign
My own seducèd heart to me,
Accompanied with thine.
Beat on, proud billows; Boreas, blow;
Swell, curlèd waves, high as Jove’s roof;
Your incivility doth show
That innocence is tempest-proof:

div.p: Though surly Nereus frown, my thoughts are calm; 5

lg.l: Then strike, Affliction, for thy wounds are balm.
That which the world miscalls a jail,
A private closet is to me,
Whilst a good conscience is my bail,

div.p: And innocence my liberty: 10

lg.l: Locks, bars, and solitude together met,
Make me no prisoner, but an anchoret.
I, whilst I wished to be retired,
Into this private room was turned;

div.p: As if their wisdom had conspired 15

lg.l: The salamander should be burned;
Or like a sophy that would drown a fish,
I am constrained to suffer what I wish.
The cynic loves his poverty;

div.p: The pelican her wilderness; 20

lg.l: And ’tis the Indian’s pride to be
Naked on frozen Caucasus:
Contentment cannot smart; stoics we see
Make torments easy to their apathy.

div.p: These manacles upon my arm 25

lg.l: I, as my mistress’ favours, wear;
And for to keep my ancles warm,
I have some iron shackles there:
These walls are but my garrison; this cell,

div.p: Which men call jail, doth prove my citadel. 30

lg.l: I’m in the cabinet locked up,
Like some high-prizèd margarite,
Or like the great mogul or pope,
Am cloistered up from public sight:

div.p: Retiredness is a piece of majesty, 35

lg.l: And thus, proud sultan, I’m as great as thee.
Here sin for want of food must starve,
Where tempting objects are not seen;
And these strong walls do only serve

div.p: To keep vice out, and keep me in: 40

lg.l: Malice of late’s grown charitable, sure,
I’m not committed, but am kept secure.
So he that struck at Jason’s life,
Thinking to’ have made his purpose sure,

div.p: By a malicious friendly knife 45

lg.l: Did only wound him to a cure:
Malice, I see, wants wit; for what is meant
Mischief, ofttimes proves favour by the event.
When once my Prince affliction hath,

div.p: Prosperity doth treason seem; 50

lg.l: And for to smooth so rough a path,
I can learn patience from him:
Now not to suffer shows no loyal heart,
When kings want ease, subjects must bear a part.

div.p: What though I cannot see my King, 55

lg.l: Neither in person nor in coin;
Yet contemplation is a thing
That renders what I have not, mine:
My King from me what adamant can part,

div.p: Whom I do wear engraven on my heart? 60

lg.l: Have you not seen the nightingale,
A pilgrim, coopt into a cage,
How doth she chaunt her wonted tale
In that her narrow hermitage?

div.p: Even there her charming melody doth prove 65

lg.l: That all her bars are trees, her cage a grove.
I am that bird, whom they combine
Thus to deprive of liberty;
But though they do my corps confine,

div.p: Yet, maugre hate, my soul is free: 70

lg.l: And though immured, yet can I chirp and sing
Disgrace to rebels, glory to my King.
My soul is free as ambient air,
Although my baser part’s immewed,

div.p: Whilst loyal thoughts do still repair 75

lg.l: To’ accompany my solitude:
Although rebellion do my body bind,
My King alone can captivate my mind.
Great Monarch of the world, from whose power springs
The potency and power of [earthly] kings,
Record the royal woe my suffering sings.
Nature and law by thy divine decree,

div.p: (The only root of righteous royalty,) 5

lg.l: With this dim diadem invested me:
With it the sacred sceptre, purple robe,
The holy unction, and the royal globe;
Yet am I levelled with the life of Job.

div.p: The fiercest furies, that do daily tread 10

lg.l: Upon my grief, my grey discrownèd head,
Are they that owe my bounty for their bread.
With my own power my majesty they wound,
In the King’s name the King’s himself uncrowned;

div.p: So doth the dust destroy the diamond. 15

lg.l: They promise to erect my royal stem,
To make me great, to’ advance my diadem,
If I will first fall down, and worship them.
My life they prize at such a slender rate,

div.p: That in my absence they draw bills of hate, 20
To prove the King a traitor to the State.
Felons obtain more privilege than I;
They are allowed to answer ere they die:
’Tis death for me to ask the reason why.
But, sacred Saviour, with thy words I woo 25

lg.l: Thee to forgive, and not be bitter to
Such as Thou know’st do not know what they do.
Augment my patience, nullify my hate,
Preserve my issue, and inspire my mate;

div.p: Yet, though we perish, bless this Church and State. 30

head.label: CIII
head.hi: HORATIAN ODE UPON CROMWELL’S RETURN FROM IRELAND.

lg.l: The forward youth that would appear,
Must now forsake his Muses dear,
Nor in the shadows sing
His numbers languishing.

div.p: ’Tis time to leave the books in dust, 5

lg.l: And oil the unused armour’s rust,
Removing from the wall
The corslet of the hall.
So restless Cromwell could not cease

div.p: In the inglorious arts of peace, 10

lg.l: But through adventurous war
Urgèd his active star:
And like the three-forked lightning first,
Breaking the clouds where it was nurst,

div.p: Did thorough his own side 15

lg.l: His fiery way divide:
For ’tis all one to courage high
The emulous, or enemy;
And with such, to enclose

div.p: Is more than to oppose. 20

lg.l: Then burning through the air he went,
And palaces and temples rent;
And Cæsar’s head at last
Did through his laurels blast.

div.p: ’Tis madness to resist or blame 25

lg.l: The face of angry heaven’s flame;
And if we would speak true,
Much to the Man is due,
Who, from his private gardens, where

div.p: He lived reservèd and austere 30

lg.l: (As if his highest plot
To plant the bergamot,)
Could by industrious valour climb
To ruin the great work of time,

div.p: And cast the Kingdoms old 35

lg.l: Into another mould.
Though Justice against Fate complain,
And plead the ancient Rights in vain—
But those do hold or break

div.p: As men are strong or weak. 40

lg.l: Nature, that hateth emptiness,
Allows of penetration less,
And therefore must make room,
Where greater spirits come.

div.p: What field of all the Civil War 45

lg.l: Where his were not the deepest scar?
And Hampton shows what part
He had of wiser art,
Where, twining subtle fears with hope,

div.p: He wove a net of such a scope 50

lg.l: That Charles himself might chase
To Carsbrook’s narrow case;
That thence the royal actor borne
The tragic scaffold might adorn:

div.p: While round the armèd bands 55

lg.l: Did clap their bloody hands;
He nothing common did or mean
Upon that memorable scene,
But with his keener eye

div.p: The axe’s edge did try; 60

lg.l: Nor called the Gods, with vulgar spite,
To vindicate his helpless right;
But bowed his comely head
Down, as upon a bed.

div.p: —This was that memorable hour 65

lg.l: Which first assured the forcèd power:
So when they did design
The Capitol’s first line,
A Bleeding Head, where they begun,

div.p: Did fright the architects to run; 70

lg.l: And yet in that the State
Foresaw its happy fate!
And now the Irish are ashamed
To see themselves in one year tamed:

div.p: So much one man can do 75

lg.l: That does both act and know.
They can affirm his praises best,
And have, though overcome, confessed
How good he is, how just

div.p: And fit for highest trust; 80

lg.l: Nor yet grown stiffer with command,
But still in the Republic’s hand—
How fit he is to sway
That can so well obey!

div.p: He to the Commons’ feet presents 85

lg.l: A Kingdom for his first year’s rents,
And (what he may) forbears
His fame, to make it theirs:
And has his sword and spoils ungirt

div.p: To lay them at the Public’s skirt. 90

lg.l: So when the falcon high
Falls heavy from the sky,
She, having killed, no more does search
But on the next green bough to perch,

div.p: Where, when he first does lure, 95
The falconer has her sure.
—What may not then our Isle presume,
While victory his crest does plume?
What may not others fear,
If thus he crowns each year! 100

lg.l: As Cæsar he, ere long, to Gaul,
To Italy an Hannibal,
And to all states not free
Shall climacteric be.

div.p: The Pict no shelter now shall find 105

lg.l: Within his parti-coloured mind,
But from this valour, sad
Shrink underneath the plaid—
Happy, if in the tufted brake

div.p: The English hunter him mistake, 110

lg.l: Nor lay his hounds in near
The Caledonian deer.
But thou, the War’s and Fortune’s son,
March indefatigably on;

div.p: And for the last effect 115

lg.l: Still kept the sword erect:
Besides the force it has to fright
The spirits of the shady night,
The same arts that did gain

div.p: A power, must it maintain. 120

head.label: CIV
head.hi: ON THE LATE MASSACRE IN PIEMONT.

lg.l: Avenge, O Lord, thy slaughtered saints, whose bones
Lie scattered on the Alpine mountains cold;
Even them who kept thy truth so pure of old,
When all our fathers worshipped stocks and stones,

div.p: Forget not: in thy book record their groans 5
Who were thy sheep, and in their ancient fold
Slain by the bloody Piemontese that rolled
Mother with infant down the rocks. Their moans
The vales redoubled to the hills, and they
To heaven. Their martyred blood and ashes sow 10

lg.l: O’er all the Italian fields, where still doth sway
The triple tyrant; that from these may grow
A hundred fold, who, having learned thy way,
Early may fly the Babylonian woe.
First-born of Chaos, who so fair didst come
From the old Negro’s darksome womb!
Which, when it saw the lovely child,
The melancholy mass put on kind looks and smiled:

div.p: Thou tide of glory which no rest dost know, 5
But ever ebb and ever flow!
Thou golden shower of a true Jove!
Who does in thee descend, and heaven to earth make love!
Say, from what golden quivers of the sky
Do all thy wingèd arrows fly? 10
Swiftness and power by birth are thine;
From thy great sire they came, thy sire, the Word Divine.
’Tis, I believe, this archery to show,
That so much cost in colours thou
And skill in painting dost bestow 15

lg.l: Upon thy ancient arms, the gaudy heavenly bow.
Swift as light thoughts their empty carriere run,
Thy race is finished when begun;
Let a post-angel start with thee,

div.p: And thou the goal of earth shalt reach as soon as he. 20

lg.l: Thou in the moon’s bright chariot proud and gay
Dost thy bright wood of stars survey;
And all the year dost with thee bring
Of thousand flowery lights thine own nocturnal spring.

div.p: Thou, Scythian-like, dost round thy lands, above 25

lg.l: The sun’s gilt tent, for ever move;
And still as thou in pomp dost go,
The shining pageants of the world attend thy show.
Nor amidst all these triumphs dost thou scorn

div.p: The humble glowworms to adorn, 30

lg.l: And with those living spangles gild
(O greatness without pride!) the bushes of the field.
Night and her ugly subjects dost thou fright,
And sleep, the lazy owl of night;

div.p: Ashamed and fearful to appear, 35

lg.l: They screen their horrid shapes with the black hemisphere.
With them there hastes, and wildly takes the alarm,
Of painted dreams a busy swarm;
At the first opening of thine eye

div.p: The various clusters break, the antic atoms fly. 40

lg.l: When, Goddess, thou lift’st up thy wakened head
Out of the Morning’s purple bed,
Thy choir of birds about thee play,
And all thy joyful world salutes the rising day.

div.p: All the world’s bravery that delights our eyes, 45

lg.l: Is but thy several liveries;
Thou the rich dye on them bestowest,
Thy nimble pencil paints this landscape as thou goest.
A crimson garment in the rose thou wear’st;

div.p: A crown of studded gold thou bear’st; 50

lg.l: The virgin lilies, in their white,
Are clad but with the lawn of almost naked light.
The violet, spring’s little infant, stands
Girt in thy purple swaddling-bands;

div.p: On the fair tulip thou dost dote, 55

lg.l: Thou cloth’st it in a gay and parti-coloured coat.
With flame condensed thou dost thy jewels fix,
And solid colours in it mix:
Flora herself envies to see

div.p: Flowers fairer than her own, and durable as she. 60

lg.l: Through the soft ways of heaven and air and sea,
Which open all their pores to thee,
Like a clear river thou dost glide,
And with thy living stream through the close channels slide.

div.p: But where firm bodies thy free course oppose, 65

lg.l: Gently thy source the land o’erflows;
Takes there possession, and does make,
Of colours’ mingled light, a thick and standing lake:
But the vast ocean of unbounded day

div.p: In the empyrean heaven does stay; 70
Thy rivers, lakes, and springs below
From thence took first their rise, thither at last must flow.

lg.l: Philosophy! the great and only heir
Of all that human knowledge which has been
Unforfeited by man’s rebellious sin,
Though full of years he do appear,

div.p: (Philosophy! I say, and call it He, 5

lg.l: For whatsoe’er the painter’s fancy be,
It a male virtue seems to me)
Has still been kept in nonage till of late,
Nor managed or enjoyed his vast estate.

div.p: Three or four thousand years, one would have thought, 10

lg.l: To ripeness and perfection might have brought
A science so well bred and nursed,
And of such hopeful parts, too, at the first;
But oh! the guardians and the tutors then,

div.p: (Some negligent, some ambitious men) 15

lg.l: Would ne’er consent to set him free,
Or his own natural powers to let him see,
Lest that should put an end to their authority.
That his own business he might quite forget,

div.p: They’ amused him with the sports of wanton wit; 20

lg.l: With the deserts of poetry they fed him,
Instead of solid meats to’ increase his force;
Instead of vigorous exercise they led him
Into the pleasant labyrinths of ever-fresh discourse:

div.p: Instead of carrying him to see 25
The riches which do hoarded for him lie
In Nature’s endless treasury,
They chose his eye to entertain
(His curious, but not covetous, eye)
With painted scenes and pageants of the brain. 30
Some few exalted spirits this latter age has shown,
That laboured to assert the liberty
(From guardians who were now usurpers grown)
Of this old minor still, captived Philosophy;
But ’twas rebellion called, to fight 35

lg.l: For such a long-oppressèd right.
Bacon, at last, a mighty man! arose,
Whom a wise King and Nature chose
Lord Chancellor of both their laws,

div.p: And boldly undertook the injured pupil’s cause. 40

lg.l: Authority, which did a body boast,
Though ’twas but air condensed, and stalked about
Like some old giant’s more gigantic ghost,
To terrify the learnèd rout,

div.p: With the plain magic of true reason’s light 45

lg.l: He chased out of our sight,
Nor suffered living men to be misled
By the vain shadows of the dead:
To graves, from whence it rose, the conquered phantom fled.

div.p: He broke that monstrous god which stood, 50

lg.l: In midst of the orchard, and the whole did claim,
Which with a useless scythe of wood,
And something else not worth a name,
(Ridiculous and senseless terrors!) made

div.p: Children and superstitious men afraid. 55

lg.l: The orchard’s open now, and free:
Bacon has broke that scarecrow deity:
Come, enter all that will,
Behold the ripened fruit, come, gather now your fill!

div.p: Yet still, methinks, we fain would be 60

lg.l: Catching at the forbidden tree;
We would be like the Deity;
When truth and falsehood, good and evil, we
Without the senses’ aid within ourselves would see;

div.p: For ’tis God only who can find 65
All nature in his mind.
From words, which are but pictures of the thought
(Though we our thoughts from them perversely drew,)
To things, the mind’s right object, he it brought;
Like foolish birds to painted grapes we flew. 70

lg.l: He sought and gathered for our use the true;
And when on heaps the chosen bunches lay,
He pressed them wisely the mechanic way,
Till all their juice did in one vessel join,

div.p: Ferment into a nourishment divine, 75

lg.l: The thirsty soul’s refreshing wine.
Who to the life an exact piece would make,
Must not from others’ work a copy take;
No, not from Rubens or Vandyck;

div.p: Much less content himself to make it like 80

lg.l: The ideas and the images which lie
In his own fancy or his memory:
No, he before his sight must place
The natural and the living face;

div.p: The real object must command 85

lg.l: Each judgment of his eye and motion of his hand.
From these, and all long errors of the way,
In which our wandering predecessors went,
And, like the old Hebrews, many years did stray

div.p: In deserts, but of small extent, 90

lg.l: Bacon! like Moses, led us forth at last;
The barren wilderness he passed,
Did on the very border stand
Of the blessed Promised Land,

div.p: And from the mountain’s top of his exalted wit, 95

lg.l: Saw it himself, and showed us it.
But life did never to one man allow
Time to discover worlds, and conquer too;
Nor can so short a line sufficient be

div.p: To fathom the vast deeps of Nature’s sea: 100

lg.l: The work he did we ought to admire,
And were unjust if we should more require
From his few years, divided ’twixt the excess
Of low affliction and high happiness:

div.p: For who on things remote can fix his sight, 105

lg.l: That’s always in a triumph or a fight?
From you, great champions! we expect to get
These spacious countries but discovered yet;
Countries where yet, instead of Nature, we

div.p: Her images and idols worshipped see: 110

lg.l: These large and wealthy regions to subdue,
Though Learning has whole armies at command,
Quartered about in every land,
A better troop she ne’er together drew.

div.p: Methinks, like Gideon’s little band, 115

lg.l: God with design has picked out you,
To do these noble wonders by a few.
When the whole host He saw, they are, said He,
Too many to o’ercome for Me:

div.p: And now He chooses out his men, 120

lg.l: Much in the way that He did then:
Not those many, whom He found
Idly extended on the ground,
To drink, with their dejected head,

div.p: The stream, just so as by their mouths it fled: 125

lg.l: No; but those few who took the waters up,
And made of their laborious hands the cup.
Thus you prepared, and in the glorious fight
Their wondrous pattern too you take:

div.p: Their old and empty pitchers first they brake, 130

lg.l: And with their hands then lifted up the light.
Iö! sound too the trumpets here!
Already your victorious lights appear;
New scenes of heaven already we espy,

div.p: And crowds of golden worlds on high, 135

lg.l: Which from the spacious plains of earth and sea
Could never yet discovered be
By sailor’s or Chaldean’s watchful eye.
Nature’s great works no distance can obscure,

div.p: No smallness her near objects can secure: 140

lg.l: You’ have taught the curious sight to press
Into the privatest recess
Of her imperceptible littleness:
You’ have learned to read her smallest hand,

div.p: And well begun her deepest sense to understand. 145

lg.l: Mischief and true dishonour fall on those
Who would to laughter or to scorn expose
So virtuous and so noble a design,
So human for its use, for knowledge so divine.

div.p: The things which these proud men despise, and call 150

lg.l: Impertinent, and vain, and small,
Those smallest things of nature let me know,
Rather than all their greatest actions do.
Whoever would deposèd truth advance

div.p: Into the throne usurped from it, 155

lg.l: Must feel at first the blows of ignorance,
And the sharp points of envious wit.
So when, by various turns of the celestial dance,
In many thousand years

div.p: A star, so long unknown, appears, 160

lg.l: Though heaven itself more beauteous by it grow,
It troubles and alarms the world below,
Does to the wise a star, to fools a meteor, show.
With courage and success you the bold work begin;

div.p: Your cradle has not idle been; 165

lg.l: None e’er but Hercules and you would be
At five years’ age worthy a history:
And ne’er did fortune better yet
The historian to the story fit.

div.p: As you from all old errors free 170

lg.l: And purge the body of Philosophy,
So from all modern follies he
Has vindicated eloquence and wit:
His candid style like a clean stream does slide,

div.p: And his bright fancy all the way 175

lg.l: Does, like the sunshine, in it play;
It does like Thames, the best of rivers, glide,
Where the god does not rudely overturn,
But gently pour, the crystal urn,
And with judicious hand does the whole current guide.

div.p: ’T has all the beauties Nature can impart, 181
And all the comely dress, without the paint, of Art.

lg.l: No victor that in battle spent,
When he at night asleep doth lie
Rich in a conquered monarch’s tent,
E’er had so vain a dream as I.

div.p: Methought I saw the earliest shade 5

lg.l: And sweetest that the spring can spread,
Of jasmin, briar, and woodbine made;
And there I saw Clorinda dead.
Though dead she lay, yet could I see

div.p: No cypress nor no mourning yew; 10

lg.l: Nor yet the injured lover’s tree;
No willow near her coffin grew.
But all showed unconcerned to be,
As if just Nature there did strive

div.p: To be as pitiless as she 15

lg.l: Was to her lover when alive.
And now, methought, I lost all care,
In losing her; and was as free
As birds let loose into the air,

div.p: Or rivers that are got to sea. 20

lg.l: Methought Love’s monarchy was gone;
And whilst elective numbers sway,
Our choice and change makes power our own,
And those court us whom we obey.

div.p: Yet soon, now from my Princess free, 25

lg.l: I rather frantic grew than glad,
For subjects, getting liberty,
Get but a license to be mad.
Birds that are long in cages awed,

div.p: If they get out, awhile will roam; 30

lg.l: But straight want skill to live abroad,
Then pine and hover near their home.
And to the ocean rivers run
From being pent in banks of flowers;

div.p: Not knowing that the exhaling sun 35

lg.l: Will send them back in weeping showers.
Soon thus for pride of liberty
I low desires of bondage found;
And vanity of being free

div.p: Bred the discretion to be bound. 40

lg.l: But as dull subjects see too late
Their safety in monarchal reign,
Finding their freedom in a State
Is but proud strutting in a chain;

div.p: Then growing wiser, when undone, 45

lg.l: In winter nights sad stories sing
In praise of monarchs long since gone,
To whom their bells they yearly ring;
So now I mourned that she was dead,

div.p: Whose single power did govern me; 50
And quickly was by reason led
To find the harm of liberty.
Even so the lovers of this land
(Love’s empire in Clorinda gone)
Thought they were quit from Love’s command, 55

lg.l: And beauty’s world was all their own.
But lovers, who are Nature’s best
Old subjects, never long revolt;
They soon in passion’s war contest,

div.p: Yet in their march soon make a halt. 60
And those, when by my mandates brought
Near dead Clorinda, ceased to boast
Of freedom found, and wept for thought
Of their delightful bondage lost.
And now the day to night was turned, 65

lg.l: Or sadly night’s close mourning wore;
All maids for one another mourned,
That lovers now could love no more.
All lovers quickly did perceive

div.p: They had on earth no more to do 70

lg.l: Than civilly to take their leave,
As worthies that to dying go.
And now all quires her dirges sing,
In shades of cypress and of yew;

div.p: The bells of every temple ring, 75

lg.l: Where maids their withered garlands strew.
To such extremes did sorrow rise,
That it transcended speech and form,
And was so lost to ears and eyes

div.p: As seamen sinking in a storm. 80

lg.l: My soul, in sleep’s soft fetters bound,
Did now for vital freedom strive;
And straight, by horror waked, I found
The fair Clorinda still alive.

div.p: Yet she’s to me but such a light, 85

lg.l: As are the stars to those who know
We can at most but guess their height,
And hope they mind us here below.
What is the existence of man’s life
But open war, or slumbered strife?
Where sickness to his sense presents
The combat of the elements;

div.p: And never feels a perfect peace, 5

lg.l: Till death’s cold hand signs his release.
It is a storm, where the hot blood
Outvies in rage the boiling flood;
And each loud passion of the mind

div.p: Is like a furious gust of wind, 10

lg.l: Which bears his bark with many a wave,
Till he casts anchor in the grave.
It is a flower, which buds and grows,
And withers as the leaves disclose;

div.p: Whose spring and fall faint seasons keep, 15

lg.l: Like fits of waking before sleep:
Then shrinks into that fatal mould
Where its first being was enrolled.
It is a dream, whose seeming truth
