div.p: Is moralized in age and youth: 20

lg.l: Where all the comforts he can share
As wandering as his fancies are;
Till in the mist of dark decay
The dreamer vanish quite away.

div.p: It is a dial, which points out 25

lg.l: The sunset, as it moves about:
And shadows out in lines of night
The subtle stages of time’s flight,
Till all-obscuring earth hath laid

div.p: The body in perpetual shade. 30

lg.l: It is a weary interlude,
Which doth short joys, long woes include;
The world the stage, the prologue tears,
The acts vain hope, and varied fears:

div.p: The scene shuts up with loss of breath, 35
And leaves no epilogue but death.

lg.l: Let him that will, ascend the tottering seat
Of courtly grandeur, and become as great
As are his mounting wishes: as for me,
Let sweet repose and rest my portion be;

div.p: Give me some mean obscure recess, a sphere 5
Out of the road of business, or the fear
Of falling lower; where I sweetly may
Myself and dear retirement still enjoy:
Let not my life or name be known unto
The grandees of the time, tost to and fro 10

lg.l: By censures or applause; but let my age
Slide gently by; not overthwart the stage
Of public action; unheard, unseen,
And unconcerned, as if I ne’er had been.

div.p: And thus, while I shall pass my silent days 15
In shady privacy, free from the noise
And bustles of the mad world, then shall I
A good old innocent plebeian die.
Death is a mere surprise, a very snare
To him, that makes it his life’s greatest care 20
To be a public pageant; known to all,
But unacquainted with himself, doth fall.

lg.l: The voice which I did more esteem
Than music in her sweetest key,
Those eyes which unto me did seem
More comfortable than the day—

div.p: Those now by me, as they have been, 5

lg.l: Shall never more be heard or seen;
But what I once enjoyed in them
Shall seem hereafter as a dream.
All earthly comforts vanish thus;

div.p: So little hold of them have we, 10

lg.l: That we from them, or they from us,
May in a moment ravished be.
Yet we are neither just nor wise,
If present mercies we despise;

div.p: Or mind not how there may be made 15
A thankful use of what we had.

lg.l: In this marble casket lies
A matchless jewel of rich price;
Whom Nature in the world’s disdain
But showed, and put it up again.
False world, thou liest: thou canst not lend
The least delight:
Thy favours cannot gain a friend,
They are so slight:

div.p: Thy morning pleasures make an end 5

lg.l: To please at night:
Poor are the wants that thou suppliest:
And yet thou vaunt’st, and yet thou viest
With heaven; fond earth, thou boast’st; false world, thou liest.

div.p: Thy babbling tongue tells golden tales 10

lg.l: Of endless treasure:
Thy bounty offers easy sales
Of lasting pleasure:
Thou ask’st the conscience what she ails,

div.p: And swear’st to ease her; 15

lg.l: There’s none can want where thou suppliest,
There’s none can give where thou deniest;
Alas! fond world, thou boast’st; false world, thou liest.
What well-advisèd ear regards

div.p: What earth can say? 20

lg.l: Thy words are gold, but thy rewards
Are painted clay:
Thy cunning can but pack the cards,
Thou canst not play:

div.p: Thy game at weakest, still thou viest; 25

lg.l: If seen, and then revied, deniest:
Thou art not what thou seem’st; false world, thou liest.
Thy tinsel bosom seems a mint
Of new-coined treasure;

div.p: A paradise, that has no stint, 30

lg.l: No change, no measure;
A painted cask, but nothing in’t,
Nor wealth, nor pleasure.
Vain earth! that falsely thus compliest

div.p: With man; vain man, that thou reliest 35
On earth: vain man, thou doat’st; vain earth, thou liest.
What mean dull souls in this high measure
To haberdash
In earth’s base wares, whose greatest treasure
Is dross and trash; 40
The height of whose enchanting pleasure
Is but a flash?
Are these the goods that thou suppliest
Us mortals with? Are these the highest? 44
Can these bring cordial peace? False world, thou liest.

head.label: CXIII
head.hi: TO THE MEMORY OF MR. OLDHAM.

lg.l: Farewell, too little and too lately known,
Whom I began to think, and call my own;
For sure our souls were near allied, and thine
Cast in the same poetic mould with mine.

div.p: One common note on either lyre did strike, 5

lg.l: And knaves and fools we both abhorred alike.
To the same goal did both our studies drive;
The last set out, the soonest did arrive.
Thus Nisus fell upon the slippery place,

div.p: Whilst his young friend performed, and won the race. 10

lg.l: Oh early ripe! to thy abundant store
What could advancing age have added more?
It might (what nature never gives the young)
Have taught the numbers of thy native tongue.

div.p: But satire needs not those, and wit will shine 15

lg.l: Through the harsh cadence of a rugged line.
A noble error, and but seldom made,
When poets are by too much force betrayed;
Thy generous fruits, though gathered ere their prime,

div.p: Still showed a quickness; and maturing time 20

lg.l: But mellows what we write, to the dull sweets of rhyme.
Once more, hail, and farewell; farewell, thou young,
But, ah too short, Marcellus of our tongue!
Thy brows with ivy and with laurels bound;

div.p: But fate and gloomy night encompass thee around. 25

head.label: CXIV
head.hi: AN EPITAPH ON THE EXCELLENT COUNTESS OF HUNTINGDON.

lg.l: The chief perfection of both sexes joined,
With neither’s vice nor vanity combined;
Of this our age the wonder, love, and care,
The example of the following, and despair;

div.p: Such beauty, that from all hearts love must flow, 5

lg.l: Such majesty, that none durst tell her so;
A wisdom of so large and potent sway,
Rome’s Senate might have wished, her Conclave may:
Which did to earthly thoughts so seldom bow,

div.p: Alive she scarce was less in heaven than now; 10

lg.l: So void of the least pride, to her alone
These radiant excellencies seemed unknown;
Such once there was; but let thy grief appear,
Reader, there is not: Huntingdon lies here.
In this marble buried lies
Beauty may enrich the skies,
And add light to Phœbus’ eyes;
Sweeter than Aurora’s air,

div.p: When she paints the lilies fair, 5

lg.l: And gilds cowslips with her hair;
Chaster than the virgin spring,
Ere her blossoms she doth bring,
Or cause Philomel to sing.

div.p: If such goodness live ’mongst men, 10
Tell me it: I [shall] know then
She is come from heaven again.

head.label: CXVI
head.hi: ON THE RELIGIOUS MEMORY OF MRS. CATHERINE THOMSON, MY CHRISTIAN FRIEND.

lg.l: When Faith and Love, which parted from thee never,
Had ripened thy just soul to dwell with God,
Meekly thou didst resign this earthly load
Of death, called life; which us from life doth sever.

div.p: Thy works and alms, and all thy good endeavour, 5

lg.l: Stayed not behind, nor in the grave were trod;
But, as Faith pointed with her golden rod,
Followed thee up to joy and bliss for ever.
Love led them on, and Faith, who knew them best,

div.p: Thy handmaids, clad them o’er with purple beams 10

lg.l: And azure wings, that up they flew so drest,
And spake the truth of thee on glorious themes
Before the Judge; who thenceforth bid thee rest,
And drink thy fill of pure immortal streams.

head.label: CXVII
head.hi: AN EPITAPH UPON HUSBAND AND WIFE, WHO DIED AND WERE BURIED TOGETHER.

div.p: To these, whom death again did wed,
This grave’s their second marriage-bed;
For though the hand of Fate could force
’Twixt soul and body a divorce,
It could not sunder man and wife, 5
’Cause they both lived but one life.
Peace, good reader, do not weep;
Peace, the lovers are asleep:
They (sweet turtles) folded lie
In the last knot that love could tie. 10
And though they lie as they were dead,
Their pillow stone, their sheets of lead;
(Pillow hard, and sheets not warm)
Love made the bed, they’ll take no harm.
Let them sleep, let them sleep on, 15

lg.l: Till this stormy night be gone,
And the eternal morrow dawn;
Then the curtains will be drawn,
And they wake into that light,

div.p: Whose day shall never die in night. 20

lg.l: Here lies a piece of Christ; a star in dust;
A vein of gold; a china dish that must
Be used in heaven, when God shall feast the just.

head.label: CXIX
head.hi: EPITAPH ON COMPANIONS LEFT BEHIND IN THE NORTHERN SEAS.

lg.l: I were unkind unless that I did shed,
Before I part, some tears upon our dead:
And when my eyes be dry, I will not cease
In heart to pray their bones may rest in peace:

div.p: Their better parts (good souls) I know were given 5

lg.l: With an intent they should return to heaven:
Their lives they spent to the last drop of blood,
Seeking God’s glory and their country’s good.
And as a valiant soldier rather dies,

div.p: Than yields his courage to his enemies; 10

lg.l: And stops their way with his hewed flesh, when death
Hath quite deprived him of his strength and breath;
So have they spent themselves; and here they lie,
A famous mark of our discovery.

div.p: We that survive, perchance may end our days 15

lg.l: In some employment meriting no praise;
And in a dung-hill rot, when no man names
The memory of us, but to our shames.
They have outlived this fear, and their brave ends

div.p: Will ever be an honour to their friends. 20

lg.l: Why drop you so, mine eyes? Nay rather pour
My sad departure in a solemn shower.
The winter’s cold, that lately froze our blood,
Now were it so extreme, might do this good,

div.p: As make these tears bright pearls, which I would lay 25

lg.l: Tombed safely with you till doom’s fatal day;
That in this solitary place, where none
Will ever come to breathe a sigh or groan,
Some remnant might be extant of the true

div.p: And faithful love I ever tendered you. 30

lg.l: Oh! rest in peace, dear friends, and, let it be
No pride to say, the sometime part of me.
What pain and anguish doth afflict the head,
The heart, and stomach, when the limbs are dead;

div.p: So grieved, I kiss your graves, and vow to die, 35
A foster-father to your memory.

head.label: CXX
head.hi: EPITAPH ON THE LADY MARY VILLIERS.

lg.l: The Lady Mary Villiers lies
Under this stone: with weeping eyes
The parents that first gave her birth,
And their sad friends, laid her in earth.

div.p: If any of them, reader, were 5

lg.l: Known unto thee, shed a tear:
Or if thyself possess a gem,
As dear to thee as this to them,
Though a stranger to this place,

div.p: Bewail in their’s thine own hard case; 10
For thou perhaps at thy return
Mayst find thy darling in an urn.

lg.l: Accept, thou shrine of my dead saint,
Instead of dirges this complaint;
And for sweet flowers to crown thy hearse,
Receive a strew of weeping verse

div.p: From thy grieved friend, whom thou might’st see 5

lg.l: Quite melted into tears for thee.
Dear loss! since thy untimely fate,
My task hath been to meditate
On thee, on thee: thou art the book,

div.p: The library whereon I look, 10

lg.l: Though almost blind. For thee, loved clay,
I languish out, not live, the day,
Using no other exercise
But what I practise with mine eyes:

div.p: By which wet glasses I find out 15

lg.l: How lazily time creeps about
To one that mourns; this, only this,
My exercise and business is:
So I compute the weary hours

div.p: With sighs dissolvèd into showers. 20

lg.l: Nor wonder if my time go thus
Backward and most preposterous;
Thou hast benighted me; thy set
This eve of blackness did beget,

div.p: Who wast my day (though overcast 25

lg.l: Before thou hadst thy noontide past),
And I remember must in tears,
Thou scarce hadst seen so many years
As day tells hours. By thy clear sun

div.p: My love and fortune first did run; 30

lg.l: But thou wilt never more appear
Folded within my hemisphere,
Since both thy light and motion,
Like a fled star, is fall’n and gone,

div.p: And ’twixt me and my soul’s dear wish 35

lg.l: The earth now interposèd is,
Which such a strange eclipse doth make
As ne’er was read in almanack.
I could allow thee for a time

div.p: To darken me and my sad clime; 40

lg.l: Were it a month, a year, or ten,
I would thy exile live till then;
And all that space my mirth adjourn.
So thou wouldst promise to return;

div.p: And putting off thy ashy shroud 45
At length disperse this sorrow’s cloud.
But woe is me! the longest date
Too narrow is to calculate
These empty hopes: never shall I
Be so much blest as to descry 50

lg.l: A glimpse of thee, till that day come
Which shall the earth to cinders doom,
And a fierce fever must calcine
The body of this world like thine,

div.p: My little world! That fit of fire 55
Once off, our bodies shall aspire
To our souls’ bliss: then we shall rise,
And view ourselves with clearer eyes
In that calm region, where no night
Can hide us from each other’s sight. 60
Meantime, thou hast her, earth: much good
May my harm do thee. Since it stood
With Heaven’s will I might not call
Her longer mine, I give thee all
My short-lived right and interest 65

lg.l: In her, whom living I loved best:
With a most free and bounteous grief,
I give thee what I could not keep.
Be kind to her, and prithee look

div.p: Thou write into thy Doomsday book 70

lg.l: Each parcel of this rarity,
Which in thy casket shrined doth lie:
See that thou make thy reckoning straight,
And yield her back again by weight;

div.p: For thou must audit on thy trust 75

lg.l: Each grain and atom of this dust,
As thou wilt answer him that lent,
Not gave, thee, my dear monument.
So close the ground, and ’bout her shade

div.p: Black curtains draw; my bride is laid. 80

lg.l: Sleep on, my Love, in thy cold bed
Never to be disquieted!
My last good night! Thou wilt not wake
Till I thy fate shall overtake:

div.p: Till age, or grief, or sickness must 85
Marry my body to that dust
It so much loves; and fill the room
My heart keeps empty in thy tomb.
Stay for me there; I will not fail
To meet thee in that hallow vale. 90

lg.l: And think not much of my delay;
I am already on the way,
And follow thee with all the speed
Desire can make, or sorrows breed.

div.p: Each minute is a short degree, 95

lg.l: And every hour a step towards thee.
At night when I betake to rest,
Next morn I rise nearer my west
Of life, almost by eight hours’ sail,

div.p: Than when sleep breathed his drowsy gale. 100

lg.l: Thus from the sun my bottom steers,
And my day’s compass downward bears:
Nor labour I to stem the tide,
Through which to thee I swiftly glide.

div.p: ’Tis true, with shame and grief I yield, 105
Thou, like the van, first took’st the field,
And gotten hast the victory
In thus adventuring to die
Before me, whose more years might crave
A just precedence in the grave. 110

lg.l: But hark! my pulse, like a soft drum,
Beats my approach, tells thee I come;
And slow howe’er my marches be,
I shall at last sit down by thee.

div.p: The thought of this bids me go on, 115
And wait my dissolution
With hope and comfort. Dear (forgive
The crime) I am content to live
Divided, with but half a heart,
Till we shall meet and never part. 120

lg.l: Our life is only death! time that ensu’th
Is but the death of time that went before;
Youth is the death of childhood, age of youth;
Die once to God, and then thou diest no more.
As due by many titles, I resign
Myself to Thee, O God. First I was made
By Thee and for Thee; and, when I was decayed,
Thy blood bought that, the which before was thine:

div.p: I am thy son, made with Thyself to shine; 5

lg.l: Thy servant, whose pains Thou hast still repaid,
Thy sheep, thine image; and, till I betrayed
Myself, a temple of thy Spirit divine.
Why doth the devil then usurp on me?

div.p: Why doth he steal, nay, ravish that’s thy right? 10

lg.l: Except Thou rise, and for thine own work fight,
Oh! I shall soon despair, when I shall see
That Thou lov’st mankind well, yet wilt not choose me,
And Satan hates me, yet is loth to lose me.
Death, be not proud, though some have callèd thee
Mighty and dreadful, for thou art not so;
For those, whom thou think’st thou dost overthrow,
Die not, poor Death; nor yet canst thou kill me.

div.p: From rest and sleep, which but thy picture be, 5

lg.l: Much pleasure, then from thee much more must flow:
And soonest our best men with thee do go,
Rest of their bones, and soul’s delivery.
Thou’rt slave to fate, chance, kings, and desperate men,

div.p: And dost with poison, war, and sickness dwell; 10
And poppy’ or charms can make us sleep as well,
And better than thy stroke. Why swell’st thou then?
One short sleep past, we wake eternally;
And death shall be no more; Death, thou shalt die.

lg.l: Yet once more, O ye laurels, and once more,
Ye myrtles brown, with ivy never-sere,
I come to pluck your berries harsh and crude;
And, with forced fingers rude,

div.p: Shatter your leaves before the mellowing year: 5

lg.l: Bitter constraint, and sad occasion dear,
Compels me to disturb your season due:
For Lycidas is dead, dead ere his prime,
Young Lycidas, and hath not left his peer.

div.p: Who would not sing for Lycidas? he knew 10

lg.l: Himself to sing, and build the lofty rhyme.
He must not float upon his watery bier
Unwept, and welter to the parching wind,
Without the meed of some melodious tear.

div.p: Begin then, Sisters of the sacred well, 15

lg.l: That from beneath the seat of Jove doth spring;
Begin, and somewhat loudly sweep the string.
Hence with denial vain, and coy excuse:
So may some gentle Muse

div.p: With lucky words favour my destined urn; 20

lg.l: And as he passes turn,
And bid fair peace be to my sable shroud.
For we were nursed upon the self-same hill,
Fed the same flock, by fountain, shade, and rill.

div.p: Together both, ere the high lawns appeared 25

lg.l: Under the opening eyelids of the Morn,
We drove a-field, and both together heard
What time the gray-fly winds her sultry horn,
Battening our flocks with the fresh dews of night,

div.p: Oft till the star that rose at evening, bright, 30

lg.l: Toward heaven’s descent had sloped his westering wheel.
Meanwhile the rural ditties were not mute,
Tempered to the oaten flute;
Rough Satyrs danced, and Fauns with cloven heel

div.p: From the glad sound would not be absent long; 35

lg.l: And old Damœtas loved to hear our song.
But, oh the heavy change, now thou art gone,
Now thou art gone and never must return!
Thee, Shepherd, thee the woods and desert caves,

div.p: With wild thyme and the gadding vine o’ergrown, 40

lg.l: And all their echoes, mourn:
The willows and the hazel copses green
Shall now no more be seen
Fanning their joyous leaves to thy soft lays.

div.p: As killing as the canker to the rose, 45

lg.l: Or taint-worm to the weanling herds that graze,
Or frost to flowers, that their gay wardrobe wear,
When first the white-thorn blows;
Such, Lycidas, thy loss to shepherds’ ear.

div.p: Where were ye, Nymphs, when the remorseless deep 50

lg.l: Closed o’er the head of your loved Lycidas?
For neither were ye playing on the steep,
Where your old bards, the famous Druids, lie,
Nor on the shaggy top of Mona high,

div.p: Nor yet where Deva spreads her wizard stream: 55

lg.l: Ay me! I fondly dream!
Had ye been there—for what could that have done
What could the Muse herself that Orpheus bore,
The Muse herself, for her enchanting son,

div.p: Whom universal Nature did lament, 60

lg.l: When by the rout that made the hideous roar
His gory visage down the stream was sent,
Down the swift Hebrus, to the Lesbian shore?
Alas! what boots it with incessant care

div.p: To tend the homely, slighted, shepherd’s trade, 65

lg.l: And strictly meditate the thankless Muse?
Were it not better done, as others use,
To sport with Amaryllis in the shade,
Or with the tangles of Neæra’s hair?

div.p: Fame is the spur that the clear spirit doth raise— 70

lg.l: That last infirmity of noble mind—
To scorn delights, and live laborious days;
But the fair guerdon when we hope to find,
And think to burst out into sudden blaze,

div.p: Comes the blind Fury with the abhorrèd shears, 75

lg.l: And slits the thin-spun life. ‘But not the praise,’
Phœbus replied, and touched my trembling ears;
‘Fame is no plant that grows on mortal soil,
Nor in the glistering foil

div.p: Set-off to the world, nor in broad rumour lies; 80

lg.l: But lives, and spreads aloft by those pure eyes,
And perfect witness of all-judging Jove;
As he pronounces lastly on each deed,
Of so much fame in heaven expect thy meed.’

div.p: O fountain Arethuse, and thou honoured flood, 85

lg.l: Smooth-sliding Mincius, crowned with vocal reeds,
That strain I heard was of a higher mood:
But now my oat proceeds,
And listens to the herald of the sea

div.p: That came in Neptune’s plea. 90

lg.l: He asked the waves, and asked the felon winds,
What hard mishap hath doomed this gentle swain?
And questioned every gust of rugged wings
That blows from off each beakèd promontory:

div.p: They knew not of his story; 95

lg.l: And sage Hippotades their answer brings,
That not a blast was from his dungeon strayed;
The air was calm, and on the level brine
Sleek Panope with all her sisters played.

div.p: It was that fatal and perfidious bark, 100

lg.l: Built in the eclipse, and rigged with curses dark,
That sunk so low that sacred head of thine.
Next Camus, reverend sire, went footing slow,
His mantle hairy, and his bonnet sedge,

div.p: Inwrought with figures dim, and on the edge 105

lg.l: Like to that sanguine flower inscribed with woe.
‘Ah! who hath reft (quoth he) my dearest pledge?’
Last came, and last did go,
The pilot of the Galilean lake;

div.p: Two massy keys he bore of metals twain, 110
(The golden opes, the iron shuts amain,)
He shook his mitred locks, and stern bespake,
‘How well could I have spared for thee, young swain,
Enow of such as for their bellies’ sake
Creep, and intrude, and climb into the fold! 115

lg.l: Of other care they little reckoning make,
Than how to scramble at the shearers’ feast,
And shove away the worthy bidden guest;
Blind mouths! that scarce themselves know how to hold

div.p: A sheep-hook, or have learned aught else the least 120

lg.l: That to the faithful herdman’s art belongs!
What recks it them? What need they? They are sped;
And, when they list, their lean and flashy songs
Grate on their scrannel pipes of wretched straw;

div.p: The hungry sheep look up, and are not fed, 125

lg.l: But, swoln with wind and the rank mist they draw,
Rot inwardly, and foul contagion spread:
Beside what the grim wolf with privy paw
Daily devours apace, and nothing said:

div.p: But that two-handed engine at the door 130

lg.l: Stands ready to smite once, and smite no more.’
Return, Alpheus, the dread voice is past
That shrunk thy streams; return, Sicilian Muse,
And call the vales, and bid them hither cast

div.p: Their bells, and flowerets of a thousand hues. 135

lg.l: Ye valleys low, where the mild whispers use
Of shades, and wanton winds, and gushing brooks,
On whose fresh lap the swart-star sparely looks,
Throw hither all your quaint enamelled eyes,

div.p: That on the green turf suck the honied showers, 140

lg.l: And purple all the ground with vernal flowers.
Bring the rathe primrose that forsaken dies,
The tufted crow-toe, and pale jessamine,
The white pink, and the pansy freaked with jet,

div.p: The glowing violet, 145

lg.l: The musk-rose, and the well-attired woodbine,
With cowslips wan that hang the pensive head,
And every flower that sad embroidery wears:
Bid amaranthus all his beauty shed,

div.p: And daffodillies fill their cups with tears, 150

lg.l: To strew the laureat hearse where Lycid lies.
For, so to interpose a little ease,
Let our frail thoughts dally with false surmise;
Ay me! whilst thee the shores and sounding seas

div.p: Wash far away, where’er thy bones are hurled, 155

lg.l: Whether beyond the stormy Hebrides,
Where thou perhaps, under the whelming tide,
Visit’st the bottom of the monstrous world;
Or whether thou, to our moist vows denied,

div.p: Sleep’st by the fable of Bellerus old, 160

lg.l: Where the great Vision of the guarded Mount
Looks towards Namancos and Bayona’s hold.
Look homeward, Angel, now, and melt with ruth:
And, O ye dolphins, waft the hapless youth.

div.p: Weep no more, woful shepherds, weep no more; 165

lg.l: For Lycidas, your sorrow, is not dead,
Sunk though he be beneath the watery floor;
So sinks the day-star in the ocean-bed,
And yet anon repairs his drooping head,

div.p: And tricks his beams, and with new-spangled ore 170

lg.l: Flames in the forehead of the morning sky:
So Lycidas sunk low, but mounted high,
Through the dear might of Him that walked the waves,
Where, other groves and other streams along,

div.p: With nectar pure his oozy locks he laves, 175

lg.l: And hears the unexpressive nuptial song,
In the blest kingdoms meek of joy and love.
There entertain him all the saints above
In solemn troops and sweet societies,

div.p: That sing and, singing, in their glory move, 180

lg.l: And wipe the tears for ever from his eyes.
Now, Lycidas, the shepherds weep no more;
Henceforth thou art the Genius of the shore,
In thy large recompense, and shalt be good

div.p: To all that wander in that perilous flood. 185

lg.l: Thus sang the uncouth swain to the oaks and rills,
While the still Morn went out with sandals gray;
He touched the tender stops of various quills,
With eager thought warbling his Doric lay:

div.p: And now the sun had stretched out all the hills, 190

lg.l: And now was dropt into the western bay;
At last he rose, and twitched his mantle blue;
To-morrow to fresh woods and pastures new.

head.label: CXXVI
head.hi: THE CHRISTIAN’S REPLY TO THE PHILOSOPHER.

lg.l: The good in graves as heavenly seed are sown;
And at the saints’ first spring, the general doom,
Will rise, not by degrees, but fully blown;
When all the angels to their harvest come.

div.p: Cannot Almighty Heaven (since flowers which pass 5

lg.l: Thawed through a still, and there melt mingled too,
Are raised distinct in a poor chymist’s glass)
Do more in graves than men in limbecs do?
God bred the arts, to make us more believe

div.p: (By seeking nature’s covered mysteries,) 10

lg.l: His darker works, that faith may thence conceive
He can do more than what our reason sees.
O coward faith! religion’s trembling guide!
Whom ev’n the dim-eyed arts must lead to see

div.p: What nature only from our sloth does hide, 15

lg.l: Causes remote, which faith’s dark dangers be.
Religion, ere imposed, should first be taught;
Not seem to dull obedience ready laid,
Then swallowed straight for ease, but long be sought;

div.p: And be by reason counselled, though not swayed. 20

lg.l: God has enough to human kind disclosed;
Our fleshly garments He a while received,
And walked as if the Godhead were deposed,
Yet could be then but by a few believed.

div.p: The faithless Jews will this at doom confess, 25

lg.l: Who did suspect Him for his low disguise:
But, if He could have made his virtue less,
He had been more familiar to their eyes.
Frail life! in which, through mists of human breath

div.p: We grope for truth, and make our progress slow, 30

lg.l: Because by passion blinded; till, by death
Our passions ending, we begin to know.
O reverend death! whose looks can soon advise
Even scornful youth, whilst priests their doctrine waste;

div.p: Yet mocks us too; for he does make us wise, 35

lg.l: When by his coming our affairs are past.
O harmless death! whom still the valiant brave,
The wise expect, the sorrowful invite,
And all the good embrace, who know the grave
A short dark passage to eternal light.
How soon doth man decay!
When clothes are taken from a chest of sweets
To swaddle infants, whose young breath
Scarce knows the way;

div.p: Those clouts are little winding-sheets, 5

lg.l: Which do consign and send them unto death.
When boys go first to bed,
They step into their voluntary graves;
Sleep binds them fast; only their breath

div.p: Makes them not dead. 10

lg.l: Successive nights, like rolling waves,
Convey them quickly, who are bound for death.
When youth is frank and free,
And calls for music, while his veins do swell,

div.p: All day exchanging mirth and breath 15

lg.l: In company;
That music summons to the knell,
Which shall befriend him at the house of death.
When man grows staid and wise,

div.p: Getting a house and home, where he may move 20

lg.l: Within the circle of his breath,
Schooling his eyes;
That dumb inclosure maketh love
Unto the coffin, that attends his death.

div.p: When age grows low and weak, 25

lg.l: Marking his grave, and thawing every year,
Till all do melt, and drown his breath,
When he would speak;
A chair or litter shows the bier

div.p: Which shall convey him to the house of death. 30

lg.l: Man, ere he is aware,
Hath put together a solemnity,
And dressed his hearse, while he has breath
As yet to spare.

div.p: Yet, Lord, instruct us so to die, 35
That all these dyings may be life in death.

lg.l: Happy those early days, when I
Shined in my angel-infancy!
Before I understood this place
Appointed for my second race,

div.p: Or taught my soul to fancy aught 5

lg.l: But a white celestial thought;
When yet I had not walked above
A mile or two from my first Love,
And looking back, at that short space,

div.p: Could see a glimpse of his bright face; 10

lg.l: When on some gilded cloud or flower
My gazing soul would dwell an hour,
And in those weaker glories spy
Some shadows of eternity;

div.p: Before I taught my tongue to wound 15

lg.l: My conscience with a sinful sound,
Or had the black art to dispense
A several sin to every sense,
But felt through all this fleshly dress

div.p: Bright shoots of everlastingness. 20

lg.l: Oh how I long to travel back,
And tread again that ancient track!
That I might once more reach that plain
Where first I left my glorious train;

div.p: From whence the enlightened spirit sees 25

lg.l: That shady City of palm-trees.
But ah! my soul with too much stay
Is drunk, and staggers in the way!
Some men a forward motion love,

div.p: But I by backward steps would move; 30
And when this dust falls to the urn,
In that state I came return.

lg.l: See, how the orient dew,
Shed from the bosom of the morn
Into the blowing roses,
Yet careless of its mansion new,

div.p: For the clear region where ’twas born, 5

lg.l: Round in itself incloses,
And in its little globe’s extent,
Frames, as it can, its native element.
How it the purple flower does slight,

div.p: Scarce touching where it lies; 10

lg.l: But gazing back upon the skies,
Shines with a mournful light,
Like its own tear,
Because so long divided from the sphere;

div.p: Restless it rolls, and unsecure, 15

lg.l: Trembling, lest it grow impure;
Till the warm sun pities its pain,
And to the skies exhales it back again.
So the soul, that drop, that ray,

div.p: Of the clear fountain of eternal day, 20

lg.l: Could it within the human flower be seen,
Remembering still its former height,
Shuns the sweet leaves, the blossoms green;
And, recollecting its own light,

div.p: Does, in its pure and circling thoughts, express 25

lg.l: The greater heaven in a heaven less.
In how coy a figure wound,
Every way it turns away:
So the world excluding round,

div.p: Yet receiving in the day; 30

lg.l: Dark beneath, but bright above;
Here disdaining, there in love.
How loose and easy hence to go;
How girt and ready to ascend;

div.p: Moving but on a point below, 35

lg.l: It all about does upward bend.
Such did the manna’s sacred dew distil,
White and entire, although congealed and chill;
Congealed on earth; but does, dissolving, run

div.p: Into the glories of the almighty Sun. 40

lg.l: My soul, there is a country,
Afar beyond the stars,
Where stands a wingèd sentry,
All skilful in the wars.

div.p: There, above noise and danger, 5

lg.l: Sweet peace sits crowned with smiles,
And One born in a manger
Commands the beauteous files.
He is thy gracious friend,

div.p: And (O my soul, awake!) 10

lg.l: Did in pure love descend,
To die here for thy sake.
If thou canst get but thither,
There grows the flower of peace,

div.p: The rose that cannot wither, 15

lg.l: Thy fortress, and thy ease.
Leave then thy foolish ranges;
For none can thee secure,
But One who never changes,

div.p: Thy God, thy Life, thy Cure. 20

lg.l: The night is come, like to the day;
Depart not Thou, great God, away.
Let not my sins, black as the night,
Eclipse the lustre of thy light.

div.p: Keep still in my horizon; for to me 5

lg.l: The sun makes not the day, but Thee.
Thou whose nature cannot sleep,
On my temples sentry keep!
Guard me ’gainst those watchful foes,

div.p: Whose eyes are open while mine close; 10

lg.l: Let no dreams my head infest,
But such as Jacob’s temples blest.
While I do rest, my soul advance;
Make me to sleep a holy trance.

div.p: That I may, my rest being wrought, 15

lg.l: Awake into some holy thought;
And with as active vigour run
My course as doth the nimble sun.
Sleep is a death; oh! make me try,

div.p: By sleeping, what it is to die: 20

lg.l: And as gently lay my head
On my grave, as now my bed.
Howe’er I rest, great God, let me
Awake again at last with Thee.

div.p: And thus assured, behold I lie 25

lg.l: Securely, or to wake or die.
These are my drowsy days; in vain
I do now wake to sleep again:
Oh! come that hour, when I shall never

div.p: Sleep again, but wake for ever. 30

lg.l: Vain world, what is in thee?
What do poor mortals see,
Which should esteemèd be
Worthy their pleasure?

div.p: Is it the mother’s womb, 5

lg.l: Or sorrows which soon come,
Or a dark grave and tomb,
Which is their treasure?
How dost thou man deceive

div.p: By thy vain glory? 10

lg.l: Why do they still believe
Thy false history?
Is it children’s book and rod,
The labourer’s heavy load,

div.p: Poverty undertrod, 15

lg.l: The world desireth?
Is it distracting cares,
Or heart-tormenting fears,
Or pining grief and tears,

div.p: Which man requireth? 20
Or is it youthful rage,
Or childish toying;
Or is decrepit age
Worth man’s enjoying?
Is it deceitful wealth, 25

lg.l: Got by care, fraud, or stealth,
Or short uncertain health,
Which thus befool men?
Or do the serpent’s lies,

div.p: By the world’s flatteries 30

lg.l: And tempting vanities,
Still overrule them?
Or do they in a dream
Sleep out their season?

div.p: Or borne down by lust’s stream, 35

lg.l: Which conquers reason?
The silly lambs to-day
Pleasantly skip and play,
Whom butchers mean to slay

div.p: Perhaps to-morrow; 40

lg.l: In a more brutish sort
Do careless sinners sport,
Or in dead sleep still snort,
As near to sorrow;

div.p: Till life, not well begun, 45

lg.l: Be sadly ended,
And the web they have spun
Can ne’er be mended.
What is the time that’s gone,

div.p: And what is that to come? 50
Is it not now as none?
The present stays not.
Time posteth, oh how fast!
Unwelcome death makes haste;
None can call back what’s past— 55

lg.l: Judgment delays not.
Though God bring in the light,
Sinners awake not;
Because hell’s out of sight

div.p: They sin forsake not. 60

lg.l: Man walks in a vain show;
They know, yet will not know;
Sit still, when they should go;
But run for shadows;

div.p: While they might taste and know 65

lg.l: The living streams that flow,
And crop the flowers that grow,
In Christ’s sweet meadows.
Life’s better slept away

div.p: Than as they use it; 70

lg.l: In sin and drunken play
Vain men abuse it.
Malignant world, adieu!
Where no foul vice is new—

div.p: Only to Satan true, 75

lg.l: God still offended;
Though taught and warned by God,
And his chastising rod,
Keeps still the way that’s broad,

div.p: Never amended. 80
Baptismal vows some make,
But ne’er perform them;
If angels from heaven spake,
’Twould not reform them.
They dig for hell beneath, 85

lg.l: They labour hard for death,
Run themselves out of breath
To overtake it.
Hell is not had for naught,

div.p: Damnation’s dearly bought, 90

lg.l: And with great labour sought;
They’ll not forsake it.
Their souls are Satan’s fee—
He’ll not abate it;

div.p: Grace is refused that’s free, 95

lg.l: Mad sinners hate it.
Is this the world men choose,
For which they heaven refuse,
And Christ and grace abuse,

div.p: And not receive it? 100

lg.l: Shall I not guilty be
Of this in some degree,
If hence God would me free,
And I’d not leave it;

div.p: My soul, from Sodom fly, 105
Lest wrath there find thee;
Thy refuge-rest is nigh;
Look not behind thee!
There’s none of this ado, 110

lg.l: None of the hellish crew;
God’s promise is most true,
Boldly believe it.
My friends are gone before,

div.p: And I am near the shore; 115

lg.l: My soul stands at the door,
O Lord, receive it!
It trusts Christ and his merits,
The dead He raises;

div.p: Join it with blessed spirits, 120
Who sing thy praises.

head.label: CXXXIII
head.hi: HYMN FOR ADVENT; OR CHRIST’S COMING TO JERUSALEM IN TRIUMPH.

lg.l: Lord, come away,
Why dost Thou stay?
Thy road is ready: and thy paths, made strait,
With longing expectation wait

div.p: The consecration of thy beauteous feet. 5
Ride on triumphantly; behold we lay
Our lusts and proud wills in thy way.
Hosanna! welcome to our hearts. Lord, here
Thou hast a temple too, and full as dear
As that of Sion; and as full of sin; 10

lg.l: Nothing but thieves and robbers dwell therein,
Enter, and chase them forth, and cleanse the floor;
Crucify them, that they may never more
Profane that holy place,

div.p: Where Thou hast chose to set thy face. 15
And then if our stiff tongues shall be
Mute in the praises of thy Deity,
The stones out of the temple wall
Shall cry aloud, and call
Hosanna! and thy glorious footsteps greet. 20

lg.l: They are all gone into the world of light,
And I alone sit lingering here;
Their very memory is fair and bright,
And my sad thoughts doth clear.

div.p: It glows and glitters in my cloudy breast, 5

lg.l: Like stars upon some gloomy grove,
Or those faint beams in which this hill is drest,
After the sun’s remove.
I see them walking in an air of glory,

div.p: Whose light doth trample on my days; 10
My days, which are at best but dull and hoary,
Mere glimmering and decays.
O holy Hope! and high Humility!
High as the heavens above! 15

lg.l: These are your walks, and you have showed them me
To kindle my cold love.
Dear, beauteous death; the jewel of the just,
Shining nowhere but in the dark;

div.p: What mysteries do, lie beyond thy dust, 20

lg.l: Could man outlook that mark!
He that hath found some fledged bird’s nest may know,
At first sight, if the bird be flown;
But what fair dell or grove he sings in now,

div.p: That is to him unknown. 25

lg.l: And yet, as angels in some brighter dreams
Call to the soul when man doth sleep,
So some strange thoughts transcend our wonted themes,
And into glory peep.

div.p: If a star were confined into a tomb, 30

lg.l: Her captive flames must needs burn there;
But when the hand that locked her up gives room,
She’ll shine through all the sphere.
O Father of eternal life, and all

div.p: Created glories under Thee, 35

lg.l: Resume thy spirit from this world of thrall
Into true liberty.
Either disperse these mists, which blot and fill
My pérspective still as they pass;

div.p: Or else remove me hence unto that hill, 40
Where I shall need no glass.

lg.l: Happy the man, whose wish and care
A few paternal acres bound,
Content to breathe his native air,
In his own ground.

div.p: Whose herds with milk, whose fields with bread, 5

lg.l: Whose flocks supply him with attire;
Whose trees in summer yield him shade,
In winter fire.
Blest, who can unconcern’dly find

div.p: Hours, days, and years slide soft away, 10

lg.l: In health of body, peace of mind,
Quiet by day,
Sound sleep by night; study and ease,
Together mixed; sweet recreation,

div.p: And innocence, which most does please 15

lg.l: With meditation.
Thus let me live, unseen, unknown;
Thus unlamented let me die,
Steal from the world, and not a stone

div.p: Tell where I lie. 20

lg.l: All travellers at first incline
Where’er they see the fairest sign;
And, if they find the chambers neat,
And like the liquor and the meat,

div.p: Will call again, and recommend 5

lg.l: The Angel-inn to every friend.
What though the painting grows decayed,
The house will never lose its trade:
Nay, though the treacherous tapster Thomas

div.p: Hangs a new Angel two doors from us, 10

lg.l: As fine as daubers’ hands can make it,
In hopes that strangers may mistake it,
We think it both a shame and sin
To quit the true old Angel-inn.

div.p: Now this is Stella’s case in fact, 15

lg.l: An angel’s face a little cracked:
(Could poets or could painters fix
How angels look at thirty-six:)
This drew us in at first to find

div.p: In such a form an angel’s mind; 20

lg.l: And every virtue now supplies
The fainting rays of Stella’s eyes.
See at her levee crowding swains,
Whom Stella freely entertains

div.p: With breeding, humour, wit, and sense; 25

lg.l: And puts them but to small expense;
Their mind so plentifully fills,
And makes such reasonable bills,
So little gets for what she gives,

div.p: We really wonder how she lives; 30

lg.l: And, had her stock been less, no doubt
She must have long ago run out.
Then who can think we’ll quit the place,
When Doll hangs out a newer face?

div.p: Or stop and light at Chloe’s head, 35

lg.l: With scraps and leavings to be fed?
Then, Chloe, still go on to prate
Of thirty-six and thirty-eight;
Pursue your trade of scandal-picking,

div.p: Your hints that Stella is no chicken; 40

lg.l: Your inuendos, when you tell us
That Stella loves to talk with fellows;
And let me warn you to believe
A truth, for which your soul should grieve;

div.p: That, should you live to see the day 45

lg.l: When Stella’s locks must all be grey,
When age must print a furrowed trace
On every feature of her face;
Though you, and all your senseless tribe,

div.p: Could art, or time, or nature bribe, 50

lg.l: To make you look like Beauty’s Queen,
And hold for ever at fifteen;
No bloom of youth can ever blind
The cracks and wrinkles of your mind:

div.p: All men of sense will pass your door, 55
And crowd to Stella’s at fourscore.

head.label: CXXXVII
head.hi: ON THE PROSPECT OF PLANTING ARTS AND LEARNING IN AMERICA.

lg.l: The Muse, disgusted at an age and clime
Barren of every glorious theme,
In distant lands now waits a better time,
Producing subjects worthy fame.

div.p: In happy climes, where from the genial sun 5

lg.l: And virgin earth such scenes ensue,
The force of art by nature seems outdone,
And fancied beauties by the true.
In happy climes, the seat of innocence,

div.p: Where nature guides, and virtue rules, 10

lg.l: Where men shall not impose for truth and sense
The pedantry of courts and schools.
There shall be sung another Golden Age,
The rise of empire and of arts,

div.p: The good and great inspiring epic rage, 15

lg.l: The wisest heads and noblest hearts:
Not such as Europe breeds in her decay;
Such as she bred when fresh and young,
When heavenly flame did animate her clay,

div.p: By future poets shall be sung. 20

lg.l: Westward the course of empire take its way;
The four first acts already past,
A fifth shall close the drama with the day;
Time’s noblest offspring is the last.

head.label: CXXXVIII
head.hi: THE LAWYER’S FAREWELL TO HIS MUSE.

lg.l: As, by some tyrant’s stem command,
A wretch forsakes his native land,
In foreign climes condemned to roam,
An endless exile from his home;

div.p: Pensive he treads the destined way; 5

lg.l: And dreads to go; nor dares to stay;
Till on some neighbouring mountain’s brow
He stops, and turns his eyes below;
There, melting at the well-known view,

div.p: Drops a last tear, and bids adieu: 10

lg.l: So I, thus doomed from thee to part,
Gay Queen of fancy and of art,
Reluctant move, with doubtful mind,
Oft stop, and often look behind.

div.p: Companion of my tender age, 15

lg.l: Serenely gay, and sweetly sage,
How blithsome were we wont to rove
By verdant hill, or shady grove,
Where fervent bees with humming voice

div.p: Around the honied oak rejoice, 20

lg.l: And agèd elms with awful bend
In long cathedral walks extend!
Lulled by the lapse of gliding floods,
Cheered by the warbling of the woods,

div.p: How blest my days, my thoughts how free, 25

lg.l: In sweet society with thee!
Then all was joyous, all was young,
And years unheeded rolled along:
But now the pleasing dream is o’er,

div.p: These scenes must charm me now no more. 30

lg.l: Lost to the fields, and torn from you,—
Farewell! a long, a last adieu!
Me wrangling courts, and stubborn law,
To smoke, and crowds, and cities draw:

div.p: There selfish faction rules the day, 35

lg.l: And pride and avarice throng the way;
Diseases taint the murky air,
And midnight conflagrations glare;
Loose revelry, and riot bold,

div.p: In frighted streets their orgies hold; 40

lg.l: Or, where in silence all is drowned,
Fell murder walks his lonely round;
No room for peace, no room for you;
Adieu, celestial Nymph, adieu!

div.p: Shakspeare no more, thy sylvan son, 45

lg.l: Nor all the art of Addison,
Pope’s heaven-strung lyre, nor Waller’s ease,
Nor Milton’s mighty self, must please:
Instead of these a formal band,

div.p: In furs and coifs, around me stand; 50

lg.l: With sounds uncouth and accents dry,
That grate the soul of harmony,
Each pedant sage unlocks his store
Of mystic, dark, discordant lore;

div.p: And points with tottering hand the ways 55

lg.l: That lead me to the thorny maze.
There, in a winding close retreat,
Is Justice doomed to fix her seat;
There fenced by bulwarks of the law,

div.p: She keeps the wondering world in awe; 60

lg.l: And there, from vulgar sight retired,
Like eastern queens, is more admired.
O let me pierce the secret shade
Where dwells the venerable maid!

div.p: There humbly mark, with reverend awe, 65

lg.l: The guardian of Britannia’s law;
Unfold with joy her sacred page,
The united boast of many an age;
Where mixed, yet uniform, appears

div.p: The wisdom of a thousand years; 70

lg.l: In that pure spring the bottom view,
Clear, deep, and regularly true;
And other doctrines thence imbibe
Than lurk within the sordid scribe;

div.p: Observe how parts with parts unite 75

lg.l: In one harmonious rule of right;
See countless wheels distinctly tend
By various laws to one great end:
While mighty Alfred’s piercing soul

div.p: Pervades and regulates the whole. 80

lg.l: Then welcome business, welcome strife,
Welcome the cares, the thorns of life,
The visage wan, the pore-blind sight,
The toil by day, the lamp at night,

div.p: The tedious forms, the solemn prate, 85

lg.l: The pert dispute, the dull debate,
The drowsy bench, the babbling hall,
For thee, fair Justice, welcome all!
Thus though my noon of life be passed,

div.p: Yet let my setting sun, at last, 90

lg.l: Find out the still, the rural cell,
Where sage Retirement loves to dwell!
There let me taste the homefelt bliss
Of innocence, and inward peace;

div.p: Untainted by the guilty bribe, 95

lg.l: Uncursed amid the harpy tribe;
No orphan’s cry to wound my ear;
My honour and my conscience clear;
Thus may I calmly meet my end,

div.p: Thus to the grave in peace descend. 100

lg.l: A Juggler long through all the town
Had rais’d his fortune and renown;
You’d think (so far his art transcends)
The devil at his fingers’ ends.

div.p: Vice heard his fame, she read his bill; 5

lg.l: Convinced of his inferior skill,
She sought his booth, and from the crowd
Defied the man of art aloud.
‘Is this then he so famed for sleight?

div.p: Can this slow bungler cheat your sight? 10
Dares he with me dispute the prize?
I leave it to impartial eyes.’
Provoked, the Juggler cried, ’Tis done;
In science I submit to none.’
Thus said, the cups and balls he played; 15

lg.l: By turns this here, that there, conveyed.
The cards, obedient to his words,
Are by a fillip turned to birds.
His little boxes change the grain:

div.p: Trick after trick deludes the train. 20

lg.l: He shakes his bag, he shows all fair;
His fingers spread, and nothing there;
Then bids it rain with showers of gold;
And now his ivory eggs are told;

div.p: But, when from thence the hen he draws, 25

lg.l: Amazed spectators hum applause.
Vice now stept forth, and took the place,
With all the forms of his grimace.
‘This magic looking-glass,’ she cries,

div.p: ‘(There, hand it round) will charm your eyes.’ 30

lg.l: Each eager eye the sight desired,
And every man himself admired.
Next, to a senator addressing,
‘See this bank-note; observe the blessing.

div.p: Breathe on the bill. Heigh, pass! ’tis gone.’ 35

lg.l: Upon his lips a padlock shown.
A second puff the magic broke;
The padlock vanished, and he spoke.
Twelve bottles ranged upon the board,

div.p: All full, with heady liquor stored, 40

lg.l: By clean conveyance disappear,
And now two bloody swords are there.
A purse she to a thief exposed;
At once his ready fingers closed.

div.p: He opes his fist, the treasure’s fled: 45
He sees a halter in its stead.
She bids Ambition hold a wand;
He grasps a hatchet in his hand.
A box of charity she shows.
‘Blow here;’ and a churchwarden blows. 50
’Tis vanish’d with conveyance neat,
And on the table smokes a treat.
She shakes the dice, the board she knocks,
And from all pockets fills her box.
A counter, in a miser’s hand, 55

lg.l: Grew twenty guineas at command.
She bids his heir the sum retain,
And ’tis a counter now again.
A guinea with her touch you see

div.p: Take every shape but Charity; 60

lg.l: And not one thing you saw, or drew,
But changed from what was first in view.
The Juggler now, in grief of heart,
With this submission owned her art:

div.p: ‘Can I such matchless sleight withstand? 65
How practice hath improved your hand!
But now and then I cheat the throng;
You every day, and all day long.’

lg.l: When Britain first at Heaven’s command
Arose from out the azure main,
This was the charter of her land,
And guardian angels sung the strain:

div.p: Rule Britannia! Britannia rules the waves! 5

lg.l: Britons never shall be slaves.
The nations not so blest as thee
Must in their turn to tyrants fall,
Whilst thou shalt flourish great and free,

div.p: The dread and envy of them all. 10

lg.l: Still more majestic shalt thou rise,
More dreadful from each foreign stroke;
As the loud blast that tears the skies
Serves but to root thy native oak.

div.p: Thee haughty tyrants ne’er shall tame; 15

lg.l: All their attempts to bend thee down
Will but arouse thy generous flame,
And work their woe and thy renown.
To thee belongs the rural reign;

div.p: Thy cities shall with commerce shine; 20

lg.l: All thine shall be the subject main,
And every shore it circles thine!
The Muses, still with Freedom found,
Shall to thy happy coast repair;

div.p: Blest Isle, with matchless beauty crowned, 25
And manly hearts to guard the fair:—
Rule Britannia! Britannia rules the waves!
Britons never shall be slaves!
ON THE TAKING OF PORTO-BELLO BY ADMIRAL VERNON. NOV. 22, 1739.

lg.l: As near Porto-Bello lying
On the gently swelling flood,
At midnight with streamers flying
Our triumphant navy rode:

div.p: There while Vernon sat all-glorious 5

lg.l: From the Spaniards’ late defeat;
And his crews, with shouts victorious,
Drank success to England’s fleet;
On a sudden, shrilly sounding,

div.p: Hideous yells and shrieks were heard; 10

lg.l: Then each heart with fear confounding,
A sad troop of ghosts appeared,
All in dreary hammocks shrouded,
Which for winding-sheets they wore,

div.p: And with looks by sorrow clouded, 15

lg.l: Frowning on that hostile shore.
On them gleamed the moon’s wan lustre,
When the shade of Hosier brave
His pale bands was seen to muster,

div.p: Rising from their watery grave: 20

lg.l: O’er the glimmering wave he hied him,
Where the Burford reared her sail,
With three thousand ghosts beside him,
And in groans did Vernon hail:

div.p: ‘Heed, O heed, our fatal story. 25

lg.l: I am Hosier’s injured ghost,
You, who now have purchased glory
At this place where I was lost;
Though in Porto-Bello’s ruin

div.p: You now triumph free from fears, 30

lg.l: When you think on our undoing,
You will mix your joy with tears.
‘See these mournful spectres, sweeping
Ghastly o’er this hated wave,

div.p: Whose wan cheeks are stained with weeping; 35

lg.l: These were English captains brave:
Mark those numbers pale and horrid,
Those were once my sailors bold,
Lo! each hangs his drooping forehead,

div.p: While his dismal tale is told. 40

lg.l: ‘I, by twenty sail attended,
Did this Spanish town affright:
Nothing then its wealth defended
But my orders not to fight:

div.p: Oh! that in this rolling ocean 45

lg.l: I had cast them with disdain,
And obeyed my heart’s warm motion,
To have quelled the pride of Spain.
‘For resistance I could fear none,

div.p: But with twenty ships had done 50

lg.l: What thou, brave and happy Vernon,
Hast achieved with six alone.
Then the Bastimentos never
Had our foul dishonour seen,

div.p: Nor the sea the sad receiver 55

lg.l: Of this gallant train had been.
‘Thus, like thee, proud Spain dismaying,
And her galleons leading home,
Though condemned for disobeying,

div.p: I had met a traitor’s doom; 60

lg.l: To have fall’n, my country crying
He has played an English part,
Had been better far than dying
Of a grieved and broken heart.

div.p: ‘Unrepining at thy glory, 65

lg.l: Thy successful arms we hail;
But remember our sad story,
And let Hosier’s wrongs prevail;
Sent in this foul clime to languish,

div.p: Think what thousands fell in vain, 70

lg.l: Wasted with disease and anguish,
Not in glorious battle slain.
‘Hence, with all my train attending
From their oozy tombs below,

div.p: Through the hoary foam ascending, 75

lg.l: Here I feed my constant woe:
Here the Bastimentos viewing,
We recall our shameful doom,
And our plaintive cries renewing,

div.p: Wander through the midnight gloom. 80

lg.l: ‘O’er these waves for ever mourning
Shall we roam, deprived of rest,
If to Britain’s shores returning,
You neglect my just request.

div.p: After this proud foe subduing, 85

lg.l: When your patriot friends you see,
Think on vengeance for my ruin,
And for England shamed in me.’

div.p: I’ve heard them lilting at our ewe-milking,
Lasses a’ lilting before dawn o’ day;
But now they are moaning on ilka green loaning—
The Flowers of the Forest are a’ wede away. 4

lg.l: At bughts, in the morning, nae blythe lads are scorning,
Lassies are lonely and dowie and wae;
Nae daffin’, nae gabbin’, but sighing and sabbing,
Ilk ane lifts her leglin, and hies her away.
In har’st, at the shearing, nae youths now are jeering,

div.p: Bandsters are lyart, and runkled, and gray; 10
At fair or at preaching, nae wooing, nae fleeching—
The Flowers of the Forest are a’ wede away.
At e’en, in the gloaming, nae younkers are roaming
’Bout stacks wi’ the lasses at bogle to play;
But ilk ane sits drearie, lamenting her dearie— 15
The Flowers of the Forest are weded away.
’Dool and wae for the order, sent our lads to the Border!
The English, for ance, by guile wan the day;
The Flowers of the Forest, that fought aye the foremost,
The prime of our land, are cauld in the clay. 20

lg.l: We’ll hear nae mair lilting at the ewe-milking;
Women and bairns are heartless and wae;
Sighing and moaning on ilka green loaning—
The Flowers of the Forest are a’ wede away.
A wee bird came to our ha’ door;
He warbled sweet and clearly;
And aye the o’ercome o’ his sang
Was ‘Wae’s me for Prince Charlie!’

div.p: Oh! when I heard the bonny, bonny bird, 5

lg.l: The tears came drapping rarely;
I took my bonnet aff my head,
For weel I lo’ed Prince Charlie.
Quoth I; ‘My bird, my bonny, bonny bird,

div.p: Is that a tale ye borrow? 10

lg.l: Or is’t some words ye’ve learned by rote,
Or a lilt o’ dool and sorrow?’
Oh no, no, no,’ the wee bird sang,
‘I’ve flown sin’ morning early;

div.p: But sic a day o’ wind and rain— 15

lg.l: Oh wae’s me for Prince Charlie!
O’er hills that are by right his ain
He roams a lonely stranger;
On ilka hand he’s pressed by want,

div.p: On ilka side by danger. 20

lg.l: Yestreen I met him in the glen,
My heart near bursted fairly:
For sadly changed indeed was he—
Oh! wae’s me for Prince Charlie!

div.p: ‘Dark night came on; the tempest howled 25

lg.l: Out owre the hills and valleys;
And whare was’t that your Prince lay down,
Whase hame should be a palace?
He rowed him in a Highland plaid,

div.p: Which covered him but sparely, 30

lg.l: And slept beneath a bush o’ broom—
Oh! wae’s me for Prince Charlie!’
But now the bird saw some red coats,
And he shook his wings wi’ anger:

div.p: ‘Oh, this is no a land for me— 35

lg.l: I’ll tarry here nae langer.’
A while he hovered on the wing,
Ere he departed fairly;
But weel I mind the farewell strain—

div.p: ’Twas ‘Wae’s me for Prince Charlie!’ 40
IN IMITATION OF ALCÆUS.

lg.l: What constitutes a State?
Not high-raised battlement or laboured mound,
Thick wall or moated gate;
Not cities proud with spires and turrets crowned;

div.p: Not bays and broad-armed ports, 5

lg.l: Where, laughing at the storm, rich navies ride;
Not starred and spangled courts,
Where low-browed baseness wafts perfume to pride.
No:—men, high-minded men,

div.p: With powers as far above dull brutes endued 10

lg.l: In forest, brake, or den,
As beasts excel cold rocks and brambles rude;
Men, who their duties know,
But know their rights, and, knowing, dare maintain,

div.p: Prevent the long-aimed blow, 15

lg.l: And crush the tyrant while they rend the chain:
These constitute a State,
And sovereign Law, that State’s collected will,
O’er thrones and globes elate,

div.p: Sits Empress, crowning good, repressing ill. 20

lg.l: Smit by her sacred frown,
The fiend, Dissension, like a vapour sinks,
And e’en the all-dazzling Crown
Hides his faint rays, and at her bidding shrinks.

div.p: Such was this heaven-loved isle, 25
Than Lesbos fairer and the Cretan shore!
No more shall Freedom smile?
Shall Britons languish, and be men no more?
Since all must life resign,
Those sweet rewards, which decorate the brave, 30
’Tis folly to decline,
And steal inglorious to the silent grave.
WRITTEN IN THE YEAR 1746.

lg.l: How sleep the brave, who sink to rest,
By all their country’s wishes blest!
When Spring, with dewy fingers cold,
Returns to deck their hallowed mould,

div.p: She there shall dress a sweeter sod 5

lg.l: Than Fancy’s feet have ever trod.
By fairy hands their knell is rung;
By forms unseen their dirge is sung;
There Honour comes, a pilgrim gray,

div.p: To bless the turf that wraps their clay; 10
And Freedom shall awhile repair,
To dwell a weeping hermit there!
Hail, beauteous stranger of the grove!
Thou messenger of spring!
Now Heaven repairs thy rural seat,
And woods thy welcome sing.
What time the daisy decks the green, 5

lg.l: Thy certain voice we hear;
Hast thou a star to guide thy path,
Or mark the rolling year?
Delightful visitant! with thee

div.p: I hail the time of flowers, 10

lg.l: And hear the sound of music sweet
From birds among the bowers.
The schoolboy, wandering through the wood
To pull the primrose gay,

div.p: Starts, the new voice of spring to hear, 15

lg.l: And imitates thy lay.
What time the pea puts on the bloom,
Thou fliest thy vocal vale,
An annual guest in other lands,

div.p: Another spring to hail. 20

lg.l: Sweet bird! thy bower is ever green,
Thy sky is ever clear;
Thou hast no sorrow in thy song,
No winter in thy year!

div.p: Oh could I fly, I’d fly with thee! 25

lg.l: We’d make, with joyful wing,
Our annual visit o’er the globe,
Companions of the spring.
If aught of oaten stop, or pastoral song,
May hope, chaste Eve, to soothe thy modest ear,
Like thy own solemn springs,
Thy springs, and dying gales;

div.p: O Nymph reserved, while now the bright-haired Sun 5

lg.l: Sits in yon western tent, whose cloudy skirts,
With brede ethereal wove,
O’erhang his wavy bed:
Now air is hushed, save where the weak-eyed bat,

div.p: With short shrill shriek flits by on leathern wing; 10

lg.l: Or where the beetle winds
His small but sullen horn,
As oft he rises ’midst the twilight path,
Against the pilgrim borne in heedless hum;

div.p: Now teach me, Maid composed, 15

lg.l: To breathe some softened strain,
Whose numbers, stealing through thy darkening vale,
May not unseemly with its stillness suit;
As, musing slow, I hail

div.p: Thy genial loved return! 20
For when thy folding-star arising shows
His paly circlet, at his warning lamp
The fragrant Hours, and Elves
Who slept in buds the day,
And many a Nymph who wreathes her brows with sedge, 25

lg.l: And sheds the freshening dew, and, lovelier still,
The pensive Pleasures sweet,
Prepare thy shadowy car.
Then let me rove some wild and heathy scene;

div.p: Or find some ruin ’midst its dreary dells, 30

lg.l: Whose walls more awful nod
By thy religious gleams.
Or, if chill blustering winds, or driving rain,
Prevent my willing feet, be mine the hut,

div.p: That from the mountain’s side 35

lg.l: Views wilds, and swelling floods,
And hamlets brown, and dim-discovered spires;
And hears their simple bell, and marks o’er all
Thy dewy fingers draw

div.p: The gradual dusky veil. 40

lg.l: While Spring shall pour his showers, as oft he wont,
And bathe thy breathing tresses, meekest Eve!
While Summer loves to sport
Beneath thy lingering light;

div.p: While sallow Autumn fills thy lap with leaves; 45

lg.l: Or Winter, yelling through the troublous air,
Affrights thy shrinking train,
And rudely rends thy robes;
So long, regardful of thy quiet rule,

div.p: Shall Fancy, Friendship, Science, smiling Peace, 50
Thy gentlest influence own,
And love thy favourite name!

lg.l: Wee, modest, crimson-tippèd flower,
Thou’s met me in an evil hour;
For I maun crush amang the stoure
Thy slender stem:

div.p: To spare thee now is past my power, 5

lg.l: Thou bonnie gem.
Alas! it’s no thy neebor sweet,
The bonnie lark, companion meet!
Bending thee ’mang the dewy weet

div.p: Wi’ speckled breast, 10

lg.l: When upward-springing, blithe, to greet
The purpling east.
Cauld blew the bitter-biting north
Upon thy early, humble birth;

div.p: Yet cheerfully thou glinted forth 15

lg.l: Amid the storm;
Scarce reared above the parent-earth
Thy tender form.
The flaunting flowers our gardens yield,

div.p: High sheltering woods and wa’s maun shield, 20

lg.l: But thou, beneath the random bield
O’ clod, or stane,
Adorns the histie stubble-field,
Unseen, alane.

div.p: There, in thy scanty mantle clad, 25

lg.l: Thy snawie bosom sunward spread,
Thou lifts thy unassuming head
In humble guise;
But now the share uptears thy bed,

div.p: And low thou lies! 30

lg.l: Such is the fate of artless maid,
Sweet floweret of the rural shade!
By love’s simplicity betrayed,
And guileless trust,

div.p: Till she, like thee, all soiled, is laid 35

lg.l: Low i’ the dust.
Such is the fate of simple bard,
On life’s rough ocean luckless-starred!
Unskilful he to note the card

div.p: Of prudent lore, 40

lg.l: Till billows rage, and gales blow hard,
And whelm him o’er!
Such fate to suffering worth is given,
Who long with wants and woes has striven,

div.p: By human pride or cunning driven 45

lg.l: To misery’s brink,
Till, wrenched of every stay but Heaven,
He, ruined, sink!
Even thou who mourn’st the Daisy’s fate,

div.p: That fate is thine—no distant date; 50

lg.l: Stern Ruin’s ploughshare drives, elate,
Full on thy bloom,
Till crushed beneath the furrow’s weight,
Shall be thy doom.

head.label: CXLIX
head.hi: ON THE DEATH OF RICHARD WEST.

lg.l: In vain to me the smiling mornings shine,
And reddening Phœbus lifts his golden fire,
The birds in vain their amorous descant join,
Or cheerful fields resume their green attire.

div.p: These ears, alas! for other notes repine, 5

lg.l: A different object do these eyes require;
My lonely anguish melts no heart but mine,
And in my breast the imperfect joys expire;
Yet morning smiles the busy race to cheer,

div.p: And new-born pleasure brings to happier men; 10

lg.l: The fields to all their wonted tribute bear,
To warm their little loves the birds complain;
I fruitless mourn to him that cannot hear,
And weep the more, because I weep in vain.
Bloom of beauty, early flower
Of the blissful bridal bower,
Thou, thy parents’ pride and care,
Fairest offspring of the fair,

div.p: Lovely pledge of mutual love, 5

lg.l: Angel seeming from above,
Was it not thou day by day
Dost thy very sex betray,
Female more and more appear,

div.p: Female, more than angel dear, 10
How to speak thy face and mien,
(Soon too dangerous to be seen)
How shall I, or shall the Muse,
Language of resemblance choose,
Language like thy mien and face, 15

lg.l: Full of sweetness, full of grace?
By the next returning spring,
When again the linnets sing,
When again the lambkins play,

div.p: Pretty sportlings full of May, 20

lg.l: When the meadows next are seen,
Sweet enamel, white and green,
And the year in fresh attire
Welcomes every gay desire,

div.p: Blooming on shalt thou appear 25

lg.l: More inviting than the year,
Fairer sight than orchard shows,
Which beside a river blows:
Yet another spring I see,

div.p: And a brighter bloom in thee: 30

lg.l: And another round of time,
Circling, still improves thy prime:
And beneath the vernal skies
Yet a verdure more shall rise,

div.p: Ere thy beauties, kindling slow, 35

lg.l: In each finished feature glow,
Ere in smiles and in disdain
Thou exert thy maiden reign,
Absolute to save or kill

div.p: Fond beholders at thy will. 40

lg.l: Happy thrice, and thrice again,
Happiest he of happy men,
Who, in courtship greatly sped,
Wins the damsel to his bed,

div.p: Bears the virgin prize away, 45

lg.l: Counting life one nuptial day:
For the dark-brown dusk of hair,
Shadowing thick thy forehead fair,
Down the veiny temples growing,

div.p: O’er the sloping shoulders flowing, 50

lg.l: And the smoothly penciled brow,
Mild to him in every vow,
And the fringèd lid below,
Thin as thinnest blossoms blow,

div.p: And the hazely-lucid eye, 55

lg.l: Whence heart-winning glances fly,
And that cheek of health, o’erspread
With soft-blended white and red,
And the witching smiles which break

div.p: Round those lips, which sweetly speak, 60

lg.l: And thy gentleness of mind,
Gentle from a gentle kind,
These endowments, heavenly dower!
Brought him in the promised hour,

div.p: Shall for ever bind him to thee, 65
Shall renew him still to woo thee.

lg.l: Little charm of placid mien,
Miniature of Beauty’s Queen,
Numbering years, a scanty nine,
Stealing hearts without design,

div.p: Young inveigler, fond in wiles, 5

lg.l: Prone to mirth, profuse in smiles,
Yet a novice in disdain,
Pleasure giving without pain,
Still caressing, still caressed,

div.p: Thou and all thy lovers blessed, 10

lg.l: Never teased, and never teasing,
Oh for ever pleased and pleasing!
Hither, British Muse of mine,
Hither, all the Grecian Nine,

div.p: With the lovely Graces Three, 15

lg.l: And your promised nursling see:
Figure on her waxen mind
Images of life refined;
Make it as a garden gay,

div.p: Every bud of thought display, 20

lg.l: Till, improving year by year,
The whole culture shall appear,
Voice, and speech, and action, rising,
All to human sense surprising.

div.p: Is the silken web so thin 25
As the texture of her skin?

lg.l: Can the lily and the rose
Such unsullied hue disclose?
Are the violets so blue
As her veins exposed to view?

div.p: Do the stars in wintry sky 30
Twinkle brighter than her eye?
Has the morning lark a throat
Sounding sweeter than her note?
Who e’er knew the like before thee? 35

lg.l: They who knew the nymph that bore thee.
From thy pastime and thy toys,
From thy harmless cares and joys,
Give me now a moment’s time:

div.p: When thou shalt attain thy prime, 40

lg.l: And thy bosom feel desire,
Love the likeness of thy sire,
One ordained through life to prove
Still thy glory, still thy love.

div.p: Like thy sister, and like thee, 45

lg.l: Let thy nurtured daughters be:
Semblance of the fair who bore thee,
Trace the pattern set before thee.
Where the Liffy meets the main,

div.p: Has thy sister heard my strain: 50

lg.l: From the Liffy to the Thames,
Minstrel echoes, sing their names,
Wafting to the willing ear
Many a cadence sweet to hear,

div.p: Smooth as gently breathing gales 55

lg.l: O’er the ocean and the vales,
While the vessel calmly glides
O’er the level glassy tides,
While the summer flowers are springing,

div.p: And the new-fledged birds are singing. 60

lg.l: Dear Love, let me this evening die,
Oh smile not to prevent it;
Dead with my rivals let me lie,
Or we shall both repent it.

div.p: Frown quickly then, and break my heart, 5

lg.l: That so my way of dying
May, though my life was full of smart,
Be worth the world’s envying.
Some, striving knowledge to refine,

div.p: Consume themselves with thinking; 10

lg.l: And some, who friendship seal in wine,
Are kindly killed with drinking.
And some are wrecked on the Indian coast,
Thither by gain invited;

div.p: Some are in smoke of battle lost, 15

lg.l: Whom drums, not lutes, delighted.
Alas! how poorly these depart,
Their graves still unattended!
Who dies not of a broken heart

div.p: Is not of Death commended. 20

lg.l: His memory is only sweet,
All praise and pity moving,
Who kindly at his mistress’ feet
Does die with over-loving.

div.p: And now thou frown’st, and now I die, 25

lg.l: My corpse by lovers followed;
Which straight shall by dead lovers lie;
That ground is only hallowed.
If priests are grieved I have a grave,

div.p: My death not well approving, 30

lg.l: The poets my estate shall have,
To teach them the Art of Loving.
And now let lovers ring their bells
For me, poor youth departed,

div.p: Who kindly in his love excels, 35

lg.l: By dying broken-hearted.
My grave with flowers let lovers strow,
Which, if thy tears fall near them,
May so transcend in scent and show,

div.p: As thou wilt shortly wear them. 40

lg.l: Such flowers how much will florists prize,
On lover’s grave that growing,
Are watered by his mistress’ eyes,
With pity ever-flowing.

div.p: A grave so deckt will, though thou art 45

lg.l: Yet fearful to come nigh me,
Provoke thee straight to break thy heart,
And lie down boldly by me.
Then everywhere all bells shall ring,

div.p: All light to darkness turning; 50

lg.l: While every quire shall sadly sing,
And nature’s self wear mourning.
Yet we hereafter may be found,
By destiny’s right placing,

div.p: Making, like flowers, love underground, 55
Whose roots are still embracing.
And are ye sure the news is true?
And are ye sure he’s weel?
Is this a time to think o’ wark?
Ye jades, lay by your wheel;
Is this the time to spin a thread, 5

lg.l: When Colin’s at the door?
Reach down my cloak, I’ll to the quay,
And see him come ashore.
For there’s nae luck about the house,

div.p: There’s nae luck at a’; 10

lg.l: There’s little pleasure in the house,
When our gudeman’s awa’.
And gie to me my bigonet,
My bishop’s satin gown;

div.p: For I maun tell the baillie’s wife 15

lg.l: That Colin’s in the town.
My Turkey slippers maun gae on,
My stockins pearly blue;
It’s a’ to pleasure our gudeman,

div.p: For he’s baith leal and true. 20

lg.l: Rise, lass, and mak a clean fireside,
Put on the muckle pot;
Gie little Kate her button gown
And Jock his Sunday coat;

div.p: And mak their shoon as black as slaes, 25

lg.l: Their hose as white as snaw;
It’s a’ to please my ain gudeman,
For he’s been long awa.
There’s twa fat hens upo’ the coop

div.p: Been fed this month and mair; 30

lg.l: Mak haste and thraw their necks about,
That Colin weel may fare;
And spread the table neat and clean,
Gar ilka thing look braw,

div.p: For wha can tell how Colin fared 35

lg.l: When he was far awa?
Sae true his heart, sae smooth his speech,
His breath like caller air;
His very foot has music in’t

div.p: As he comes up the stair— 40
And will I see his face again?
And will I hear him speak?
I’m downright dizzy wi’ the thought,
In troth I’m like to greet!
If Colin’s weel, and weel content, 45

lg.l: I hae nae mair to crave:
And gin I live to keep him sae,
I’m blest aboon the lave:
And will I see his face again,

div.p: And will I hear him speak? 50

lg.l: I’m downright dizzy wi’ the thought,
In troth I’m like to greet.
For there’s nae luck about the house,
There’s nae luck at a’;

div.p: There’s little pleasure in the house, 55
When our gudeman’s awa’.

lg.l: Ye banks and braes o’ bonnie Doon,
How can ye bloom sae fair!
How can ye chant, ye little birds,
And I sae fu’ o’ care!

div.p: Thou’ll break my heart, thou bonnie bird 5

lg.l: That sings upon the bough;
Thou minds me o’ the happy days
When my fause Luve was true.
Thou’ll break my heart, thou bonnie bird

div.p: That sings beside thy mate; 10

lg.l: For sae I sat, and sae I sang,
And wist na o’ my fate.
Aft hae I roved by bonnie Doon
To see the woodbine twine,

div.p: And ilka bird sang o’ its love; 15

lg.l: And sae did I o’ mine.
Wi’ lightsome heart I pu’d a rose,
Frae aff its thorny tree;
And my fause luver staw the rose,

div.p: But left the thorn wi’ me. 20

lg.l: A. ‘Busk ye, busk ye, my bonnie, bonnie bride,
Busk ye, busk ye, my winsome marrow,
Busk ye, busk ye, my bonnie, bonnie bride,
And think nae mair of the braes of Yarrow.’

div.p: B. ‘Where gat ye that bonnie, bonnie bride, 5

lg.l: Where gat ye that winsome marrow?’
A. ‘I gat her where I daurna weel be seen,
Pu’ing the birks on the braes of Yarrow.’
‘Weep not, weep not, my bonnie, bonnie bride,

div.p: Weep not, weep not, my winsome marrow, 10
Nor let thy heart lament to leave
Pu’ing the birks on the braes of Yarrow.’
B. ‘Why does she weep, thy bonnie, bonnie bride?
Why does she weep, thy winsome marrow?
And why daur ye nae mair well be seen 15

lg.l: Pu’ing the birks on the braes of Yarrow?’
A. ‘Lang maun she weep, lang lang maun she weep,
Lang maun she weep wi’ dule and sorrow,
And lang maun I nae mair weel be seen

div.p: Pu’ing the birks on the braes of Yarrow. 20

lg.l: ‘For she has tint her lover dear,
Her lover dear, the cause of sorrow;
And I ha’e slain the comeliest swain
That ever pu’ed birks on the braes of Yarrow.

div.p: ‘Why runs thy stream, O Yarrow, reid? 25
Why on thy braes heard the voice of sorrow?
And why yon melancholious weeds,
Hung on the bonnie birks of Yarrow?
‘What’s yonder floats on the rueful flood?
What’s yonder floats? Oh, dule and sorrow! 30

lg.l: Oh! ’tis the comely swain I slew
Upon the duleful banks of Yarrow!
‘Wash, oh, wash his wounds in tears,
His wounds in tears of dule and sorrow,

div.p: And wrap his limbs in mourning weeds, 35

lg.l: And lay him on the banks of Yarrow!
‘Then build, then build, ye sisters sad,
Ye sisters sad, his tomb wi’ sorrow,
And weep around in waeful wise,

div.p: His helpless fate on the braes of Yarrow. 40

lg.l: ‘Curse ye, curse ye his useless shield,
The arm that wrought the deed of sorrow,
The fatal spear that pierced his breast,
His comely breast, on the braes of Yarrow.

div.p: ‘Did I not warn thee not to love, 45

lg.l: And warn from fight? but, to my sorrow,
Too rashly bold, a stronger arm
Thou met’st, and fell on the braes of Yarrow,
‘Sweet smells the birk; green grows the grass,

div.p: Yellow on Yarrow’s braes the gowan, 50

lg.l: Fair hangs the apple frae the rock,
Sweet the wave of Yarrow flowin’.
‘Flows Yarrow sweet? as sweet flows Tweed,
As green its grass, its gowan as yellow,

div.p: As sweet smells on its braes the birk, 55

lg.l: The apple from its rocks as mellow.
‘Fair was thy love! fair, fair indeed thy love!
In flowery bands thou didst him fetter;
Though he was fair, and well-beloved again,

div.p: Than me he never loved thee better. 60

lg.l: ‘Busk ye, then, busk, my bonnie, bonnie bride,
Busk ye, busk ye, my winsome marrow,
Busk ye, and lo’e me on the banks of Tweed,
And think nae mair on the braes of Yarrow.’

div.p: C. ‘How can I busk, a bonnie, bonnie bride, 65

lg.l: How can I busk, a winsome marrow?
How lo’e him on the banks of Tweed,
That slew my Love on the braes of Yarrow?
‘Oh, Yarrow fields! may never rain,

div.p: Nor dew thy tender blossoms cover, 70

lg.l: For there was basely slain my Love,
My Love, as he had not been a lover!
‘The boy put on his robes of green,
His purple vest, ’twas my ain sewin’:

div.p: Ah, wretched me! I little, little knew, 75

lg.l: He was in these to meet his ruin.
‘The boy took out his milk-white steed,
Unmindful of my dule and sorrow;
But, ere the toofal of the night,

div.p: He lay a corpse on the banks of Yarrow. 80

lg.l: ‘Much I rejoiced that waeful day,
I sang, my voice the woods returning;
But lang ere night the spear was flown
That slew my Love, and left me mourning.

div.p: ‘What can my barbarous father do, 85

lg.l: But with his cruel rage pursue me?
My lover’s blood is on thy spear;
How canst thou, barbarous man, then woo me?
‘My happy sisters may be proud;

div.p: With cruel and ungentle scoffing 90

lg.l: May bid me seek on Yarrow’s braes
My lover nailèd in his coffin.
‘My brother Douglas may upbraid,
And strive with threatening words to move me;

div.p: My lover’s blude is on thy spear, 95

lg.l: How canst thou ever bid me love thee?
‘Yes, yes, prepare the bed, the bed of love,
With bridal-sheets my body cover;
Unbar, ye bridal maids, the door,

div.p: Let in the expected husband-lover! 100
‘But who the expected husband is?
His hands, methinks, are bathed in slaughter.
Ah me! what ghastly spectre’s yon,
Comes in his pale shroud bleeding after?
‘Pale as he is, here lay him down, 105

lg.l: Oh, lay his cold head on my pillow!
Take aff, take aff these bridal weeds,
And crown my careful head with willow.
‘Pale though thou art, yet best beloved,

div.p: Oh, could my warmth to life restore thee! 110

lg.l: Yet lie all night between my breasts;
No youth lay ever there before thee.
‘Pale, pale indeed, O lovely youth!
Forgive, forgive so foul a slaughter,

div.p: And lie all night between my breasts; 115

lg.l: No youth shall ever lie there after.’
A. Return, return, O mournful bride!
Return, and dry thy useless sorrow:
Thy lover heeds naught of thy sighs;

div.p: He lies a corpse on the braes of Yarrow! 120

lg.l: When the sheep are in the fauld, and the kye at hame,
And a’ the warld to rest are gane,
The waes o’ my heart fa’ in showers frae my e’e,
While my gudeman lies sound by me.

div.p: Young Jamie lo’ed me weel, and sought me for his bride; 5

lg.l: But saving a croun he had naething else beside:
To make the croun a pund, young Jamie gaed to sea;
And the croun and the pund were baith for me.
He hadna been awa’ a week but only twa,

div.p: When my father brak his arm, and the cow was stown awa; 10

lg.l: My mother she fell sick, and my Jamie at the sea—
And auld Robin Gray came a-courtin’ me.
My father couldna work, and my mother couldna spin;
I toiled day and night, but their bread I couldna win;

div.p: Auld Rob maintained them baith, and wi’ tears in his e’e 15

lg.l: Said, Jennie, for their sakes, oh marry me!
My heart it said nay; I looked for Jamie back;
But the wind it blew high, and the ship it was a wrack;
His ship it was a wrack—why didna Jamie dee?

div.p: Or why do I live to cry, Wae’s me? 20

lg.l: My father urgit sair: my mother didna speak;
But she looked in my face till my heart was like to break:
They gi’ed him my hand, but my heart was at the sea;
Sae auld Robin Gray he was gudeman to me.

div.p: I hadna been a wife a week but only four, 25

lg.l: When mournfu’ as I sat on the stane at the door,
I saw my Jamie’s wraith, for I couldna think it he—
Till he said, I’m come hame to marry thee.
O sair, sair did we greet, and muckle did we say;

div.p: We took but ae kiss, and I bad him gang away: 30

lg.l: I wish that I were dead, but I’m no like to dee;
And why was I born to say, Wae’s me!
I gang like a ghaist, and I carena to spin;
I daurna think on Jamie, for that wad be a sin;

div.p: But I’ll do my best a gude wife aye to be 35
For auld Robin Gray he is kind unto me.
A PINDARIC ODE.

lg.l: Awake, Æolian lyre, awake,
And give to rapture all thy trembling strings.
From Helicon’s harmonious springs
A thousand rills their mazy progress take:

div.p: The laughing flowers, that round them blow, 5
