lg.l: Drink life and fragrance as they flow,
Now the rich stream of music winds along,
Deep, majestic, smooth, and strong,
Through verdant vales, and Ceres’ golden reign:

div.p: Now rolling down the steep amain, 10

lg.l: Headlong, impetuous, see it pour:
The rocks and nodding groves rebellow to the roar.
O Sovereign of the willing soul,
Parent of sweet and solemn-breathing airs,

div.p: Enchanting shell! the sullen Cares 15

lg.l: And frantic Passions hear thy soft control:
On Thracia’s hills the Lord of War
Has curbed the fury of his car,
And dropped his thirsty lance at thy command.

div.p: Perching on the sceptred hand 20

lg.l: Of Jove, thy magic lulls the feathered king
With ruffled plumes, and flagging wing:
Quenched in dark clouds of slumber lie
The terror of his beak, and lightnings of his eye.

div.p: Thee the voice, the dance, obey, 25

lg.l: Tempered to thy warbled lay;
O’er Idalia’s velvet-green
The rosy-crownèd Loves are seen
On Cytherea’s day,

div.p: With antic Sports, and blue-eyed Pleasures, 30

lg.l: Frisking light in frolic measures;
Now pursuing, now retreating,
Now in circling troops they meet:
To brisk notes in cadence beating

div.p: Glance their many-twinkling feet. 35

lg.l: Slow-melting strains their Queen’s approach declare:
Where’er she turns, the Graces homage pay:
With arms sublime that float upon the air,
In gliding state she wins her easy way:

div.p: O’er her warm cheek and rising bosom move 40

lg.l: The bloom of young Desire and purple light of Love.
Man’s feeble race what ills await,
Labour and penury, the racks of pain,
Disease, and sorrow’s weeping train,

div.p: And death, sad refuge from the storms of fate! 45

lg.l: The fond complaint, my song, disprove,
And justify the laws of Jove.
Say, has he given in vain the heavenly Muse?
Night, and all her sickly dews,

div.p: Her spectres wan, and birds of boding cry, 50

lg.l: He gives to range the dreary sky;
Till down the eastern cliffs afar
Hyperion’s march they spy, and glittering shafts of war.
In climes beyond the solar road,

div.p: Where shaggy forms o’er ice-built mountains roam, 55

lg.l: The Muse has broke the twilight gloom,
To cheer the shivering native’s dull abode.
And oft, beneath the odorous shade
Of Chili’s boundless forests laid,

div.p: She deigns to hear the savage youth repeat, 60

lg.l: In loose numbers wildly sweet,
Their feather-cinctured chiefs, and dusky loves.
Her track, where’er the Goddess roves,
Glory pursue, and generous Shame,

div.p: The unconquerable Mind, and Freedom’s holy flame. 65

lg.l: Woods that wave o’er Delphi’s steep,
Isles that crown the Ægean deep,
Fields that cool Ilissus laves,
Or where Mæander’s amber waves

div.p: In lingering labyrinths creep, 70

lg.l: How do your tuneful echoes languish,
Mute, but to the voice of anguish?
Where each old poetic mountain
Inspiration breathed around;

div.p: Every shade and hallowed fountain 75

lg.l: Murmured deep a solemn sound:
Till the sad Nine, in Greece’s evil hour,
Left their Parnassus for the Latian plains.
Alike they scorn the pomp of tyrant Power,

div.p: And coward Vice, that revels in her chains. 80

lg.l: When Latium had her lofty spirit lost,
They sought, O Albion, next thy sea-encircled coast.
Far from the sun and summer-gale,
In thy green lap was Nature’s darling laid,

div.p: What time, where lucid Avon strayed, 85
To him the mighty Mother did unveil
Her awful face: the dauntless Child
Stretched forth his little arms, and smiled.
‘This pencil take (she said), whose colours clear
Richly paint the vernal year: 90

lg.l: Thine, too, these golden keys, immortal Boy!
This can unlock the gates of joy;
Of horror that, and thrilling fears,
Or ope the sacred source of sympathetic tears.’

div.p: Nor second he, that rode sublime 95

lg.l: Upon the seraph-wings of Ecstasy,
The secrets of the abyss to spy.
He passed the flaming bounds of place and time:
The living Throne, the sapphire-blaze,

div.p: Where angels tremble while they gaze, 100

lg.l: He saw; but, blasted with excess of light,
Closed his eyes in endless night.
Behold, where Dryden’s less presumptuous car,
Wide o’er the fields of glory bear

div.p: Two coursers of ethereal race, 105

lg.l: With necks in thunder clothed, and long resounding pace.
Hark, his hands the lyre explore!
Bright-eyed Fancy, hovering o’er,
Scatters from her pictured urn

div.p: Thoughts that breathe, and words that burn. 110

lg.l: But ah! ’tis heard no more—
O lyre divine, what daring spirit
Wakes thee now? Though he inherit
Nor the pride, nor ample pinion,

div.p: That the Theban Eagle bear, 115
Sailing with supreme dominion
Through the azure deep of air:
Yet oft before his infant eyes would run
Such forms as glitter in the Muse’s ray
With orient hues, unborrowed of the sun: 120

lg.l: Yet shall he mount, and keep his distant way
Beyond the limits of a vulgar fate,
Beneath the good how far!—but far above the great.
When I behold thee, blameless Williamson,
Wrecked like an infant on a savage shore,
While others round on borrowed pinions soar,
My busy fancy calls thy thread misspun;

div.p: Till Faith instructs me the deceit to shun, 5

lg.l: While thus she speaks,—‘Those wings that from the store
Of virtue were not lent, howe’er they bore
In this gross air, will melt when near the sun.
The truly’ ambitious wait for nature’s time,

div.p: Content by certain, though by slow, degrees 10

lg.l: To mount above the reach of vulgar flight;
Nor is that man confined to this low clime,
Who but the extremest skirts of glory sees,
And hears celestial echoes with delight.’
Ah! what a weary race my feet have run,
Since first I trod thy banks with alders crowned,
And thought my way was all through fairy ground,
Beneath thy azure sky and golden sun;

div.p: Where first my Muse to lisp her notes begun! 5

lg.l: While pensive Memory traces back the round
Which fills the varied interval between,
Much pleasure, more of sorrow, marks the scene.
Sweet native stream! those skies and suns so pure

div.p: No more return, to cheer my evening road; 10

lg.l: Yet still one joy remains—that not obscure,
Nor useless, all my vacant days have flowed,
From youth’s gay dawn to manhood’s prime mature,
Nor with the Muse’s laurel unbestowed.
Mary! I want a lyre with other strings,
Such aid from heaven as some have feigned they drew,
An eloquence scarce given to mortals, new
And undebased by praise of meaner things,

div.p: That ere through age or woe I shed my wings, 5

lg.l: I may record thy worth with honour due,
In verse as musical as thou art true,
And that immortalizes whom it sings:—
But thou hast little need. There is a Book

div.p: By seraphs writ with beams of heavenly light, 10

lg.l: On which the eyes of God not rarely look,
A chronicle of actions just and bright—
There all thy deeds, my faithful Mary, shine;
And since thou own’st that praise, I spare thee mine.
The twentieth year is well nigh past,
Since first our sky was overcast;
Ah would that this might be the last,
My Mary!

div.p: Thy spirits have a fainter flow, 5
I see thee daily weaker grow—
’Twas my distress that brought thee low,
My Mary!
Thy needles, once a shining store,
For my sake restless heretofore, 10

lg.l: Now rust disused, and shine no more,
My Mary!
For though thou gladly wouldst fulfil
The same kind office for me still,

div.p: Thy sight now seconds not thy will, 15

lg.l: My Mary!
But well thou play’dst the housewife’s part,
And all thy threads with magic art
Have wound themselves about this heart,

div.p: My Mary! 20

lg.l: Thy indistinct expressions seem
Like language uttered in a dream;
Yet me they charm, whate’er the theme,
My Mary!

div.p: Thy silver locks, once auburn bright, 25

lg.l: Are still more lovely in my sight
Than golden beams of orient light,
My Mary!
For could I view nor them nor thee,

div.p: What sight worth seeing could I see? 30

lg.l: The sun would rise in vain for me,
My Mary!
Partakers of thy sad decline,
Thy hands their little force resign;

div.p: Yet gently pressed, press gently mine, 35

lg.l: My Mary!
Such feebleness of limbs thou prov’st
That now at every step thou mov’st
Upheld by two; yet still thou lov’st,

div.p: My Mary! 40

lg.l: And still to love, though pressed with ill,
In wintry age to feel no chill,
With me is to be lovely still,
My Mary!

div.p: But ah! by constant heed I know 45

lg.l: How oft the sadness that I show
Transforms thy smiles to looks of woe,
My Mary!
And should my future lot be cast

div.p: With much resemblance of the past, 50
Thy worn-out heart will break at last—
My Mary!

head.label: CLXII
head.hi: TO THE EARL OF WARWICK, ON THE DEATH OF ADDISON.

lg.l: If, dumb too long, the drooping Muse hath stayed,
And left her debt to Addison unpaid,
Blame not her silence, Warwick, but bemoan,
And judge, oh judge, my bosom by your own.

div.p: What mourner ever felt poetic fires! 5

lg.l: Slow comes the verse that real woe inspires:
Grief unaffected suits but ill with art,
Or flowing numbers with a bleeding heart.
Can I forget the dismal night that gave

div.p: My soul’s best part for ever to the grave! 10

lg.l: How silent did his old companions tread,
By midnight lamps, the mansions of the dead,
Through breathing statues, then unheeded things,
Through rows of warriors, and through walks of kings!

div.p: What awe did the slow solemn knell inspire; 15

lg.l: The pealing organ, and the pausing choir;
The duties by the lawn-robed prelate paid;
And the last words that dust to dust conveyed!
While speechless o’er thy closing grave we bend,

div.p: Accept these tears, thou dear departed friend. 20

lg.l: Oh, gone for ever! take this long adieu;
And sleep in peace, next thy loved Montague.
To strew fresh laurels let the task be mine,
A frequent pilgrim at thy sacred shrine;

div.p: Mine with true sighs thy absence to bemoan, 25

lg.l: And grave with faithful epitaphs thy stone.
If e’er from me thy loved memorial part,
May shame afflict this alienated heart;
Of thee forgetful if I form a song,

div.p: My lyre be broken, and untuned my tongue, 30

lg.l: My grief be doubled, from thy image free,
And mirth a torment, unchastised by thee.
Oft let me range the gloomy aisles alone,
Sad luxury! to vulgar minds unknown,

div.p: Along the walls where speaking marbles show 35

lg.l: What worthies form the hallowed mould below;
Proud names, who once the reins of empire held;
In arms who triumphed; or in arts excelled;
Chiefs, graced with scars, and prodigal of blood;

div.p: Stern patriots, who for sacred freedom stood; 40

lg.l: Just men, by whom impartial laws were given;
And saints who taught, and led, the way to heaven.
Ne’er to these chambers, where the mighty rest,
Since their foundation, came a nobler guest;

div.p: Nor e’er was to the bowers of bliss conveyed 45

lg.l: A fairer spirit or more welcome shade.
In what new region, to the just assigned,
What new employments please the unbodied mind?
A wingèd Virtue, through the ethereal sky,

div.p: From world to world unwearied does he fly? 50

lg.l: Or curious trace the long laborious maze
Of Heaven’s decrees, where wondering angels gaze?
Does he delight to hear bold seraphs tell
How Michael battled, and the dragon fell;

div.p: Or, mixed with milder cherubim, to glow 55

lg.l: In hymns of love, not ill essayed below?
Or dost thou warn poor mortals left behind,
A task well suited to thy gentle mind?
Oh! if sometimes thy spotless form descend,

div.p: To me thy aid, thou guardian Genius, lend! 60

lg.l: When rage misguides me, or when fear alarms,
When pain distresses, or when pleasure charms,
In silent whisperings purer thoughts impart,
And turn from ill a frail and feeble heart;

div.p: Lead through the paths thy virtue trod before, 65

lg.l: Till bliss shall join, nor death can part us more.
That awful form, which, so the Heavens decree,
Must still be loved and still deplored by me,
In nightly visions seldom fails to rise,

div.p: Or, roused by Fancy, meets my waking eyes. 70

lg.l: If business calls, or crowded courts invite,
The unblemished statesman seems to strike my sight;
If in the stage I seek to soothe my care,
I meet his soul which breathes in Cato there;

div.p: If pensive to the rural shades I rove, 75
His shape o’ertakes me in the lonely grove;
’Twas there of just and good he reasoned strong,
Cleared some great truth, or raised some serious song:
There patient showed us the wise course to steer,
A candid censor, and a friend severe; 80

lg.l: There taught us how to live; and (oh! too high
The price for knowledge) taught us how to die.
Thou Hill, whose brow the antique structures grace,
Reared by bold chiefs of Warwick’s noble race,

div.p: Why, once so loved, whene’er thy bower appears, 85

lg.l: O’er my dim eyeballs glance the sudden tears!
How sweet were once thy prospects fresh and fair,
Thy sloping walks, and unpolluted air!
How sweet the glooms beneath thy aged trees,

div.p: Thy noon-tide shadow, and thy evening breeze! 90

lg.l: His image thy forsaken bowers restore;
Thy walks and airy prospects charm no more;
No more the summer in thy glooms allayed,
Thy evening breezes, and thy noon-day shade.

div.p: From other ills, however Fortune frowned; 95

lg.l: Some refuge in the Muse’s art I found:
Reluctant now I touch the trembling string,
Bereft of him who taught me how to sing;
And these sad accents, murmured o’er his urn,

div.p: Betray that absence they attempt to mourn. 100

lg.l: Oh must I then (now fresh my bosom bleeds,
And Craggs in death to Addison succeeds)
The verse, begun to one lost friend, prolong,
And weep a second in the unfinished song!

div.p: These works divine, which, on his death-bed laid, 105

lg.l: To thee, O Craggs, the expiring sage conveyed,
Great, but ill-omened, monument of fame,
Nor he survived to give, nor thou to claim.
Swift after him thy social spirit flies,

div.p: And close to his, how soon! thy coffin lies. 110

lg.l: Blest pair! whose union future bards shall tell
In future tongues: each other’s boast! farewell,
Farewell! whom joined in fame, in friendship tried,
No chance could sever, nor the grave divide.

head.label: CLXIII
head.hi: ELEGY TO THE MEMORY OF AN UNFORTUNATE LADY.

div.p: What beckoning ghost, along the moonlight shade,
Invites my steps, and points to yonder glade?
’Tis she!—but why that bleeding bosom gored,
Why dimly gleams the visionary sword?
Oh ever beauteous, ever friendly! tell, 5

lg.l: Is it, in heaven, a crime to love too well?
To bear too tender, or too firm a heart,
To act a lovers, or a Roman’s part?
Is there no bright reversion in the sky,

div.p: For those who greatly think, or bravely die? 10

lg.l: Why bade ye else, ye Powers! her soul aspire
Above the vulgar flight of low desire?
Ambition first sprung from your blest abodes:
The glorious fault of angels and of gods:

div.p: Thence to their images on earth it flows, 15

lg.l: And in the breasts of kings and heroes glows.
Most souls, ’tis true, but peep out once an age,
Dull sullen prisoners in the body’s cage:
Dim lights of life, that burn a length of years,

div.p: Useless, unseen, as lamps in sepulchres; 20

lg.l: Like eastern kings a lazy state they keep,
And, close confined to their own palace, sleep.
From these perhaps (ere nature bade her die)
Fate snatched her early to the pitying sky.

div.p: As into air the purer spirits flow, 25

lg.l: And separate from their kindred dregs below;
So flew the soul to its congenial place,
Nor left one virtue to redeem her race.
But thou, false guardian of a charge too good,

div.p: Thou, mean deserter of thy brother’s blood! 30

lg.l: See on these ruby lips the trembling breath,
These cheeks now fading at the blast of death;
Cold is that breast which warmed the world before,
And those love-darting eyes must roll no more.

div.p: Thus, if eternal justice rules the ball, 35

lg.l: Thus shall your wives, and thus your children fall;
On all the line a sudden vengeance waits,
And frequent hearses shall besiege your gates;
There passengers shall stand, and pointing say,

div.p: (While the long funerals blacken all the way) 40

lg.l: Lo! these were they, whose souls the Furies steeled,
And curst with hearts unknowing how to yield.
Thus unlamented pass the proud away,
The gaze of fools, and pageant of a day!

div.p: So perish all, whose breast ne’er learned to glow 45
For others’ good, or melt at others’ woe.
What can atone (O ever injured shade!)
Thy fate unpitied, and thy rites unpaid?
No friend’s complaint, no kind domestic tear,
Pleased thy pale ghost, or graced thy mournful bier: 50

lg.l: By foreign hands thy dying eyes were closed,
By foreign hands thy decent limbs composed,
By foreign hands thy humble grave adorned,
By strangers honoured, and by strangers mourned!

div.p: What though no friends in sable weeds appear; 55

lg.l: Grieve for an hour, perhaps, then mourn a year,
And bear about the mockery of woe
To midnight dances, and the public show?
What though no weeping Loves thy ashes grace,

div.p: Nor polished marble emulate thy face? 60

lg.l: What though no sacred earth allow thee room,
Nor hallowed dirge be muttered o’er thy tomb?
Yet shall thy grave with rising flowers be drest,
And the green turf lie lightly on thy breast:

div.p: There shall the Morn her earliest tears bestow, 65

lg.l: There the first roses of the year shall blow;
While angels with their silver wings o’ershade
The ground now sacred by thy relics made.
So, peaceful rests, without a stone, a name,

div.p: What once had beauty, titles, wealth, and fame. 70
How loved, how honoured once, avails thee not,
To whom related, or by whom begot;
A heap of dust alone remains of thee;
’Tis all thou art, and all the proud shall be!
Poets themselves must fall, like those they sung, 75

lg.l: Deaf the praised ear, and mute the tuneful tongue.
Even he, whose soul now melts in mournful lays,
Shall shortly want the generous tear he pays;
Then from his closing eyes thy form shall part,

div.p: And the last pang shall tear thee from his heart, 80
Life’s idle business at one gasp be o’er,
The Muse forgot, and thou beloved no more!

div.head:
CLXIV
ON THE DEATH OF MR. ROBERT LEVET,
div.p: A PRACTISER IN PHYSIC.

lg.l: Condemned to Hope’s delusive mine,
As on we toil from day to day,
By sudden blasts, or slow decline,
Our social comforts drop away.

div.p: Well tried through many a varying year, 5

lg.l: See Levet to the grave descend,
Officious, innocent, sincere,
Of every friendless name the friend.
Yet still he fills affection’s eye,

div.p: Obscurely wise, and coarsely kind; 10

lg.l: Nor, lettered Arrogance, deny
Thy praise to merit unrefined.
When fainting nature called for aid,
And hovering death prepared the blow,

div.p: His vigorous remedy displayed 15

lg.l: The power of art without the show.
In Misery’s darkest cavern known,
His useful care was ever nigh,
Where hopeless Anguish poured his groan,

div.p: And lonely Want retired to die. 20

lg.l: No summons mocked by chill delay,
No petty gain disdained by pride,
The modest wants of every day
The toil of every day supplied.

div.p: His virtues walked their narrow round, 25

lg.l: Nor made a pause, nor left a void;
And sure the Eternal Master found
The single talent well employed.
The busy day—the peaceful night,

div.p: Unfelt, uncounted, glided by; 30

lg.l: His frame was firm, his powers were bright,
Though now his eightieth year was nigh.
Then with no fiery throbbing pain,
No cold gradations of decay,

div.p: Death broke at once the vital chain, 35
And freed his soul the nearest way.

lg.l: Ye banks and braes and streams around
The castle o’ Montgomery,
Green be your woods, and fair your flowers,
Your waters never drumlie!

div.p: There simmer first unfauld her robes, 5

lg.l: And there the langest tarry;
For there I took the last fareweel
O’ my sweet Highland Mary.
How sweetly bloomed the gay green birk,

div.p: How rich the hawthorn’s blossom, 10

lg.l: As underneath their fragrant shade
I clasped her to my bosom!
The golden hours on angel wings
Flew o’er me and my dearie;

div.p: For dear to me as light and life 15

lg.l: Was my sweet Highland Mary.
Wi’ mony a vow and locked embrace
Our parting was fu’ tender;
And pledging aft to meet again,

div.p: We tore oursels asunder; 20

lg.l: But, oh! fell Deaths untimely frost,
That nipt my flower sae early!
Now green’s the sod, and cauld’s the clay,
That wraps my Highland Mary!

div.p: O pale, pale now, those rosy lips, 25

lg.l: I aft hae kissed sae fondly!
And closed for aye the sparkling glance
That dwelt on me sae kindly;
And mouldering now in silent dust

div.p: That heart that lo’ed me dearly! 30
But still within my bosom’s core
Shall live my Highland Mary.

lg.l: Obscurest night involved the sky;
The Atlantic billows roared,
When such a destined wretch as I,
Washed headlong from on board,

div.p: Of friends, of hope, of all bereft, 5

lg.l: His floating home for ever left.
No braver chief could Albion boast,
Than he, with whom he went,
Nor ever ship left Albion’s coast

div.p: With warmer wishes sent. 10

lg.l: He loved them both, but both in vain,
Nor him beheld, nor her again.
Not long beneath the whelming brine,
Expert to swim, he lay:

div.p: Nor soon he felt his strength decline, 15

lg.l: Or courage die away;
But waged with death a lasting strife,
Supported by despair of life.
He shouted; nor his friends had failed

div.p: To check the vessel’s course, 20

lg.l: But so the furious blast prevailed,
That, pitiless perforce,
They left their outcast mate behind,
And scudded still before the wind.

div.p: Some succour yet they could afford; 25

lg.l: And, such as storms allow,
The cask, the coop, the floated cord,
Delayed not to bestow.
But he, they knew, nor ship nor shore,

div.p: Whate’er they gave, should visit more. 30

lg.l: Nor, cruel as it seemed, could he
Their haste himself condemn,
Aware that flight, in such a sea,
Alone could rescue them;

div.p: Yet bitter felt it still to die 35

lg.l: Deserted, and his friends so nigh.
He long survives, who lives an hour
In ocean, self-upheld:
And so long he, with unspent power,

div.p: His destiny repelled: 40

lg.l: And ever as the minutes flew,
Entreated help, or cried—‘Adieu!’
At length, his transient respite past,
His comrades, who before

div.p: Had heard his voice in every blast, 45

lg.l: Could catch the sound no more.
For then by toil subdued, he drank
The stifling wave, and then he sank.
No poet wept him; but the page

div.p: Of narrative sincere, 50

lg.l: That tells his name, his worth, his age,
Is wet with Anson’s tear.
And tears by bards or heroes shed
Alike immortalize the dead.

div.p: I therefore purpose not, or dream, 55

lg.l: Descanting on his fate,
To give the melancholy theme
A more enduring date;
But misery still delights to trace

div.p: Its semblance in another’s case. 60

lg.l: No voice divine the storm allayed,
No light propitious shone,
When snatched from all effectual aid
We perished, each alone:

div.p: But I beneath a rougher sea, 65
And whelmed in deeper gulfs than he.

lg.l: I’m wearing awa’, John,
Like snaw when its thaw, John,
I’m wearing awa’
To the land o’ the leal.

div.p: There’s nae sorrow there, John, 5

lg.l: There’s neither cauld nor care, John,
The day is aye fair
In the land o’ the leal.
Ye were aye leal and true, John,

div.p: Your task’s ended noo, John, 10

lg.l: And I’ll welcome you
To the land o’ the leal.
Our bonnie bairn’s there, John,
She was baith guid and fair, John;

div.p: Oh we grudged her right sair 15

lg.l: To the land o’ the leal!
Then dry that tearfu’ e’e, John,
My soul langs to be free, John,
And angels wait on me

div.p: To the land o’ the leal. 20

lg.l: Now fare ye weel, my ain John,
This warld’s care is vain, John;
We’ll meet and aye be fain
In the land o’ the leal.

head.label: CLXVIII
head.hi: ELEGY, WRITTEN IN A COUNTRY CHURCHYARD.

lg.l: The curfew tolls the knell of parting day,
The lowing herds wind slowly o’er the lea,
The ploughman homeward plods his weary way,
And leaves the world to darkness and to me.

div.p: Now fades the glimmering landscape on the sight, 5

lg.l: And all the air a solemn stillness holds,
Save where the beetle wheels his droning flight,
And drowsy tinklings lull the distant folds;
Save that from yonder ivy-mantled tower

div.p: The moping owl does to the moon complain 10

lg.l: Of such, as wandering near her secret bower,
Molest her ancient solitary reign.
Beneath those rugged elms, that yew-tree’s shade,
Where heaves the turf in many a mouldering heap,

div.p: Each in his narrow cell for ever laid, 15

lg.l: The rude forefathers of the hamlet sleep.
The breezy call of incense-breathing Morn,
The swallow twittering from the straw-built shed,
The cock’s shrill clarion, or the echoing horn,

div.p: No more shall rouse them from their lowly bed. 20

lg.l: For them no more the blazing hearth shall burn,
Or busy housewife ply her evening care:
No children run to lisp their sire’s return,
Or climb his knees the envied kiss to share.

div.p: Oft did the harvest to their sickle yield, 25

lg.l: Their furrow oft the stubborn glebe has broke:
How jocund did they drive their team afield!
How bowed the woods beneath their sturdy stroke!
Let not Ambition mock their useful toil,

div.p: Their homely joys, and destiny obscure; 30

lg.l: Nor Grandeur hear with a disdainful smile
The short and simple annals of the poor.
The boast of heraldry, the pomp of power,
And all that beauty, all that wealth e’er gave,

div.p: Await alike the inevitable hour; 35

lg.l: The paths of glory lead but to the grave.
Nor you, ye proud, impute to these the fault,
If memory o’er their tomb no trophies raise,
Where through the long-drawn aisle and fretted vault

div.p: The pealing anthem swells the note of praise. 40

lg.l: Can storied urn, or animated bust,
Back to its mansion call the fleeting breath?
Can Honour’s voice provoke the silent dust,
Or Flattery soothe the dull cold ear of Death?

div.p: Perhaps in this neglected spot is laid 45

lg.l: Some heart once pregnant with celestial fire;
Hands, that the rod of empire might have swayed,
Or waked to ecstasy the living lyre.
But knowledge to their eyes her ample page,

div.p: Rich with the spoils of time, did ne’er unroll; 50

lg.l: Chill penury repressed their noble rage,
And froze the genial current of the soul.
Full many a gem of purest ray serene
The dark unfathomed caves of ocean bear:

div.p: Full many a flower is born to blush unseen, 55

lg.l: And waste its sweetness on the desert air.
Some village Hampden, that with dauntless breast
The little tyrant of his fields withstood;
Some mute inglorious Milton here may rest,

div.p: Some Cromwell guiltless of his country’s blood. 60

lg.l: The applause of listening senates to command,
The threats of pain and ruin to despise,
To scatter plenty o’er a smiling land,
And read their history in a nation’s eyes,

div.p: Their lot forbade: nor circumscribed alone 65

lg.l: Their growing virtues, but their crimes confined;
Forbade to wade through slaughter to a throne,
And shut the gates of mercy on mankind;
The struggling pangs of conscious truth to hide,

div.p: To quench the blushes of ingenuous shame, 70

lg.l: Or heap the shrine of luxury and pride
With incense kindled at the Muse’s flame.
Far from the madding crowd’s ignoble strife,
Their sober wishes never learned to stray;

div.p: Along the cool sequestered vale of life 75

lg.l: They kept the noiseless tenour of their way.
Yet e’en these bones from insult to protect
Some frail memorial still erected nigh,
With uncouth rhymes and shapeless sculpture decked,

div.p: Implores the passing tribute of a sigh. 80

lg.l: Their names, their years, spelt by the unlettered Muse,
The place of fame and elegy supply;
And many a holy text around she strews,
That teach the rustic moralist to die.

div.p: For who, to dumb forgetfulness a prey, 85

lg.l: This pleasing anxious being e’er resigned,
Left the warm precincts of the cheerful day,
Nor cast one longing, lingering look behind?
On some fond breast the parting soul relies,

div.p: Some pious drops the closing eye requires; 90

lg.l: E’en from the tomb the voice of Nature cries,
E’en in our ashes live their wonted fires.
For thee, who, mindful of the unhonoured dead,
Dost in these lines their artless tales relate;

div.p: If chance, by lonely Contemplation led, 95

lg.l: Some kindred spirit shall inquire thy fate,
Haply some hoary-headed swain may say,
‘Oft have we seen him at the peep of dawn,
Brushing with hasty steps the dews away,

div.p: To meet the sun upon the upland lawn. 100

lg.l: ‘There at the foot of yonder nodding beech,
That wreathes its old fantastic roots so high,
His listless length at noontide would he stretch,
And pore upon the brook that babbles by.

div.p: ‘Hard by yon wood, now smiling as in scorn, 105

lg.l: Muttering his wayward fancies he would rove;
Now drooping, woful-wan, like one forlorn,
Or crazed with care, or crossed in hopeless love.
‘One morn, I missed him on the customed hill,

div.p: Along the heath, and near his favourite tree; 110

lg.l: Another came, nor yet beside the rill,
Nor up the lawn, nor at the wood was he;
‘The next with dirges due in sad array,
Slow through the churchway path we saw him borne:

div.p: Approach and read (for thou canst read) the lay, 115
Graved on the stone beneath yon aged thorn.’

div.head: THE EPITAPH.
div.p: Here rests his head upon the lap of Earth
A Youth, to Fortune and to Fame unknown:
Fair Science frowned not on his humble birth,
And Melancholy marked him for her own. 120

lg.l: Large was his bounty, and his soul sincere;
Heaven did a recompense as largely send:
He gave to misery all he had, a tear;
He gained from Heaven, ’twas all he wished, a friend.

div.p: No farther seek his merits to disclose, 125
Or draw his frailties from their dread abode,
(There they alike in trembling hope repose;)
The bosom of his Father and his God.

lg.l: Come, O Thou traveller unknown,
Whom still I hold, but cannot see,
My company before is gone,
And I am left alone with Thee;

div.p: With Thee all night I mean to stay, 5

lg.l: And wrestle till the break of day.
I need not tell Thee who I am,
My misery or sin declare;
Thyself hast called me by my name;

div.p: Look on thy hands, and read it there! 10

lg.l: But who, I ask Thee, who art Thou?
Tell me thy Name, and tell me now.
In vain Thou strugglest to get free,
I never will unloose my hold;

div.p: Art Thou the Man that died for me? 15

lg.l: The secret of thy love untold.
Wrestling, I will not let Thee go,
Till I thy Name, thy nature know.
Wilt Thou not yet to me reveal

div.p: Thy new, unutterable Name? 20

lg.l: Tell me, I still beseech Thee, tell:
To know it now, resolved I am:
Wrestling, I will not let Thee go,
Till I thy Name, thy nature know.

div.p: ’Tis all in vain to hold thy tongue, 25

lg.l: Or touch the hollow of my thigh;
Though every sinew be unstrung,
Out of my arms Thou shalt not fly:
Wrestling, I will not let Thee go,

div.p: Till I thy Name, thy nature know. 30

lg.l: What though my shrinking flesh complain,
And murmur to contend so long?
I rise superior to my pain;
When I am weak, then am I strong:

div.p: And when my all of strength shall fail, 35

lg.l: I shall with the God-Man prevail.
My strength is gone; my nature dies;
I sink beneath thy weighty hand;
Faint to revive, and fall to rise;

div.p: I fall, and yet by faith I stand: 40

lg.l: I stand, and will not let Thee go,
Till I thy Name, thy nature know.
Yield to me now, for I am weak,
But confident in self-despair;

div.p: Speak to my heart, in blessings speak, 45
Be conquered by my instant prayer!
Speak, or Thou never hence shall move,
And tell me, if thy Name be Love?
’Tis Love! ’tis Love! Thou diedst for me!
I hear thy whisper in my heart! 50

lg.l: The morning breaks, the shadows flee;
Pure universal Love Thou art!
To me, to all, thy bowels move;
Thy nature and thy Name is Love!

div.p: My prayer hath power with God; the grace 55

lg.l: Unspeakable I now receive;
Through faith I see Thee face to face,
I see Thee face to face, and live:
In vain I have not wept and strove;

div.p: Thy nature and thy Name is Love. 60

lg.l: I know Thee, Saviour, who Thou art;
Jesus, the feeble sinner’s Friend!
Nor wilt Thou with the night depart,
But stay, and love me to the end!

div.p: Thy mercies never shall remove, 65

lg.l: Thy nature and thy Name is Love!
The Sun of Righteousness on me
Hath rose, with healing in his wings;
Withered my nature’s strength, from Thee

div.p: My soul its life and succour brings; 70

lg.l: My help is all laid up above;
Thy nature and thy Name is Love.
Contented now upon my thigh
I halt, till life’s short journey end;

div.p: All helplessness, all weakness, I 75

lg.l: On Thee alone for strength depend;
Nor have I power from Thee to move;
Thy nature and thy Name is Love.
Lame as I am, I take the prey,

div.p: Hell, earth, and sin, with ease o’ercome; 80

lg.l: I leap for joy, pursue my way,
And, as a bounding hart, fly home;
Through all eternity to prove,
Thy nature and thy Name is Love!
O blithe new-comer! I have heard,
I hear thee and rejoice:
O Cuckoo! shall I call thee bird,
Or but a wandering Voice?

div.p: While I am lying on the grass, 5

lg.l: Thy twofold shout I hear;
From hill to hill it seems to pass,
At once far off and near.
Though babbling only to the vale

div.p: Of sunshine and of flowers, 10

lg.l: Thou bringest unto me a tale
Of visionary hours.
Thrice welcome, darling of the Spring!
Even yet thou art to me

div.p: No bird, but an invisible thing, 15
A voice, a mystery;
The same whom in my school-boy days
I listened to; that Cry
Which made me look a thousand ways
In bush, and tree, and sky. 20

lg.l: To seek thee did I often rove
Through woods and on the green;
And thou wert still a hope, a love;
Still longed for, never seen!

div.p: And I can listen to thee yet; 25
Can lie upon the plain
And listen, till I do beget
That golden time again.
O blessèd bird! the earth we pace
Again appears to be 30
An unsubstantial, fairy place
That is fit home for thee!

lg.l: Triumphal arch that fill’st the sky,
When storms prepare to part,
I ask not proud Philosophy
To teach me what thou art.

div.p: Still seem, as to my childhood’s sight, 5

lg.l: A mid-way station given
For happy spirits to alight,
Betwixt the earth and heaven.
Can all that optics teach, unfold

div.p: Thy form to please me so, 10

lg.l: As when I dreamed of gems and gold
Hid in thy radiant bow?
When Science from Creation’s face
Enchantment’s veil withdraws,

div.p: What lovely visions yield their place 15

lg.l: To cold material laws!
And yet, fair bow, no fabling dreams,
But words of the Most High,
Have told why first thy robe of beams

div.p: Was woven in the sky. 20

lg.l: When o’er the green undeluged earth,
Heaven’s covenant thou didst shine,
How came the world’s gray fathers forth
To watch thy sacred sign!

div.p: And when its yellow lustre smiled 25

lg.l: O’er mountains yet untrod,
Each mother held aloft her child
To bless the bow of God.
Methinks, thy jubilee to keep,

div.p: The first-made anthem rang 30

lg.l: On earth, delivered from the deep,
And the first poet sang.
Nor ever shall the Muse’s eye,
Unraptured, greet thy beam;

div.p: Theme of primeval prophecy, 35

lg.l: Be still the poet’s theme!
The earth to thee her incense yields,
The lark thy welcome sings,
When, glittering in the freshened fields,

div.p: The snowy mushroom springs. 40

lg.l: How glorious is thy girdle cast
O’er mountain, tower, and town,
Or mirrored in the ocean vast,
A thousand fathoms down!

div.p: As fresh in yon horizon dark, 45

lg.l: As young thy beauties seem,
As when the eagle from the ark
First sported in thy beam.
For, faithful to its sacred page,

div.p: Heaven still rebuilds thy span, 50
Nor lets the type grow pale with age,
That first spoke peace to man.

lg.l: Once, in the flight of ages past,
There lived a man:—and WHO was HE?—
Mortal! howe’er thy lot be cast,
That Man resembled thee.

div.p: Unknown the region of his birth, 5

lg.l: The land in which he died unknown:
His name has perished from the earth;
This truth survives alone:—
That joy and grief, and hope and fear,

div.p: Alternate triumphed in his breast; 10

lg.l: His bliss and woe,—a smile, a tear!—
Oblivion hides the rest.
The bounding pulse, the languid limb,
The changing spirits’ rise and fall,

div.p: We know that these were felt by him, 15

lg.l: For these are felt by all.
He suffered,—but his pangs are o’er;
Enjoyed,—but his delights are fled;
Had friends,—his friends are now no more;

div.p: And foes,—his foes are dead. 20

lg.l: He loved,—but whom he loved, the grave
Hath lost in its unconscious womb:
Oh she was fair!—but nought could save
Her beauty from the tomb.

div.p: He saw whatever thou hast seen; 25

lg.l: Encountered all that troubles thee:
He was—whatever thou hast been;
He is—what thou shalt be.
The rolling seasons, day and night,

div.p: Sun, moon, and stars, the earth and main, 30

lg.l: Erewhile his portion, life, and light,
To him exist in vain.
The clouds and sunbeams, o’er his eye
That once their shades and glory threw,

div.p: Have left in yonder silent sky 35

lg.l: No vestige where they flew.
The annals of the human race,
Their ruins since the world began,
Of HIM afford no other trace

div.p: Than this,—THERE LIVED A MAN! 40
O Reader! hast thou ever stood to see
The Holly Tree?
The eye that contemplates it well perceives
Its glossy leaves
Ordered by an Intelligence so wise, 5

lg.l: As might confound the atheist’s sophistries.
Below, a circling fence, its leaves are seen
Wrinkled and keen;
No grazing cattle through their prickly round

div.p: Can reach to wound; 10

lg.l: But, as they grow where nothing is to fear,
Smooth and unarmed the pointless leaves appear.
I love to view these things with curious eyes,
And moralize;

div.p: And in this wisdom of the Holly Tree 15

lg.l: Can emblems see,
Wherewith perchance to make a pleasant rhyme,
One which may profit in the after-time.
Thus, though abroad perchance I might appear

div.p: Harsh and austere; 20

lg.l: To those who on my leisure would intrude,
Reserved and rude;—
Gentle at home amid my friends I’d be,
Like the high leaves upon the Holly Tree.

div.p: And should my youth, as youth is apt I know, 25

lg.l: Some harshness show,
All vain asperities I day by day
Would wear away,
Till the smooth temper of my age should be

div.p: Like the high leaves upon the Holly Tree. 30

lg.l: And as when all the summer trees are seen
So bright and green,
The Holly leaves a sober hue display
Less bright than they;

div.p: But when the bare and wintry woods we see, 35

lg.l: What then so cheerful as the Holly Tree?
So serious should my youth appear among
The thoughtless throng;
So would I seem amid the young and gay

div.p: More grave than they; 40
That in my age as cheerful I might be
As the green winter of the Holly Tree.

lg.l: A slanting ray of evening light
Shoots through the yellow pane:
It makes the faded crimson bright,
And gilds the fringe again;

div.p: The window’s gothic framework falls 5

lg.l: In oblique shadows on the walls.
And since those trappings first were new,
How many a cloudless day,
To rob the velvet of its hue,

div.p: Has come and passed away! 10

lg.l: How many a setting sun hath made
That curious lattice-work of shade!
Crumbled beneath the hillock green
The cunning hand must be,

div.p: That carved this fretted door, I ween, 15

lg.l: Acorn and fleur-de-lis;
And now the worm hath done her part
In mimicking the chisel’s art.
In days of yore (as now we call)

div.p: When the First James was king, 20

lg.l: The courtly knight from yonder Hall
His train did hither bring,
All seated round in order due,
With broidered suit and buckled shoe.

div.p: On damask cushions decked with fringe, 25

lg.l: All reverently they knelt;
Prayer-books, with brazen hasp and hinge,
In ancient English spelt,
Each holding in a lily hand,

div.p: Responsive to the priest’s command. 30

lg.l: Now, streaming down the vaulted aisle,
The sunbeam, long and lone,
Illumes the characters awhile
Of their inscription-stone:

div.p: And there, in marble hard and cold, 35

lg.l: The knight with all his train behold.
Outstretched together are exprest
He and my lady fair,
With hands uplifted on the breast,

div.p: In attitude of prayer: 40

lg.l: Long-visaged, clad in armour, he—
With ruffled arm and bodice she.
Set forth in order as they died,
Their numerous offspring bend,

div.p: Devoutly kneeling side by side, 45

lg.l: As if they did intend
For past omissions to atone
By saying endless prayers in stone.
Those mellow days are past and dim,

div.p: But generations new 50

lg.l: In regular descent from him
Have filled the stately pew,
And in the same succession go
To occupy the vaults below.

div.p: And now the polished modern Squire 55

lg.l: And his gay train appear,
Who duly to the Hall retire
A season every year,
And fill the seats with belle and beau,

div.p: As ’twas so many years ago; 60

lg.l: Perchance, all thoughtless, as they tread
The hollow-sounding floor,
Of that dark house of kindred dead,
Which shall, as heretofore,

div.p: In turn receive to silent rest 65

lg.l: Another and another guest:
The feathered hearse and sable train,
In all their wonted state,
Shall wind along the village lane,

div.p: And stand before the gate, 70

lg.l: Brought many a distant county through,
To join the final rendezvous.
And when the race is swept away,
All to their dusty beds,

div.p: Still shall the mellow evening ray 75

lg.l: Shine gaily o’er their heads;
While other faces, fresh and new,
Shall fill the Squire’s deserted pew.
Once a dream did weave a shade
O’er my angel-guarded bed,
That an emmet lost its way
Where on grass methought I lay.

div.p: Troubled, ’wildered, and forlorn, 5

lg.l: Dark, benighted, travel-worn,
Over many a tangled spray,
All heart-broke, I heard her say:
‘Oh, my children! do they cry,

div.p: Do they hear their father sigh? 10

lg.l: Now they look abroad to see,
Now return and weep for me.’
Pitying, I dropped a tear:
But I saw a glowworm near,

div.p: Who replied, ‘What wailing wight 15

lg.l: Calls the watchman of the night?
‘I am set to light the ground,
While the beetle goes his round.
Follow now the beetle’s hum,

div.p: Little wanderer, hie thee home!’ 20

lg.l: I love to rise ere gleams the tardy light,
Winter’s pale dawn; and as warm fires illume,
And cheerful tapers shine around the room,
Through misty windows bend my musing sight,

div.p: Where, round the dusky lawn, the mansions white 5

lg.l: With shutters closed peer faintly through the gloom,
That slow recedes; while yon grey spires assume,
Rising from their dark pile, an added height
By indistinctness given—Then to decree

div.p: The grateful thoughts to God, ere they unfold 10

lg.l: To friendship or the Muse, or seek with glee
Wisdom’s rich page. O hours more worth than gold,
By whose blest use we lengthen life, and, free
From drear decays of age, outlive the old!
Within a thick and spreading hawthorn bush,
That overhung a molehill large and round,
I heard from morn to morn a merry thrush
Sing hymns of rapture, while I drank the sound

div.p: With joy—and oft, an unintruding guest, 5

lg.l: I watched her secret toils from day to day;
How true she warped the moss to form her nest,
And modelled it within with wood and clay.
And by and by, like heath-bells gilt with dew,

div.p: There lay her shining eggs as bright as flowers, 10

lg.l: Ink-spotted over, shells of green and blue:
And there I witnessed in the summer hours
A brood of nature’s minstrels chirp and fly,
Glad as the sunshine and the laughing sky.
O Time! who know’st a lenient hand to lay
Softest on sorrow’s wound, and slowly thence,
Lulling to sad repose the weary sense,
The faint pang stealest unperceived away;

div.p: On thee I rest my only hope at last, 5

lg.l: And think, when thou hast dried the bitter tear
That flows in vain o’er all my soul held dear,
I may look back on every sorrow past
And meet life’s peaceful evening with a smile;

div.p: As some lone bird, at day’s departing hour, 10

lg.l: Sings in the sunbeam, of the transient shower
Forgetful, though its wings are wet the while;
Yet ah! how much must that poor heart endure,
Which hopes from thee, and thee alone, a cure.
Oh, it is pleasant, with a heart at ease,
Just after sunset, or by moonlight skies,
To make the shifting clouds be what you please,
Or let the easily-persuaded eyes

div.p: Own each quaint likeness issuing from the mould 5
Of a friend’s fancy; or, with head bent low,
And cheek aslant, see rivers flow of gold,
’Twixt crimson banks; and then a traveller go
From mount to mount, through Cloudland, gorgeous land!
Or, listening to the tide with closèd sight, 10

lg.l: Be that blind Bard, who on the Chian strand,
By those deep sounds possessed with inward light,
Beheld the Iliad and the Odyssee
Rise to the swelling of the voiceful sea.
It is a beauteous evening, calm and free;
The holy time is quiet as a nun
Breathless with adoration; the broad sun
Is sinking down in its tranquillity;

div.p: The gentleness of heaven is on the sea: 5

lg.l: Listen! the mighty Being is awake,
And doth with his eternal motion make
A sound like thunder—everlastingly.
Dear child! dear girl! that walkest with me here,

div.p: If thou appear’st untouched by solemn thought, 10

lg.l: Thy nature is not therefore less divine:
Thou liest in Abraham’s bosom all the year;
And worshipp’st at the temple’s inner shrine,
God being with thee when we know it not.
I will not praise the often-flattered rose,
Or, virgin-like, with blushing charms half seen,
Or when, in dazzling splendour, like a queen,
All her magnificence of state she shows;

div.p: No, nor that nun-like lily which but blows 5

lg.l: Beneath the valley’s cool and shady screen;
Nor yet the sun-flower, that with warrior mien
Still eyes the orb of glory where it glows;
But thou, neglected Wall-flower! to my breast

div.p: And Muse art dearest, wildest, sweetest flower! 10

lg.l: To whom alone the privilege is given
Proudly to root thyself above the rest;
As Genius does, and from thy rocky tower
Lend fragrance to the purest breath of heaven.
Hardly we breathe, although the air be free:
How massively doth awful Nature pile
The living rock, like some cathedral aisle,
Sacred to Silence and the solemn Sea.

div.p: How that clear pool lies sleeping tranquilly, 5

lg.l: And under its glassed waters seems to smile,
With many hues, a mimic grove the while
Of foliage submarine, shrub, flower, and tree.
Beautiful scene! and fitted to allure

div.p: The printless footsteps of some sea-born maid, 10

lg.l: Who here, with her green tresses disarrayed,
’Mid the clear bath, unfearing and secure,
May sport at noontide in the caverned shade—
Cold as the shadow—as the waters pure.

div.p: ’Twas on a Holy Thursday, their innocent faces clean,
The children walking two and two, in red, and blue, and green;
Grey-headed beadles walked before, with wands as white as snow,
Till into the high dome of Paul’s, they like Thames’ waters flow.
O what a multitude they seemed, these flowers of London town, 5
Seated in companies they sit, with radiance all their own:
The hum of multitudes was there, but multitudes of lambs,
Thousands of little boys and girls, raising their innocent hands.
Now like a mighty wind they raise to heaven the voice of song, 9
Or like harmonious thunderings the seats of heaven among:
Beneath them sit the agèd men, wise guardians of the poor.
Then cherish pity, lest you drive an angel from your door.

head.label: CLXXXIV
head.hi: ON AN ANTIQUE GEM BEARING THE HEADS OF PERICLES AND ASPASIA.

lg.l: This was the ruler of the land,
When Athens was the land of fame;
This was the light that led the band,
When each was like a living flame;

div.p: The centre of earth’s noblest ring— 5

lg.l: Of more than men the more than king!
Yet not by fetter, nor by spear,
His sovereignty was held or won:
Feared—but alone as freemen fear,

div.p: Loved—but as freemen love alone, 10

lg.l: He waved the sceptre o’er his kind
By nature’s first great title—mind!
Resistless words were on his tongue—
Then eloquence first flashed below;

div.p: Full armed to life the portent sprung— 15

lg.l: Minerva from the Thunderer’s brow!
And his the sole, the sacred hand
That shook her ægis o’er the land.
And throned immortal by his side,

div.p: A woman sits with eye sublime,— 20

lg.l: Aspasia, all his spirit’s bride;
But, if their solemn love were crime,
Pity the Beauty and the Sage—
Their crime was in their darkened age.

div.p: He perished, but his wreath was won— 25

lg.l: He perished in his height of fame;
Then sunk the cloud on Athens’ sun,
Yet still she conquered in his name.
Filled with his soul, she could not die;

div.p: Her conquest was posterity 30

lg.l: All thoughts, all passions, all delights,
Whatever stirs this mortal frame,
All are but ministers of Love,
And feed his sacred flame.

div.p: Oft in my waking dreams do I 5

lg.l: Live o’er again that happy hour,
When midway on the mount I lay,
Beside the ruined tower.
The moonshine stealing o’er the scene,

div.p: Had blended with the lights of eve; 10

lg.l: And she was there, my hope, my joy,
My own dear Genevieve!
She leaned against the armèd man,
The statue of the armèd knight;

div.p: She stood and listened to my lay, 15

lg.l: Amid the lingering light.
Few sorrows hath she of her own,
My hope! my joy! my Genevieve!
She loves me best, whene’er I sing

div.p: The songs that make her grieve. 20

lg.l: I played a soft and doleful air,
I sang an old and moving story—
An old rude song, that suited well
That ruin wild and hoary.

div.p: She listened with a flitting blush, 25

lg.l: With downcast eyes, and modest grace;
For well she knew, I could not choose
But gaze upon her face.
I told her of the Knight that wore

div.p: Upon his shield a burning brand; 30

lg.l: And that for ten long years he wooed
The Lady of the Land.
I told her how he pined: and ah!
The deep, the low, the pleading tone

div.p: With which I sang another’s love, 35

lg.l: Interpreted my own.
She listened with a flitting blush,
With downcast eyes, and modest grace;
And she forgave me, that I gazed

div.p: Too fondly on her face. 40

lg.l: But when I told the cruel scorn
That crazed that bold and lovely Knight,
And that he crossed the mountain-woods,
Nor rested day nor night;

div.p: That sometimes from the savage den, 45

lg.l: And sometimes from the darksome shade,
And sometimes starting up at once
In green and sunny glade,—
There came and looked him in the face

div.p: An angel beautiful and bright; 50

lg.l: And that he knew it was a fiend,
This miserable Knight!
And that unknowing what he did,
He leaped amid a murderous band,

div.p: And saved from outrage worse than death 55

lg.l: The Lady of the Land;—
And how she wept, and clasped his knees,
And how she tended him in vain;
And ever strove to expiate

div.p: The scorn that crazed his brain;— 60

lg.l: And that she nursed him in a cave;
And how his madness went away,
When on the yellow forest-leaves
A dying man he lay;—

div.p: His dying words—but when I reached 65

lg.l: That tenderest strain of all the ditty,
My faltering voice and pausing harp
Disturbed her soul with pity!
All impulses of soul and sense

div.p: Had thrilled my guileless Genevieve; 70

lg.l: The music and the doleful tale,
The rich and balmy eve;
And hopes, and fears that kindle hope,
An undistinguishable throng,

div.p: And gentle wishes long subdued, 75

lg.l: Subdued and cherished long!
She wept with pity and delight,
She blushed with love and virgin shame;
And like the murmur of a dream,

div.p: I heard her breathe my name. 80

lg.l: Her bosom heaved—she stepped aside,
As conscious of my look she stept—
Then suddenly, with timorous eye,
She fled to me and wept

div.p: She half enclosed me with her arms, 85
She pressed me with a meek embrace;
And bending back her head, looked up,
And gazed upon my face.
’Twas partly love, and partly fear,
And partly ’twas a bashful art, 90

lg.l: That I might rather feel, than see,
The swelling of her heart.
I calmed her fears, and she was calm,
And told her love with virgin pride;

div.p: And so I won my Genevieve, 95
My bright and beauteous Bride.

lg.l: She walks in beauty, like the night
Of cloudless climes and starry skies;
And all that’s best of dark and bright
Meet in her aspect and her eyes:

div.p: Thus mellowed to that tender light 5

lg.l: Which heaven to gaudy day denies.
One shade the more, one ray the less,
Had half impaired the nameless grace,
Which waves in every raven tress,

div.p: Or softly lightens o’er her face; 10

lg.l: Where thoughts serenely sweet express,
How pure, how dear their dwelling-place.
And on that cheek, and o’er that brow,
So soft, so calm, yet eloquent,

div.p: The smiles that win, the tints that glow, 15

lg.l: But tell of days in goodness spent,
A mind at peace with all below,
A heart whose love is innocent!
Oh welcome, bat and owlet gray,
Thus winging low your airy way!
And welcome, moth and drowsy fly,
That to mine ear come humming by!

div.p: And welcome, shadows dim and deep, 5

lg.l: And stars that through the pale sky peep!
O welcome all! to me ye say,
My woodland Love is on her way.
Upon the soft wind floats her hair;

div.p: Her breath is in the dewy air; 10

lg.l: Her steps are in the whispered sound,
That steals along the stilly ground.
O dawn of day, in rosy bower,
What art thou to this witching hour?

div.p: O noon of day, in sunshine bright, 15
What art thou to the fall of night?

lg.l: She was a queen of noble Nature’s crowning,
A smile of her’s was like an act of grace;
She had no winsome looks, no pretty frowning,
Like daily beauties of the vulgar race;

div.p: But if she smiled, a light was on her face, 5

lg.l: A clear, cool kindliness, a lunar beam
Of peaceful radiance, silvering o’er the stream
Of human thought with unabiding glory;
Not quite a waking truth, not quite a dream,

div.p: A visitation, bright and transitory. 10

lg.l: But she is changed,—hath felt the touch of sorrow;
No love hath she, no understanding friend;
Oh grief! when heaven is forced of earth to borrow
What the poor niggard earth has not to lend;

div.p: But when the stalk is snapt, the rose must bend. 15

lg.l: The tallest flower that skyward rears its head,
Grows from the common ground, and there must shed
Its delicate petals. Cruel fate, too surely,
That they should find so base a bridal bed,

div.p: Who lived in virgin pride, so sweet and purely! 20

lg.l: She had a brother, and a tender father;
And she was loved, but not as others are,
From whom we ask return of love,—but rather
As one might love a dream; a phantom-fair

div.p: Of something exquisitely strange and rare, 25

lg.l: Which all were glad to look on, men and maids,
Yet no one claimed—as oft, in dewy glades
The peering primrose, like a sudden gladness,
Gleams on the soul, yet unregarded fades;—

div.p: The joy is ours, but all its own the sadness. 30
’Tis vain to say—her worst of grief is only
The common lot, which all the world have known;
To her ’tis more, because her heart is lonely,
And yet she hath no strength to stand alone;—
Once she had playmates, fancies of her own, 35

lg.l: And she did love them. They are past away,
As fairies vanish at the break of day;
And like a spectre of an age departed,
Or unsphered angel wofully astray,
She glides along—the solitary-hearted.
Proud Maisie is in the wood,
Walking so early;
Sweet Robin sits on the bush,
Singing so rarely.

div.p: ‘Tell me, thou bonny bird, 5
When shall I marry me?’
—‘When six braw gentlemen
Kirkward shall carry ye.’
‘Who makes the bridal bed,
Birdie, say truly?’ 10
—‘The gray-headed sexton
That delves the grave duly.
‘The glowworm o’er grave and stone
Shall light thee steady;
The owl from the steeple sing, 15
Welcome, proud lady.’

lg.l: An hour with thee!—When earliest day
Dapples with gold the eastern gray,
Oh, what can frame my mind to bear
The toil and turmoil, cark and care,

div.p: New griefs, which coming hours unfold, 5

lg.l: And sad remembrance of the old?—
One hour with thee.
One hour with thee!—When burning June
Waves his red flag at pitch of noon;

div.p: What shall repay the faithful swain 10

lg.l: His labour on the sultry plain;
And more than cave or sheltering bough,
Cool feverish blood, and throbbing brow?—
One hour with thee.

div.p: One hour with thee!—When sun is set, 15

lg.l: Oh, what can teach me to forget
The thankless labours of the day,
The hopes, the wishes, flung away,
The increasing wants, and lessening gains,

div.p: The master’s pride, who scorns my pains?— 20
One hour with thee.

lg.l: The waters are flashing,
The white hail is dashing,
The lightnings are glancing,
The hoar-spray is dancing—

div.p: Away! 5

lg.l: The whirlwind is rolling,
The thunder is tolling,
The forest is swinging,
The minster bells ringing—

div.p: Come away! 10

lg.l: The earth is like ocean,
Wreck-strewn and in motion:
Bird, beast, man, and worm,
Have crept out of the storm—

div.p: Come away! 15
‘Our boat has one sail,
And the helmsman is pale;—A bold pilot I trow,
Who should follow us now,’
Shouted He— 20

lg.l: And She cried: ‘Ply the oar,
Put off gaily from shore!’
As she spoke bolts of death,
Mixed with hail, specked their path

div.p: O’er the sea. 25

lg.l: And from isle, tower, and rock,
The blue beacon-cloud broke,
Though dumb in the blast,
The red cannon flashed fast

div.p: From the lee. 30

lg.l: ‘And fear’st thou, and fear’st thou?
And see’st thou, and hear’st thou?
And drive we not free
O’er the terrible sea,

div.p: I and thou?’ 35

lg.l: One boat-cloak did cover
The loved and the lover—
Their blood beats one measure,
They murmur proud pleasure

div.p: Soft and low;— 40
While around the lashed ocean,
Like mountains in motion,
Is withdrawn and uplifted, Sunk,
shattered, and shifted,
To and fro. 45

lg.l: In the court of the fortress,
Beside the pale portress,
Like a bloodhound well beaten
The bridegroom stands, eaten

div.p: By shame: 50

lg.l: On the topmost watch turret,
As a death-boding spirit,
Stands the gray tyrant father,
To his voice the mad weather

div.p: Seems tame; 55

lg.l: And with curses as wild
As e’er clung to child,
He devotes to the blast
The best, loveliest, and last,

div.p: Of his name! 60

lg.l: She dwelt among the untrodden ways
Beside the springs of Dove;
A maid whom there were none to praise,
And very few to love.

div.p: A violet by a mossy stone 5
Half-hidden from the eye!
—Fair as a star, when only one
Is shining in the sky.
She lived unknown, and few could know
When Lucy ceased to be; 10
But she is in her grave, and oh!
The difference to me!

lg.l: O Goddess, hear these tuneless numbers, wrung
By sweet enforcement and remembrance dear,
And pardon that thy secrets should be sung,
Even into thine own soft-conchèd ear:

div.p: Surely I dreamt to-day, or did I see 5

lg.l: The wingèd Psyche with awakened eyes?
I wandered in a forest thoughtlessly,
And, on the sudden, fainting with surprise,
Saw two fair creatures, couchèd side by side

div.p: In deepest grass, beneath the whispering roof 10
Of leaves and trembled blossoms, where there ran
A brooklet, scarce espied:
’Mid hushed, cool-rooted flowers fragrant-eyed,
Blue, silver-white, and budded Tyrian,
They lay calm-breathing on the bedded grass; 15

lg.l: Their arms embracèd, and their pinions too;
Their lips touched not, but had not bade adieu,
As if disjoinèd by soft-handed slumber,
And ready still past kisses to outnumber

div.p: At tender eye-dawn of aurorean love: 20

lg.l: The wingèd Boy I knew;
But who wast thou, O happy, happy dove?
His Psyche true!
O latest-born and loveliest vision far

div.p: Of all Olympus’ faded hierarchy! 25

lg.l: Fairer than Phœbe’s sapphire-regioned star!
Or Vesper, amorous glowworm of the sky;
Fairer than these, though temple thou hast none,
Nor altar heaped with flowers;

div.p: Nor Virgin-choir to make delicious moan 30

lg.l: Upon the midnight hours;
No voice, no lute, no pipe, no incense sweet
From chain-swung censer teeming;
No shrine, no grove, no oracle, no heat

div.p: Of pale-mouthed prophet dreaming. 35

lg.l: O brightest! though too late for antique vows,
Too, too late for the fond believing lyre,
When holy were the haunted forest boughs,
Holy the air, the water, and the fire;

div.p: Yet even in these days so far retired 40

lg.l: From happy pieties, thy lucent fans,
Fluttering among the faint Olympians,
I see, and sing, by my own eyes inspired.
So let me be thy choir, and make a moan

div.p: Upon the midnight hours; 45

lg.l: Thy voice, thy lute, thy pipe, thy incense sweet
From swingèd censer teeming:
Thy shrine, thy grove, thy oracle, thy heat
Of pale-mouthed prophet dreaming.

div.p: Yes, I will be thy priest, and build a fane 50

lg.l: In some untrodden region of my mind,
Where branchèd thoughts, new-grown with pleasant pain,
Instead of pines shall murmur in the wind:
Far, far around shall those dark-clustered trees

div.p: Fledge the wild-ridgèd mountains steep by steep; 55

lg.l: And there by zephyrs, streams, and birds, and bees,
The moss-lain Dryads shall be lulled to sleep;
And in the midst of this wide quietness
A rosy sanctuary will I dress

div.p: With the wreathed trellis of a working brain, 60

lg.l: With buds, and bells, and stars without a name,
With all the gardener Fancy e’er could feign,
Who breeding flowers, will never breed the same:
And there shall be for thee all soft delight

div.p: That shadowy thought can win, 65
A bright torch, and a casement ope at night,
To let the warm Love in!

lg.l: Ah Sunflower! weary of time,
Who countest the steps of the sun;
Seeking after that sweet golden clime
Where the traveller’s journey is done;

div.p: Where the Youth pined away with desire, 5

lg.l: And the pale Virgin shrouded in snow,
Arise from their graves, and aspire
Where my Sunflower wishes to go.
Too true it is, my time of power was spent
In idly watering weeds of casual growth,
That wasted energy to desperate sloth
Declined, and fond self-seeking discontent;

div.p: That the huge debt for all that Nature lent 5
I sought to cancel, and was nothing loth
To deem myself an outlaw, severed both
From duty and from hope,—yea, blindly sent
Without an errand, where I would to stray:—
Too true it is, that, knowing now my state, 10

lg.l: I weakly mourn the sin I ought to hate,
Nor love the law I yet would fain obey:
But true it is, above all law and fate
Is Faith, abiding the appointed day.

head.label: CXCVI
head.hi: TO A LOFTY BEAUTY, FROM HER POOR KINSMAN.

lg.l: Fair maid, had I not heard thy baby cries,
Nor seen thy girlish, sweet vicissitude,
Thy mazy motions, striving to elude,
Yet wooing still a parents watchful eyes,

div.p: Thy humours, many as the opal’s dyes, 5

lg.l: And lovely all;—methinks thy scornful mood,
And bearing high of stately womanhood,—
Thy brow, where Beauty sits to tyrannize
O’er humble love, had made me sadly fear thee;

div.p: For never sure was seen a royal bride, 10

lg.l: Whose gentleness gave grace to so much pride—
My very thoughts would tremble to be near thee:
But when I see thee at thy father’s side,
Old times unqueen thee, and old loves endear thee.
Green little vaulter on the sunny grass,
Catching your heart up at the feel of June,
Sole voice that’s heard amidst the lazy noon,
When ev’n the bees lag at the summoning brass;

div.p: And you, warm little housekeeper, who class 5

lg.l: With those who think the candles come too soon,
Loving the fire, and with your tricksome tune
Nick the glad silent moments as they pass;
O sweet and tiny cousins, that belong,

div.p: One to the fields, the other to the hearth, 10

lg.l: Both have your sunshine; both, though small, are strong
At your clear hearts, and both seem given to earth
To sing in thoughtful ears this natural song,
In doors and out, summer and winter, mirth.

head.label: CXCVIII
head.hi: TO A BIRD THAT HAUNTED THE WATERS OF LAKEN IN THE WINTER.

lg.l: O melancholy bird!—a winter’s day
Thou standest by the margin of the pool,
And, taught by God, dost thy whole being school
To patience, which all evil can allay;

div.p: God has appointed thee the fish thy prey; 5

lg.l: And given thyself a lesson to the fool
Unthrifty, to submit to moral rule,
And his unthinking course by thee to weigh.
There need not schools, nor the professor’s chair,

div.p: Though these be good, true wisdom to impart; 10

lg.l: He, who has not enough for these to spare
Of time or gold, may yet amend his heart,
And teach his soul by brooks and rivers fair;
Nature is always wise in every part.
When in the woods I wander all alone,
The woods that are my solace and delight,
Which I more covet than a prince’s throne,
My toil by day and canopy by night;

div.p: (Light heart, light foot, light food, and slumber light, 5

lg.l: These lights shall light me to old age’s gate,
While monarchs, whom rebellious dreams affright,
Heavy with fear, death’s fearful summons wait;)
Whilst here I wander, pleased to be alone,

div.p: Weighing in thought the world’s no-happiness, 10

lg.l: I cannot choose but wonder at its moan,
Since so plain joys the woody life can bless:
Then live who may where honied words prevail,
I with the deer, and with the nightingale!
Again the violet of our early days
Drinks beauteous azure from the golden sun,
And kindles into fragrance at his blaze;
The streams, rejoiced that winter’s work is done,

div.p: Talk of to-morrow’s cowslips, as they run. 5
Wild apple! thou art bursting into bloom;
Thy leaves are coming, snowy-blossomed thorn!
Wake, buried lily! spirit, quit thy tomb;
And thou, shade-loving hyacinth, be born. 9
Then haste, sweet rose! sweet woodbine, hymn the morn,
Whose dew-drops shall illume with pearly light
Each grassy blade that thick embattled stands
From sea to sea, while daisies infinite
Uplift in praise their little glowing hands
O’er every hill that under heaven expands. 15

lg.l: The poetry of earth is never dead:
When all the birds are faint with the hot sun,
And hide in cooling trees, a voice will run
From hedge to hedge about the new-mown mead;

div.p: That is the grasshopper’s—he takes the lead 5

lg.l: In summer luxury,—he has never done
With his delights, for when tired out with fun,
He rests at ease beneath some pleasant weed.
The poetry of earth is ceasing never:

div.p: On a lone winter evening, when the frost 10

lg.l: Has wrought a silence, from the stove there shrills
The cricket’s song, in warmth increasing ever,
And seems to one in drowsiness half lost,
The grasshopper’s among some grassy hills.
Lady, I bid thee to a sunny dome,
Ringing with echoes of Italian song:
Henceforth to thee these magic halls belong,
And all the pleasant place is like a home.

div.p: Hark, on the right with full piano tone 5

lg.l: Old Dante’s voice encircles all the air:
Hark yet again, like flute-tones mingling rare,
Comes the keen sweetness of Petrarca’s moan.
Pass thou the lintel freely; without fear

div.p: Feast on the music. I do better know thee, 10

lg.l: Than to suspect this pleasure thou dost owe me
Will wrong thy gentle spirit, or make less dear
That element whence thou must draw thy life—
An English maiden, and an English wife.
The Assyrian came down like the wolf on the fold,
And his cohorts were gleaming in purple and gold;
And the sheen of their spears was like stars on the sea,
When the blue wave rolls nightly on deep Galilee.

div.p: Like the leaves of the forest when summer is green, 5

lg.l: That host with their banners at sunset were seen:
Like the leaves of the forest when autumn hath blown,
That host on the morrow lay withered and strown:
For the Angel of Death spread his wings on the blast,

div.p: And breathed in the face of the foe as he passed; 10

lg.l: And the eyes of the sleepers waxed deadly and chill,
And their hearts but once heaved, and for ever grew still!
And there lay the steed with his nostril all wide,
But through it there rolled not the breath of his pride;

div.p: And the foam of his gasping lay white on the turf, 15

lg.l: And cold as the spray of the rock-beating surf,
And there lay the rider distorted and pale,
With the dew on his brow and the rust on his mail;
And the tents were all silent, the banners alone,

div.p: The lances unlifted, the trumpet unblown: 20

lg.l: And the widows of Ashur are loud in their wail,
And the idols are broke in the temple of Baal;
And the might of the Gentile, unsmote by the sword,
Hath melted like snow in the glance of the Lord!
Is this the spot where Rome’s eternal foe
Into his snares the mighty legions drew,
Whence from the carnage, spiritless and few,
A remnant scarcely reached her gates of woe?

div.p: Is this the stream, thus gliding soft and slow, 5
That, from the gushing wounds of thousands, grew
So fierce a flood, that waves of crimson hue
Rushed on the bosom of the lake below?
The mountains that gave back the battle-cry
Are silent now;—perchance yon hillocks green 10
Mark where the bones of those old warriors lie!

lg.l: Heaven never gladdened a more peaceful scene;
Never left softer breeze a fairer sky
To sport upon thy waters, Thrasymene.

div.p: BY OBADIAH BIND-THEIR-KINGS-IN-CHAINS-AND-THEIR-NOBLES-WITH-LINKS-OF-IRON, SERJEANT IN IRETON’S REGIMENT.
Oh! wherefore come ye forth, in triumph from the North,
With your hands, and your feet, and your raiment all red?
And wherefore doth your rout send forth a joyous shout?
And whence be the grapes of the wine-press which ye tread?
Oh evil was the root, and bitter was the fruit, 5
And crimson was the juice of the vintage that we trod;
For we trampled on the throng of the haughty and the strong,
Who sate in the high places, and slew the saints of God.
It was about the noon of a glorious day of June, 9
That we saw their banners dance, and their cuirasses shine,
And the Man of Blood was there, with his long essenced hair,
And Astley, and Sir Marmaduke, and Rupert of the Rhine.
Like a servant of the Lord, with his Bible and his sword,
The General rode along us to form us to the fight,
When a murmuring sound broke out, and swelled into a shout, 15
Among the godless horsemen upon the tyrant’s right.
And hark! like the roar of the billows on the shore,
The cry of battle rises along their charging line!
For God! for the Cause! for the Church! for the Laws!
For Charles King of England, and Rupert of the Rhine! 20
The furious German comes, with his clarions and his drums,
His bravoes of Alsatia, and pages of Whitehall;
They are bursting on our flanks. Grasp your pikes, close your ranks;
For Rupert never comes but to conquer or to fall.
They are here! They rush on! We are broken! We are gone! 25
Our left is borne before them like stubble on the blast,
O Lord, put forth thy might! O Lord, defend the right!
Stand back to back, in God’s name, and fight it to the last.
Stout Skippon hath a wound; the centre hath given ground:
Hark! hark!—What means the trampling of horsemen on our rear? 30
Whose banner do I see, boys? ’Tis he, thank God, ’tis he, boys.
Bear up another minute: brave Oliver is here.
Their heads all stooping low, their points all in a row,
Like a whirlwind on the trees, like a deluge on the dykes,
Our cuirassiers have burst on the ranks of the Accurst, 35

lg.l: And at a shock have scattered the forest of his pikes.
Fast, fast, the gallants ride, in some safe nook to hide
Their coward heads, predestined to rot on Temple Bar:
And he—he turns, he flies:—shame on those cruel eyes

div.p: That bore to look on torture, and dare not look on war. 40
Ho! comrades, scour the plain; and, ere ye strip the slain,
First give another stab to make your search secure,
Then shake from sleeves and pockets their broad-pieces and lockets,
The tokens of the wanton, the plunder of the poor.
Fools! your doublets shone with gold, and your hearts were gay and bold, 45
When you kissed your lily hands to your lemans to-day;
And to-morrow shall the fox, from her chambers in the rocks,
Lead forth her tawny cubs to howl above the prey.
Where be your tongues that late mocked at heaven and hell and fate,
And the fingers that once were so busy with your blades, 50
Your perfumed satin clothes, your catches and your oaths,
Your stage-plays and your sonnets, your diamonds and your spades?
Down, down, for ever down with the Mitre and the Crown,
With the Belial of the Court, and the Mammon of the Pope;
There is woe in Oxford Halls; there is wail in Durham’s Stalls: 55
The Jesuit smites his bosom: the Bishop rends his cope.
And She of the seven hills shall mourn her children’s ills,
And tremble when she thinks on the edge of England’s sword;
And the kings of earth in fear shall shudder when they hear
What the hand of God hath wrought for the Houses and the Word. 60

lg.l: While the dawn on the mountain was misty and gray,
My true love has mounted his steed and away,
Over hill, over valley, o’er dale, and o’er down;
Heaven shield the brave Gallant that fights for the Crown!

div.p: He has doffed the silk doublet the breast-plate to bear, 5
He has placed the steel-cap o’er his long-flowing hair,
From his belt to his stirrup his broadsword hangs down,—
Heaven shield the brave Gallant that fights for the Crown!
For the rights of fair England that broadsword he draws,
Her King is his leader, her Church is his cause; 10

lg.l: His watchword is honour, his pay is renown,—
God strike with the Gallant that strikes for the Crown!
They may boast of their Fairfax, their Waller, and all
The roundheaded rebels of Westminster Hall;

div.p: But tell these bold traitors of London’s proud town, 15
That the spears of the North have encircled the Crown.
There’s Derby and Cavendish, dread of their foes;
There’s Erin’s high Ormond and Scotland’s Montrose!
Would you match the base Skippon, and Massey, and Brown,
With the Barons of England, that fight for the Crown? 20
Now joy to the crest of the brave Cavalier!

lg.l: Be his banner unconquered, resistless his spear,
Till in peace and in triumph his toils he may drown
In a pledge to Fair England, her Church, and her Crown.
Of Nelson and the North
Sing the glorious day’s renown,
When to battle fierce came forth
All the might of Denmark’s crown,

div.p: And her arms along the deep proudly shone; 5

lg.l: By each gun the lighted brand
In a bold determined hand,
And the Prince of all the land
Led them on.

div.p: Like leviathans afloat 10

lg.l: Lay their bulwarks on the brine,
While the sign of battle flew
On the lofty British line:
It was ten of April morn by the chime;

div.p: As they drifted on their path, 15

lg.l: There was silence deep as death,
And the boldest held his breath
For a time.
But the might of England flushed

div.p: To anticipate the scene; 20
And her van the fleeter rushed
O’er the deadly space between.
‘Hearts of oak!’ our captains cried; when each gun
From its adamantine lips
Spread a death-shade round the ships, 25

lg.l: Like the hurricane eclipse
Of the sun.
Again! again! again!
And the havoc did not slack,

div.p: Till a feeble cheer the Dane 30

lg.l: To our cheering sent us back;—
Their shots along the deep slowly boom:—
Then ceased—and all is wail,
As they strike the shattered sail,

div.p: Or, in conflagration pale, 35

lg.l: Light the gloom.
Out spoke the victor then,
As he hailed them o’er the wave:
‘Ye are brothers! ye are men!

div.p: And we conquer but to save: 40

lg.l: So peace instead of death let us bring;
But yield, proud foe, thy fleet,
With the crews, at England’s feet,
And make submission meet

div.p: To our King.’ 45

lg.l: Then Denmark blessed our chief
That he gave her wounds repose;
And the sounds of joy and grief
From her people wildly rose,

div.p: As death withdrew his shades from the day; 50

lg.l: While the sun looked smiling bright
O’er a wide and woeful sight,
Where the fires of funeral light
Died away.

div.p: Now joy, Old England, raise 55

lg.l: For the tidings of thy might,
By the festal cities’ blaze,
Whilst the wine-cup shines in light;
And yet, amidst that joy and uproar,

div.p: Let us think of them that sleep 60

lg.l: Full many a fathom deep,
By thy wild and stormy steep,
Elsinore!
Brave hearts! to Britain’s pride

div.p: Once so faithful and so true, 65

lg.l: On the deck of fame that died,
With the gallant good Riou:
Soft sigh the winds of heaven o’er their grave!
While the billow mournful rolls,

div.p: And the mermaid’s song condoles, 70
Singing glory to the souls
Of the brave!

lg.l: On Linden, when the sun was low,
All bloodless lay the untrodden snow;
And dark as winter was the flow
Of Iser, rolling rapidly.

div.p: But Linden saw another sight, 5

lg.l: When the drum beat at dead of night,
Commanding fires of death to light
The darkness of her scenery.
By torch and trumpet fast arrayed,

div.p: Each horseman drew his battle-blade, 10

lg.l: And furious every charger neighed
To join the dreadful revelry.
Then shook the hills, with thunder riven;
Then rushed the steed, to battle driven;

div.p: And louder than the bolts of Heaven 15

lg.l: Far flashed the red artillery.
But redder yet that light shall glow
On Linden’s hills of stainèd snow,
And bloodier yet the torrent flow

div.p: Of Iser, rolling rapidly. 20
’Tis morn; but scarce yon level sun
Can pierce the war-clouds, rolling dun,
Where furious Frank and fiery Hun
Shout in their sulphurous canopy.
The combat deepens. On, ye brave, 25

lg.l: Who rush to glory, or the grave!
Wave, Munich, all thy banners wave,
And charge with all thy chivalry!
Few, few shall part, where many meet;

div.p: The snow shall be their winding-sheet; 30
And every turf beneath their feet
Shall be a soldier’s sepulchre.

head.label: CCIX
head.hi: ON THE EXTINCTION OF THE VENETIAN REPUBLIC.

lg.l: Once did She hold the gorgeous East in fee,
And was the safeguard of the West; the worth
Of Venice did not fall below her birth,
Venice, the eldest child of liberty.

div.p: She was a maiden City, bright and free; 5

lg.l: No guile seduced, no force could violate;
And when she took unto herself a mate,
She must espouse the everlasting Sea.
And what if she had seen those glories fade,

div.p: Those titles vanish, and that strength decay,— 10

lg.l: Yet shall some tribute of regret be paid
When her long life hath reached its final day:
Men are we, and must grieve when even the shade
Of that which once was great has passed away.

head.label: CCX
head.hi: COMPOSED BY THE SEA-SIDE, NEAR CALAIS, AUGUST, 1802.

lg.l: Fair Star of Evening, Splendour of the West,
Star of my country!—on the horizon’s brink
Thou hangest, stooping, as might seem, to sink
On England’s bosom; yet well pleased to rest,

div.p: Meanwhile, and be to her a glorious crest, 5

lg.l: Conspicuous to the Nations. Thou, I think,
Should’st be my Country’s emblem; and should’st wink,
Bright Star! with laughter on her banners, drest
In thy fresh beauty. There! that dusky spot

div.p: Beneath thee, that is England; there it lies. 10

lg.l: Blessings be on you both! one hope, one lot,
One life, one glory! I with many a fear
For my dear Country, many heartfelt sighs,
Among men who do not love her, linger here.

div.p: Another year!—another deadly blow!
Another mighty empire overthrown!
And we are left, or shall be left, alone;
The last that dare to struggle with the foe.
’Tis well! from this day forward we shall know 5

lg.l: That in ourselves our safety must be sought;
That by our own right hands it must be wrought;
That we must stand unpropped, or be laid low.
O dastard whom such foretaste doth not cheer!

div.p: We shall exult, if they who rule the land 10

lg.l: Be men who hold its many blessings dear,
Wise, upright, valiant; not a servile band,
Who are to judge of danger which they fear,
And honour which they do not understand.

head.label: CCXII
head.hi: THE BURIAL OF SIR JOHN MOORE.

lg.l: Not a drum was heard, not a funeral note,
As his corpse to the rampart we hurried;
Not a soldier discharged his farewell shot
O’er the grave where our hero we buried.

div.p: We buried him darkly at dead of night, 5
