lg.l: The sods with our bayonets turning;
By the struggling moonbeam’s misty light,
And the lantern dimly burning.
No useless coffin enclosed his breast.

div.p: Not in sheet nor in shroud we wound him; 10

lg.l: But he lay like a warrior taking his rest,
With his martial cloak around him.
Few and short were the prayers we said,
And we spoke not a word of sorrow;

div.p: But we stedfastly gazed on the face that was dead, 15

lg.l: And we bitterly thought of the morrow.
We thought as we hollowed his narrow bed,
And smoothed down his lonely pillow,
That the foe and the stranger would tread o’er his head,

div.p: And we far away on the billow! 20

lg.l: Lightly they’ll talk of the spirit that’s gone,
And o’er his cold ashes upbraid him,—
But little he’ll reck, if they let him sleep on
In the grave where a Briton has laid him.

div.p: But half of our heavy task was done, 25

lg.l: When the clock struck the hour for retiring;
And we heard the distant and random gun
That the foe was sullenly firing.
Slowly and sadly we laid him down,

div.p: From the field of his fame fresh and gory; 30
We carved not a line, and we raised not a stone—
But we left him alone with his glory.
’Tis done—but yesterday a King!
And armed with Kings to strive—
And now thou art a nameless thing:
So abject—yet alive!
Is this the man of thousand thrones, 5

lg.l: Who strewed our earth with hostile bones,
And can he thus survive?
Since he, miscalled the Morning Star,
Nor man nor fiend hath fall’n so far.

div.p: Ill-minded man! why scourge thy kind 10

lg.l: Who bowed so low the knee?
By gazing on thyself grown blind,
Thou taught’st the rest to see.
With might unquestioned,—power to save,—

div.p: Thine only gift hath been the grave, 15

lg.l: To those that worshipped thee;
Nor till thy fall could mortals guess
Ambition’s less than littleness!
Thanks for that lesson—it will teach

div.p: To after-warriors more 20

lg.l: Than high Philosophy can preach,
And vainly preached before.
That spell upon the minds of men
Breaks, never to unite again,

div.p: That led them to adore 25

lg.l: Those Pagod things of sabre sway,
With fronts of brass, and feet of clay.
The triumph, and the vanity,
The rapture of the strife—

div.p: The earthquake voice of Victory, 30

lg.l: To thee the breath of life;
The sword, the sceptre, and that sway
Which man seemed made but to obey,
Wherewith renown was rife—

div.p: All quelled!—Dark Spirit! what must be 35
The madness of thy memory!
The Desolator desolate!
The Victor overthrown!
The Arbiter of others’ fate
A suppliant for his own! 40

lg.l: Is it some yet imperial hope,
That with such change can calmly cope?
Or dread of death alone?
To die a prince—or live a slave—

div.p: Thy choice is most ignobly brave! 45

lg.l: He who of old would rend the oak,
Dreamed not of the rebound:
Chained by the trunk he vainly broke—
Alone—how looked he round?

div.p: Thou, in the sternness of thy strength, 50

lg.l: An equal deed hast done at length,
And darker fate hast found:
He fell, the forest prowlers’ prey;
But thou must eat thy heart away!

div.p: The Roman, when his burning heart 55

lg.l: Was slaked with blood of Rome,
Threw down the dagger—dared depart,
In savage grandeur, home—
He dared depart in utter scorn

div.p: Of men that such a yoke had borne, 60

lg.l: Yet left him such a doom!
His only glory was that hour
Of self-upheld abandoned power.
The Spaniard, when the lust of sway

div.p: Had lost its quickening spell, 65

lg.l: Cast crowns for rosaries away,
An empire for a cell;
A strict accountant of his beads,
A subtle disputant on creeds,

div.p: His dotage trifled well: 70

lg.l: Yet better had he neither known
A bigot’s shrine, nor despot’s throne.
But thou—from thy reluctant hand
The thunderbolt is wrung—

div.p: Too late thou leav’st the high command 75

lg.l: To which thy weakness clung;
All Evil Spirit as thou art,
It is enough to grieve the heart,
To see thine own unstrung;

div.p: To think that God’s fair world hath been 80

lg.l: The footstool of a thing so mean!
And Earth hath spilt her blood for him,
Who thus can hoard his own!
And Monarchs bowed the trembling limb,

div.p: And thanked him for a throne! 85

lg.l: Fair Freedom! we may hold thee dear,
When thus thy mightiest foes their fear
In humblest guise have shown.
Oh! ne’er may tyrant leave behind

div.p: A brighter name to lure mankind! 90

lg.l: Thine evil deeds are writ in gore,
Nor written thus in vain—
Thy triumphs tell of fame no more,
Or deepen every stain:

div.p: If thou hadst died as honour dies, 95

lg.l: Some new Napoleon might arise,
To shame the world again—
But who would soar the solar height,
To set in such a starless night?

div.p: Weighed in the balance, hero dust 100

lg.l: Is vile as vulgar clay:
Thy scales, Mortality, are just
To all that pass away:
But yet methought the living great

div.p: Some higher sparks should animate, 105

lg.l: To dazzle and dismay:
Nor deemed Contempt could thus make mirth
Of these, the conquerors of the earth.
And she, proud Austria’s mournful flower,

div.p: Thy still imperial bride, 110

lg.l: How bears her breast the torturing hour?
Still clings she to thy side?
Must she too bend, must she too share
Thy late repentance, long despair,

div.p: Thou throneless Homicide? 115
If still she loves thee, hoard that gem;
’Tis worth thy vanished diadem!
Then haste thee to thy sullen Isle,
And gaze upon the sea;
That element may meet thy smile— 120

lg.l: It ne’er was ruled by thee!
Or trace with thine all-idle hand,
In loitering mood upon the sand,
That Earth is now as free,

div.p: That Corinth’s pedagogue hath now 125

lg.l: Transferred his by-word to thy brow.
Thou Timour! in his captive’s cage—
What thoughts will there be thine,
While brooding in thy prisoned rage?

div.p: But one—‘The world was mine!’ 130

lg.l: Unless, like he of Babylon,
All sense is with thy sceptre gone,
Life will not long confine
That spirit poured so widely forth—

div.p: So long obeyed—so little worth! 135

lg.l: Or, like the thief of fire from heaven,
Wilt thou withstand the shock?
And share with him, the unforgiven,
His vulture and his rock!

div.p: Foredoomed by God—by man accurst, 140

lg.l: And that last act, though not thy worst,
The very Fiend’s arch-mock;
He in his fall preserved his pride,
And, if a mortal, had as proudly died!

div.p: FOR THE ANNIVERSARY MEETING OF THE PITT CLUB OF SCOTLAND, 1814.

lg.l: O dread was the time, and more dreadful the omen,
When the brave on Marengo lay slaughtered in vain,
And beholding broad Europe bowed down by her foemen,
Pitt closed in his anguish the map of her reign!

div.p: Not the fate of broad Europe could bend his brave spirit 5

lg.l: To take for his country the safety of shame;
O then in her triumph remember his merit,
And hallow the goblet that flows to his name.
Round the husbandman’s head, while he traces the furrow,

div.p: The mists of the winter may mingle with rain, 10

lg.l: He may plough it with labour, and sow it in sorrow,
And sigh while he fears he has sowed it in vain;
He may die ere his children shall reap in their gladness,
But the blithe harvest-home shall remember his claim;

div.p: And their jubilee-shout shall be softened with sadness, 15

lg.l: While they hallow the goblet that flows to his name.
Though anxious and timeless his life was expended,
In foils for our Country preserved by his care,
Though he died ere one ray o’er the nations ascended,

div.p: To light the long darkness of doubt and despair; 20

lg.l: The storms he endured in our Britain’s December,
The perils his wisdom foresaw and o’ercame,
For her glory’s rich harvest shall Britain remember
And hallow the goblet that flows to his name.

div.p: Nor forget this gray head, who, all dark in affliction, 25

lg.l: Is deaf to the tale of our victories won,
And to sounds the most dear to paternal affection,
The shout of his people applauding his son;
By his firmness unmoved in success or disaster,

div.p: By his long reign of virtue, remember his claim! 30

lg.l: With our tribute to Pitt join the praise of his Master,
Though a tear stain the goblet that flows to his name.
Yet again fill the wine-cup, and change the sad measure,
The rites of our grief and our gratitude paid,

div.p: To our Prince, to our Heroes, devote the bright treasure, 35

lg.l: The wisdom that planned, and the zeal that obeyed!
Fill Wellington’s cup till it beam like his glory,
Forget not our own brave Dalhousie and Græme,
A thousand years hence hearts shall bound at their story,

div.p: And hallow the goblet that flows to their fame. 40

div.head:
CCXV
TO THE MEMORY OF PIETRO D’ALESSANDRO,
div.p: SECRETARY TO THE PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENT OF SICILY IN 1848, WHO DIED AN EXILE AT MALTA IN JANUARY 1855.

lg.l: Beside the covered grave
Linger the exiles, though their task is done.
Yes, brethren; from your band one more is gone,
A good man and a brave.

div.p: Scanty the rites, and train; 5

lg.l: How many’ of all the storied marbles, set
In all thy churches, City of La Valette,
Hide nobler heart and brain?
Ah! had his soul been cold,

div.p: Tempered to make a sycophant or spy, 10

lg.l: To love hard truth less than an easy lie,
His country less than gold,—
Then, not the spirit’s strife,
Nor sickening pangs at sight of conquering crime,

div.p: Nor anxious watching of an evil time, 15

lg.l: Had worn his chords of life:
Nor here, nor thus with tears
Untimely shed, but there whence o’er the sea
The great Volcano looks, his rest might be,

div.p: The close of prosperous years. 20

lg.l: No! Different hearts are bribed;
And therefore, in his cause’s sad eclipse,
Here died he, with ‘Palermo’ on his lips,
A poor man, and proscribed.

div.p: Wrecked all thy hopes, O friend,— 25

lg.l: Hopes for thyself, thine Italy, thine own,—
High gifts defeated of their due renown,—
Long toil—and this the end!
The end? not ours to scan:

div.p: Yet grieve not, children, for your father’s worth; 30

lg.l: Oh! never wish that in his native earth
He lay, a baser man.
What to the dead avail
The chance success, the blundering praise of fame?

div.p: Oh! rather trust, somewhere the noble aim 35

lg.l: Is crowned, though here it fail.
Kind, generous, true wert thou:
This meed at least to goodness must belong,
That such it was. Farewell; the world’s great wrong

div.p: Is righted for thee now. 40

lg.l: Rest in thy foreign grave,
Sicilian! whom our English hearts have loved,—
Italian! such as Dante had approved,—
An exile—not a slave!

head.label: CCXVI
head.hi: HYMN BEFORE SUNRISE, IN THE VALE OF CHAMOUNI.

div.p: Hast thou a charm to stay the morning star
In his steep course? So long he seems to pause
On thy bald awful head, O sovran Blanc!
The Arvé and Arveiron at thy base
Rave ceaselessly; but thou, most awful Form! 5

lg.l: Risest from forth thy silent sea of pines,
How silently! Around thee and above
Deep is the air, and dark, substantial, black,
An ebon mass: methinks thou piercest it

div.p: As with a wedge! But when I look again, 10

lg.l: It is thine own calm home, thy crystal shrine,
Thy habitation from eternity!
O dread and silent Mount! I gazed upon thee,
Till thou, still present to the bodily sense,

div.p: Didst vanish from my thought: entranced in prayer 15

lg.l: I worshipped the Invisible alone.
Yet, like some sweet beguiling melody,
So sweet, we know not we are listening to it,
Thou, the meanwhile, wast blending with my thought,

div.p: Yea, with my life and life’s own secret joy, 20

lg.l: Till the dilating soul, enrapt, transfused,
Into the mighty vision passing—there,
As in her natural form, swelled vast to Heaven!
Awake my soul! not only passive praise

div.p: Thou owest! not alone these swelling tears, 25
Mute thanks, and secret ecstasy! Awake,
Voice of sweet song! Awake, my heart, awake!
Green vales and icy cliffs, all join my Hymn.
Thou first and chief, sole sovran of the Vale!
Oh, struggling with the darkness all the night, 30

lg.l: And visited all night by troops of stars,
Or when they climb the sky, or when they sink:
Companion of the morning star at dawn,
Thyself Earth’s rosy star, and of the dawn

div.p: Co-herald: wake, oh wake, and utter praise! 35
Who sank thy sunless pillars deep in earth?
Who filled thy countenance with rosy light;
Who made thee parent of perpetual streams?
And you, ye five wild torrents, fiercely glad!
Who called you forth from night and utter death, 40

lg.l: From dark and icy caverns called you forth,
Down those precipitous, black, jagged rocks,
For ever shattered and the same for ever?
Who gave you your invulnerable life,

div.p: Your strength, your speed, your fury, and your joy, 45

lg.l: Unceasing thunder and eternal foam?
And who commanded (and the silence came,)
Here let the billows stiffen and have rest?
Ye ice-falls! ye that from the mountain’s brow

div.p: Adown enormous ravines slope amain— 50

lg.l: Torrents, methinks, that heard a mighty voice,
And stopped at once amid their maddest plunge!
Motionless torrents! silent cataracts!
Who made you glorious as the gates of Heaven

div.p: Beneath the keen full moon? Who bade the sun 55
Clothe you with rainbows? Who, with living flowers
Of loveliest blue, spread garlands at your feet?—
God! let the torrents, like a shout of nations,
Answer! and let the ice-plains echo, God! 59
God! sing, ye meadow-streams, with gladsome voice!
Ye pine-groves, with your soft and soul-like sounds!
And they too have a voice, yon piles of snow,
And in their perilous fall shall thunder, God!
Ye living flowers that skirt the eternal frost!
Ye wild goats sporting round the eagle’s nest! 65
Ye eagles, playmates of the mountain-storm!

lg.l: Ye lightnings, the dread arrows of the clouds!
Ye signs and wonders of the elements,
Utter forth God, and fill the hills with praise!
Thou, too, hoar Mount! with thy sky-pointing peaks,

div.p: Oft from whose feet the avalanche, unheard, 71
Shoots downward, glittering through the pure serene,
Into the depth of clouds that veil thy breast—
Thou too again, stupendous Mountain! thou,
That as I raise my head, awhile bowed low 75

lg.l: In adoration, upward from thy base
Slow travelling with dim eyes suffused with tears,
Solemnly seemest, like a vapoury cloud,
To rise before me—rise, oh, ever rise,

div.p: Rise like a cloud of incense from the earth! 80

lg.l: Thou kingly Spirit throned among the hills,
Thou dread ambassador from Earth to Heaven,
Great hierarch! tell thou the silent sky,
And tell the stars, and tell yon rising sun,

div.p: Earth, with her thousand voices, praises God. 85

lg.l: Between two sister moorland rills
There is a spot that seems to lie
Sacred to flowerets of the hills,
And sacred to the sky.

div.p: And in this smooth and open dell 5

lg.l: There is a tempest-stricken tree;
A corner-stone by lightning cut,
The last stone of a lonely hut;
And in this dell you see

div.p: A thing no storm can e’er destroy, 10

lg.l: The shadow of a Danish boy.
In clouds above the lark is heard,
But drops not here to earth for rest;
Within this lonesome nook the bird

div.p: Did never build her nest. 15

lg.l: No beast, no bird hath here his home;
Bees, wafted on the breezy air,
Pass high above those fragrant bells
To other flowers; to other dells

div.p: Their burdens do they bear. 20

lg.l: The Danish boy walks here alone:
The lovely dell is all his own.
A Spirit of noonday is he,
Yet seems a form of flesh and blood;

div.p: Nor piping shepherd shall he be, 25

lg.l: Nor herd-boy of the wood.
A regal vest of fur he wears,
In colour like a raven’s wing;
It fears not rain, nor wind, nor dew;

div.p: But in the storm ’tis fresh and blue 30

lg.l: As budding pines in Spring;
His helmet has a vernal grace,
Fresh as the bloom upon his face.
A harp is from his shoulder slung;

div.p: Resting the harp upon his knee, 35

lg.l: To words of a forgotten tongue
He suits its melody.
Of flocks upon the neighbouring hills
He is the darling and the joy;

div.p: And often, when no cause appears, 40
The mountain ponies prick their ears,
—They hear the Danish boy,
While in the dell he sings alone
Beside the tree and corner-stone.
There sits he: in his face you spy 45

lg.l: No trace of a ferocious air;
Nor ever was a cloudless sky
So steady or so fair.
The lovely Danish boy is blest,

div.p: And happy in his flowery cove: 50

lg.l: From bloody deeds his thoughts are far;
And yet he warbles songs of war,
That seem like songs of love,
For calm and gentle is his mien;

div.p: Like a dead boy he is serene. 55

head.label: CCXVIII
head.hi: ON REVISITING THE BANKS OF THE WYE.

div.p: Five years have passed; five summers, with the length
Of five long winters! and again I hear
These waters, rolling from their mountain springs
With a soft inland murmur.—Once again
Do I behold these steep and lofty cliffs, 5
Which on a wild secluded scene impress
Thoughts of more deep seclusion; and connect
The landscape with the quiet of the sky.
The day is come when I again repose
Here, under this dark sycamore, and view 10

lg.l: These plots of cottage ground, these orchard tufts,
Which, at this season, with their unripe fruits,
Are clad in one green hue, and lose themselves
Mid groves and copses. Once again I see

div.p: These hedge-rows, hardly hedge-rows, little lines 15
Of sportive wood run wild; these pastoral farms
Green to the very door; and wreaths of smoke
Sent up, in silence, from among the trees
With some uncertain notice, as might seem,
Of vagrant dwellers in the houseless woods, 20
Or of some hermit’s cave, where by his fire
The hermit sits alone.
These beauteous forms
Through a long absence have not been to me
As is a landscape to a blind man’s eye: 25

lg.l: But oft, in lonely rooms, and ’mid the din
Of towns and cities, I have owed to them,
In hours of weariness, sensations sweet,
Felt in the blood, and felt along the heart;

div.p: And passing even into my purer mind 30

lg.l: With tranquil restoration:—feelings too
Of unremembered pleasure: such, perhaps,
As have no slight or trivial influence
On that best portion of a good man’s life,

div.p: His little, nameless, unremembered acts 35

lg.l: Of kindness and of love. Nor less, I trust,
To them I may have owed another gift,
Of aspect more sublime; that blessèd mood,
In which the burthen of the mystery,

div.p: In which the heavy and the weary weight 40

lg.l: Of all this unintelligible world,
Is lightened:—that serene and blessèd mood,
In which the affections gently lead us on,—
Until, the breath of this corporeal frame,

div.p: And even the motion of our human blood, 45

lg.l: Almost suspended, we are laid asleep
In body, and become a living soul:
While with an eye made quiet by the power
Of harmony, and the deep power of joy,

div.p: We see into the life of things. 50
If this
Be but a vain belief, yet, oh! how oft,
In darkness, and amid the many shapes
Of joyless daylight; when the fretful stir
Unprofitable, and the fever of the world, 55

lg.l: Have hung upon the beatings of my heart,
How oft, in spirit, have I turned to thee,
O sylvan Wye! thou wanderer through the woods,
How often has my spirit turned to thee!

div.p: And now, with gleams of half-extinguished thought, 60

lg.l: With many recognitions dim and faint,
And somewhat of a sad perplexity,
The picture of the mind revives again:
While here I stand, not only with the sense

div.p: Of present pleasure, but with pleasing thoughts 65
That in this moment there is life and food
For future years. And so I dare to hope,
Though changed, no doubt, from what I was when first
I came among these hills; when like a roe
I bounded o’er the mountains, by the sides 70
Of the deep rivers, and the lonely streams,
Wherever Nature led: more like a man
Flying from something that he dreads, than one
Who sought the thing he loved. For Nature then
(The coarser pleasures of my boyish days, 75

lg.l: And their glad animal movements all gone by,)
To me was all in all.—I cannot paint
What then I was. The sounding cataract
Haunted me like a passion: the tall rock,

div.p: The mountain, and the deep and gloomy wood, 80

lg.l: Their colours and their forms, were then to me
An appetite: a feeling and a love,
That had no need of a remoter charm,
By thought supplied, or any interest

div.p: Unborrowed from the eye.—That time is past, 85

lg.l: And all its aching joys are now no more,
And all its dizzy raptures. Not for this
Faint I, nor mourn nor murmur; other gifts
Have followed, for such loss, I would believe,

div.p: Abundant recompense. For I have learned 90
To look on Nature, not as in the hour
Of thoughtless youth; but hearing oftentimes
The still, sad music of humanity,
Nor harsh nor grating, though of ample power
To chasten and subdue. And I have felt 95

lg.l: A presence that disturbs me with the joy
Of elevated thoughts; a sense sublime
Of something far more deeply interfused,
Whose dwelling is the light of setting suns,

div.p: And the round ocean and the living air, 100

lg.l: And the blue sky, and in the mind of man:
A motion and a spirit, that impels
All thinking things, all objects of all thought,
And rolls through all things. Therefore am I still

div.p: A lover of the meadows and the woods, 105
And mountains; and of all that we behold
From this green earth; of all the mighty world
Of eye and ear, both what they half create,
And what perceive; well pleased to recognize
In Nature and the language of the sense, 110

lg.l: The anchor of my purest thoughts, the nurse,
The guide, the guardian of my heart, and soul
Of all my moral being.
Nor perchance,

div.p: If I were not thus taught, should I the more 115

lg.l: Suffer my genial spirits to decay:
For thou art with me, here, upon the banks
Of this fair river; thou, my dearest Friend,
My dear, dear Friend; and in thy voice I catch

div.p: The language of my former heart, and read 120

lg.l: My former pleasures in the shooting lights
Of thy wild eyes. Oh! yet a little while
May I behold in thee what I was once,
My dear, dear Sister! And this prayer I make,

div.p: Knowing that Nature never did betray 125
The heart that loved her; ’tis her privilege,
Through all the years of this our life, to lead
From joy to joy: for she can so inform
The mind that is within us, so impress
With quietness and beauty, and so feed 130

lg.l: With lofty thoughts, that neither evil tongues,
Rash judgments, nor the sneers of selfish men,
Nor greetings where no kindness is, nor all
The dreary intercourse of daily life,

div.p: Shall e’er prevail against us, or disturb 135
Our cheerful faith that all which we behold
Is full of blessings. Therefore let the moon
Shine on thee in thy solitary walk;
And let the misty mountain-winds be free
To blow against thee: and, in after years, 140
When these wild ecstasies shall be matured
Into a sober pleasure, when thy mind
Shall be a mansion for all lovely forms,
Thy memory be as a dwelling-place
For all sweet sounds and harmonies; oh! then, 145

lg.l: If solitude, or fear, or pain, or grief,
Should be thy portion, with what healing thoughts
Of tender joy wilt thou remember me,
And these my exhortations! Nor, perchance,

div.p: If I should be where I no more can hear 150
Thy voice, nor catch from thy wild eyes these gleams
Of past existence, wilt thou then forget
That on the banks of this delightful stream
We stood together; and that I, so long
A worshipper of Nature, hither came, 155
Unwearied in that service; rather say
With warmer love, oh! with far deeper zeal
Of holier love. Nor wilt thou then forget,
That after many wanderings, many years
Of absence, these steep woods and lofty cliffs, 160
And this green pastoral landscape, were to me
More dear, both for themselves and for thy sake.

head.label: CCXIX
head.hi: DEDICATION OF THE REVOLT OF ISLAM TO HIS WIFE.

lg.l: So now my summer-task is ended, Mary,
And I return to thee, mine own heart’s home;
As to his Queen some victor Knight of Faëry,
Earning bright spoils for her enchanted dome;

div.p: Nor thou disdain, that ere my fame become 5

lg.l: A star among the stars of mortal night,
If it indeed may cleave its natal gloom,
Its doubtful promise thus I would unite
With thy belovèd name, thou Child of love and light.

div.p: The toil which stole from thee so many an hour, 10

lg.l: Is ended,—and the fruit is at thy feet!
No longer where the woods to frame a bower
With interlacèd branches mix and meet,
Or where with sound like many voices sweet,

div.p: Water-falls leap among wild islands green, 15

lg.l: Which framed for my lone boat a lone retreat
Of moss-grown trees and weeds, shall I be seen:
But beside thee, where still my heart has ever been.
Thoughts of great deeds were mine, dear Friend, when first
The clouds which wrap this world from youth did pass.

div.p: I do remember well the hour which burst 21
My spirit’s sleep: a fresh May-dawn it was,
When I walked forth upon the glittering grass,
And wept, I knew not why; until there rose
From the near school-room voices, that, alas! 25

lg.l: Were but one echo from a world of woes—
The harsh and grating strife of tyrants and of foes.
And then I clasped my hands and looked around—
But none was near to mock my streaming eyes,
Which poured their warm drops on the sunny ground—

div.p: So without shame I spake:—‘I will be wise, 31
And just, and free, and mild, if in me lies
Such power, for I grow weary to behold
The selfish and the strong still tyrannise
Without reproach or check.’ I then controlled 35

lg.l: My tears, my heart grew calm, and I was meek and bold.
And from that hour did I with earnest thought
Heap knowledge from forbidden mines of lore,
Yet nothing that my tyrants knew or taught

div.p: I cared to learn, but from that secret store 40
Wrought linkèd armour for my soul, before
It might walk forth to war among mankind;
Thus power and hope were strengthened more and more
Within me, till there came upon my mind
A sense of loneliness, a thirst with which I pined. 45

lg.l: Alas, that love should be a blight and snare
To those who seek all sympathies in one!—
Such once I sought in vain; then black despair,
The shadow of a starless night, was thrown

div.p: Over the world in which I moved alone:— 50

lg.l: Yet never found I one not false to me,
Hard hearts, and cold, like weights of icy stone,
Which crushed and withered mine, that could not be
Aught but a lifeless clog, until revived by thee.

div.p: Thou Friend, whose presence on my wintry heart 55

lg.l: Fell, like bright spring upon some herbless plain,
How beautiful and calm and free thou wert
In thy young wisdom, when the mortal chain
Of Custom thou didst burst and rend in twain,

div.p: And walked as free as light the clouds among, 60

lg.l: Which many an envious slave then breathed in vain
From his dim dungeon, and my spirit sprung
To meet thee from the woes which had begirt it long.
No more alone through the world’s wilderness,

div.p: Although I trod the paths of high intent, 65

lg.l: I journeyed now: no more companionless,
Where solitude is like despair, I went.—
There is the wisdom of a stern content,
When Poverty can blight the just and good,

div.p: When Infamy dares mock the innocent, 70

lg.l: And cherished friends turn with the multitude
To trample: this was ours, and we unshaken stood!
Now has descended a serener hour,
And, with inconstant fortune, friends return;

div.p: Though suffering leaves the knowledge and the power 75

lg.l: Which says:—Let scorn be not repaid with scorn;
And from thy side two gentle babes are born
To fill our home with smiles, and thus are we
Most fortunate beneath life’s beaming morn;

div.p: And these delights, and thou, have been to me 80

lg.l: The parents of the Song I consecrate to thee.
Is it, that now my inexperienced fingers
But strike the prelude of a loftier strain?
Or must the lyre on which my spirit lingers

div.p: Soon pause in silence, ne’er to sound again, 85

lg.l: Though it might shake the Anarch Custom’s reign,
And charm the minds of men to Truth’s own sway,
Holier than was Amphion’s? I would fain
Reply in hope—but I am worn away,
And Death and Love are yet contending for their prey.

div.p: And what art thou? I know, but dare not speak: 91
Time may interpret to his silent years.
Yet in the paleness of thy thoughtful cheek,
And in the light thine ample forehead wears,
And in thy sweetest smiles, and in thy tears, 95

lg.l: And in thy gentle speech, a prophecy
Is whispered, to subdue my fondest fears:
And through thine eyes, even in thy soul I see
A lamp of vestal fire burning internally.

div.p: They say that thou wert lovely from thy birth, 100

lg.l: Of glorious parents, thou aspiring Child:
I wonder not—for one then left this earth,
Whose life was like a setting planet mild,
Which clothed thee in the radiance undefiled

div.p: Of its departing glory; still her fame 105

lg.l: Shines on thee through the tempests dark and wild,
Which shake these latter days; and thou canst claim
The shelter, from thy Sire, of an immortal name.
Truth’s deathless voice pauses among mankind!

div.p: If there must be no response to my cry— 110

lg.l: If men must rise and stamp with fury blind
On his pure name who loves them—thou and I,
Sweet Friend! can look from our tranquillity
Like lamps into the world’s tempestuous night,—

div.p: Two tranquil stars, while clouds are passing by 115
Which wrap them from the foundering seaman’s sight,
That burn from year to year with unextinguished light.

lg.l: Ye clouds! that far above me float and pause,
Whose pathless march no mortal may control!
Ye ocean-waves! that, wheresoe’er ye roll,
Yield homage only to eternal laws!

div.p: Ye woods! that listen to the night-birds singing, 5

lg.l: Midway the smooth and perilous slope reclined,
Save when your own imperious branches swinging
Have made a solemn music of the wind!
Where, like a man beloved of God,

div.p: Through glooms, which never woodman trod, 10

lg.l: How oft, pursuing fancies holy,
My moonlight way o’er flowering weeds I wound,
Inspired, beyond the guess of folly,
By each rude shape and wild unconquerable sound!

div.p: O ye loud waves! and O ye forests high! 15
And O ye clouds that far above me soared!
Thou rising sun! thou blue rejoicing sky!
Yea, every thing that is and will be free!
Bear witness for me, wheresoe’er ye be,
With what deep worship I have still adored 20

lg.l: The spirit of divinest Liberty.
When France in wrath her giant-limbs upreared,
And with that oath, which smote air, earth, and sea,
Stamped her strong foot, and said she would be free,

div.p: Bear witness for me, how I hoped and feared! 25

lg.l: With what a joy my lofty gratulation
Unawed I sang, amid a slavish band:
And when to whelm the disenchanted nation,
Like fiends embattled by a wizard’s wand,

div.p: The Monarchs marched in evil day 30

lg.l: And Britain joined the dire array;
Though dear her shores and circling ocean,
Though many friendships, many youthful loves
Had swoln the patriot emotion

div.p: And flung a magic light o’er all her hills and groves; 35

lg.l: Yet still my voice, unaltered, sang defeat
To all that braved the tyrant-quelling lance,
And shame too long delayed and vain retreat!
For ne’er, O Liberty! with partial aim

div.p: I dimmed thy light or damped thy holy flame; 40

lg.l: But blessed the pæans of delivered France,
And hung my head and wept at Britain’s name.
‘And what,’ I said, ‘though Blasphemy’s loud scream
With that sweet music of deliverance strove?

div.p: Though all the fierce and drunken passions wove 45

lg.l: A dance more wild than e’er was maniac’s dream?
Ye storms, that round the dawning east assembled,
The sun was rising, though ye hid his light!’
And when, to soothe my soul, that hoped and trembled,
The dissonance ceased, and all seemed calm and bright;

div.p: When France her front deep-scarred and gory 51
Concealed with clustering wreaths of glory;
When, insupportably advancing,
Her arm made mockery of the warrior’s tramp;
While timid looks of fury glancing, 55

lg.l: Domestic Treason, crushed beneath her fatal stamp,
Writhed like a wounded dragon in his gore;
Then I reproached my fears that would not flee;
‘And soon,’ I said, ‘shall Wisdom teach her lore

div.p: In the low huts of them that toil and groan! 60

lg.l: And, conquering by her happiness alone,
Shall France compel the nations to be free,
Till Love and Joy look round, and call the earth their own.’
Forgive me, Freedom! O forgive those dreams!

div.p: I hear thy voice, I hear thy loud lament, 65

lg.l: From bleak Helvetia’s icy caverns sent—
I hear thy groans upon her blood-stained streams!
Heroes, that for your peaceful country perished,
And ye that, fleeing, spot your mountain-snows

div.p: With bleeding wounds; forgive me, that I cherished 70

lg.l: One thought that ever blessed your cruel foes!
To scatter rage and traitorous guilt,
Where Peace her jealous home had built;
A patriot-race to disinherit

div.p: Of all that made their stormy wilds so dear; 75

lg.l: And with inexpiable spirit
To taint the bloodless freedom of the mountaineer—
O France, that mockest Heaven, adulterous, blind,
And patriot only in pernicious toils,

div.p: Are these thy boasts, Champion of human kind? 80

lg.l: To mix with kings in the low lust of sway,
Yell in the hunt, and share the murderous prey;
To’ insult the shrine of Liberty with spoils
From freemen torn? to tempt and to betray?

div.p: The Sensual and the Dark rebel in vain, 85
Slaves by their own compulsion! In mad game
They burst their manacles and wear the name
Of Freedom, graven on a heavier chain!
O Liberty! with profitless endeavour
Have I pursued thee, many a weary hour; 90
But thou nor swell’st the victor’s strain, nor ever
Didst breathe thy soul in forms of human power.
Alike from all, howe’er they praise thee,
(Nor prayer, nor boastful name delays thee)
Alike from Priestcraft’s harpy minions, 95

lg.l: And factious Blasphemy’s obscener slaves,
Thou speedest on thy subtle pinions,
The guide of homeless winds, and playmate of the waves!
And there I felt thee!—on that sea-cliff’s verge,

div.p: Whose pines, scarce travelled by the breeze above, 100

lg.l: Had made one murmur with the distant surge!
Yes, while I stood and gazed, my temples bare,
And shot my being through earth, sea, and air,
Possessing all things with intensest love,

div.p: O Liberty! my spirit felt thee there. 105

lg.l: O wild West Wind, thou breath of Autumn’s being,
Thou, from whose unseen presence the leaves dead
Are driven, like ghosts from an enchanter fleeing,
Yellow, and black, and pale, and hectic red,

div.p: Pestilence-stricken multitudes: O thou, 5
Who chariotest to their dark wintry bed
The wingèd seeds, where they lie cold and low,
Each like a corpse within its grave, until
Thine azure sister of the spring shall blow
Her clarion o’er the dreaming earth, and fill 10
(Driving sweet buds like flocks to feed in air,)
With living hues and odours plain and hill:
Wild Spirit, which art moving everywhere;
Destroyer and Preserver; hear, O hear!
Thou on whose stream, ’mid the steep sky’s commotion, 15

lg.l: Loose clouds like earth’s decaying leaves are shed,
Shook from the tangled boughs of heaven and ocean,
Angels of rain and lightning; there are spread
On the blue surface of thine airy surge,

div.p: Like the bright hair uplifted from the head 20
Of some fierce Mænad, ev’n from the dim verge
Of the horizon to the zenith’s height—
The locks of the approaching storm. Thou dirge
Of the dying year, to which this closing night
Will be the dome of a vast sepulchre, 25
Vaulted with all thy congregated might
Of vapours, from whose solid atmosphere
Black rain, and fire, and hail, will burst: O hear!
Thou who didst waken from his summer-dreams
The blue Mediterranean, where he lay, 30

lg.l: Lulled by the coil of his crystalline streams,
Beside a pumice isle in Baiæ’s bay,
And saw in sleep old palaces and towers
Quivering within the wave’s intenser day,

div.p: All overgrown with azure moss and flowers 35
So sweet, the sense faints picturing them! Thou
For whose path the Atlantic’s level powers
Cleave themselves into chasms, while far below
The sea-blooms and the oozy woods which wear
The sapless foliage of the ocean, know 40

lg.l: Thy voice, and suddenly grow gray with fear,
And tremble and despoil themselves: O hear!
If I were a dead leaf thou mightest bear;
If I were a swift cloud to fly with thee;

div.p: A wave to pant beneath thy power, and share 45
The impulse of thy strength, only less free
Than thou, O uncontrollable! If even
I were as in my boyhood, and could be
The comrade of thy wanderings over heaven,
As then, when to outstrip the skyey speed 50
Scarce seemed a vision, I would ne’er have striven
As thus with thee in prayer in my sore need.
O lift me as a wave, a leaf, a cloud!
I fall upon the thorns of life! I bleed!
A heavy weight of hours has chained and bowed 55

lg.l: One too like thee: tameless, and swift, and proud.
Make me thy lyre, ev’n as the forest is:
What if my leaves are falling like its own!
The tumult of thy mighty harmonies

div.p: Will take from both a deep autumnal tone, 60

lg.l: Sweet though in sadness. Be thou, Spirit fierce,
My spirit! be thou me, impetuous One!
Drive my dead thoughts over the universe
Like withered leaves to quicken a new birth;

div.p: And, by the incantation of this verse, 65

lg.l: Scatter, as from an unextinguished hearth
Ashes and sparks, my words among mankind!
Be through my lips to unawakened earth
The trumpet of a prophecy! O Wind,

div.p: If winter comes, can spring be far behind? 70

lg.l: My heart aches, and a drowsy numbness pains
My sense, as though of hemlock I had drunk,
Or emptied some dull opiate to the drains
One minute past, and Lethe-wards had sunk:

div.p: ’Tis not through envy of thy happy lot, 5

lg.l: But being too happy in thy happiness,—
That thou, light-wingèd Dryad of the trees,
In some melodious plot
Of beechen green, and shadows numberless,

div.p: Singest of summer in full-throated ease. 10

lg.l: O for a draught of vintage, that hath been
Cooled a long age in the deep-delvèd earth,
Tasting of Flora and the country-green,
Dance, and Provençal song, and sun-burnt mirth!

div.p: O for a beaker full of the warm South, 15

lg.l: Full of the true, the blushful Hippocrene,
With beaded bubbles winking at the brim,
And purple-stainèd mouth;
That I might drink, and leave the world unseen,

div.p: And with thee fade away into the forest dim: 20

lg.l: Fade far away, dissolve, and quite forget
What thou among the leaves hast never known,
The weariness, the fever, and the fret
Here, where men sit and hear each other groan;

div.p: Where palsy shakes a few, sad, last gray hairs, 25

lg.l: Where youth grows pale, and spectre-thin, and dies;
Where but to think is to be full of sorrow
And leaden-eyed despairs;
Where Beauty cannot keep her lustrous eyes,

div.p: Or new Love pine at them beyond to-morrow. 30

lg.l: Away! away! for I will fly to thee,
Not charioted by Bacchus and his pards,
But on the viewless wings of Poesy,
Though the dull brain perplexes and retards:

div.p: Already with thee! tender is the night, 35

lg.l: And haply the Queen-Moon is on her throne,
Clustered around by all her starry Fays;
But here there is no light,
Save what from heaven is with the breezes blown

div.p: Through verdurous glooms and winding mossy ways. 40

lg.l: I cannot see what flowers are at my feet,
Nor what soft incense hangs upon the boughs,
But, in embalmèd darkness, guess each sweet
Wherewith the seasonable month endows

div.p: The grass, the thicket, and the fruit-tree wild; 45

lg.l: White hawthorn, and the pastoral eglantine;
Fast-fading violets covered up in leaves;
And mid-May’s eldest child,
The coming musk-rose, full of dewy wine,

div.p: The murmurous haunt of flies on summer eves. 50

lg.l: Darkling I listen; and for many a time
I have been half in love with easeful Death,
Called him soft names in many a musèd rhyme,
To take into the air my quiet breath;

div.p: Now more than ever seems it rich to die, 55

lg.l: To cease upon the midnight with no pain,
While thou art pouring forth thy soul abroad
In such an ecstasy!
Still wouldst thou sing, and I have ears in vain—

div.p: To thy high requiem become a sod. 60

lg.l: Thou wast not born for death, immortal Bird!
No hungry generations tread thee down;
The voice I hear this passing night was heard
In ancient days by emperor and clown:

div.p: Perhaps the self-same song that found a path 65

lg.l: Through the sad heart of Ruth, when, sick for home,
She stood in tears amid the alien corn;
The same that oft-times hath
Charmed magic casements, opening on the foam

div.p: Of perilous seas, in faery lands forlorn. 70

lg.l: Forlorn! the very word is like a bell
To toll me back from thee to my sole self!
Adieu! the Fancy cannot cheat so well
As she is famed to do, deceiving elf.

div.p: Adieu! adieu! thy plaintive anthem fades 75

lg.l: Past the near meadows, over the still stream,
Up the hill-side; and now ’tis buried deep
In the next valley-glades:
Was it a vision, or a waking dream?

div.p: Fled is that music:—do I wake or sleep? 80

lg.l: Hail to thee, blithe Spirit!
Bird thou never wert,
That from heaven, or near it
Pourest thy full heart

div.p: In profuse strains of unpremeditated art. 5

lg.l: Higher still and higher
From the earth thou springest,
Like a cloud of fire;
The blue deep thou wingest,

div.p: And singing still dost soar, and soaring ever singest. 10

lg.l: In the golden lightning
Of the sunken sun,
O’er which clouds are brightening,
Thou dost float and run,

div.p: Like an unbodied Joy whose race is just begun. 15
The pale purple even
Melts around thy flight;
Like a star of heaven
In the broad daylight
Thou art unseen, but yet I hear thy shrill delight: 20

lg.l: Keen as are the arrows
Of that silver sphere,
Whose intense lamp narrows
In the white dawn clear,

div.p: Until we hardly see, we feel that it is there. 25

lg.l: All the earth and air
With thy voice is loud,
As, when night is bare,
From one lonely cloud
The moon rains out her beams, and heaven is overflowed.

div.p: What thou art we know not; 31
What is most like thee?
From rainbow clouds there flow not
Drops so bright to see
As from thy presence showers a rain of melody. 35

lg.l: Like a poet hidden
In the light of thought,
Singing hymns unbidden,
Till the world is wrought

div.p: To sympathy with hopes and fears it heeded not: 40
Like a high-born maiden
In a palace tower,
Soothing her love-laden
Soul in secret hour
With music sweet as love, which overflows her bower: 45
Like a glowworm golden
In a dell of dew,
Scattering unbeholden
Its aerial hue
Among the flowers and grass, which screen it from the view: 50

lg.l: Like a rose embowered
In its own green leaves,
By warm winds deflowered,
Till the scent it gives

div.p: Makes faint with too much sweet these heavy-winged thieves. 55
Sound of vernal showers
On the twinkling grass,
Rain-awakened flowers,
All that ever was
Joyous, and clear, and fresh, thy music doth surpass. 60

lg.l: Teach us, sprite or bird,
What sweet thoughts are thine:
I have never heard
Praise of love or wine

div.p: That panted forth a flood of rapture so divine. 65
Chorus hymeneal,
Or triumphal chaunt,
Matched with thine, would be all
But an empty vaunt—
A thing wherein we feel there is some hidden want. 70
What objects are the fountains
Of thy happy strain?
What fields, or waves, or mountains?
What shapes of sky or plain?
What love of thine own kind? what ignorance of pain? 75
With thy clear keen joyance
Languor cannot be:
Shadow of annoyance
Never came near thee:
Thou lovest; but ne’er knew love’s sad satiety. 80

lg.l: Waking or asleep,
Thou of death must deem
Things more true and deep
Than we mortals dream,

div.p: Or how could thy notes flow in such a crystal stream? 85

lg.l: We look before and after,
And pine for what is not:
Our sincerest laughter
With some pain is fraught;
Our sweetest songs are those that tell of saddest thought.

div.p: Yet if we could scorn 91
Hate, and pride, and fear;
If we were things born
Not to shed a tear,
I know not how thy joy we ever should come near. 95

lg.l: Better than all measures
Of delightful sound,
Better than all treasures
That in books are found,

div.p: Thy skill to poet were, thou scorner of the ground! 100

lg.l: Teach me half the gladness
That thy brain must know,
Such harmonious madness
From my lips would flow,

div.p: The world should listen then, as I am listening now! 105

head.label: CCXXIV
head.hi: ‘ON THIS DAY I COMPLETE MY THIRTY-SIXTH YEAR.’

div.p: ’Tis time this heart should be unmoved,
Since others it hath ceased to move:
Yet, though I cannot be beloved,
Still let me love!
My days are in the yellow leaf; 5

lg.l: The flowers and fruits of love are gone;
The worm, the canker, and the grief
Are mine alone!
The fire that on my bosom preys

div.p: Is lone as some volcanic isle; 10

lg.l: No torch is kindled at its blaze—
A funeral pile.
The hope, the fear, the jealous care,
The exalted portion of the pain

div.p: And power of love, I cannot share, 15

lg.l: But wear the chain.
But ’tis not thus—and ’tis not here—
Such thoughts should shake my soul, nor now,
Where glory decks the hero’s bier,

div.p: Or binds his brow. 20

lg.l: The sword, the banner, and the field,
Glory and Greece, around me see!
The Spartan, borne upon his shield,
Was not more free.

div.p: Awake! (not Greece—she is awake!) 25

lg.l: Awake, my spirit! Think through whom
Thy life-blood tracks its parent lake,
And then strike home!
Tread those reviving passions down,

div.p: Unworthy manhood!—unto thee 30

lg.l: Indifferent should the smile or frown
Of beauty be.
If thou regret’st thy youth, why live?
The land of honourable death

div.p: Is here:—up to the field, and give 35

lg.l: Away thy breath!
Seek out— less often sought than found—
A soldier’s grave, for thee the best;
Then look around, and choose thy ground,

div.p: And take thy rest. 40
What voice did on my spirit fall,
Peschiera, when thy bridge I crost?
‘’Tis better to have fought and lost,
Than never to have fought at all.’
The tricolor—a trampled rag 5

lg.l: Lies, dirt and dust; the lines I track
By sentry boxes yellow-black,
Lead up to no Italian flag.
I see the Croat soldier stand

div.p: Upon the grass of your redoubts; 10

lg.l: The eagle with his black wings flouts
The breadth and beauty of your land.
Yet not in vain, although in vain,
O men of Brescia, on the day

div.p: Of loss past hope, I heard you say 15
Your welcome to the noble pain.
You said, ‘Since so it is,—good bye
Sweet life, high hope; but whatsoe’er
May be, or must, no tongue shall dare
To tell, “The Lombard feared to die!”’ 20
You said, (there shall be answer fit,)
‘And if our children must obey,
They must; but thinking on this day,
’Twill less debase them to submit.’
You said, (oh, not in vain you said,) 25

lg.l: ‘Haste, brothers, haste, while yet we may;
The hours ebb fast of this one day,
When blood may yet be nobly shed.’
Ah! not for idle hatred, not

div.p: For honour, fame, nor self-applause, 30

lg.l: But for the glory of the cause,
You did, what will not be forgot.
And though the stranger stand, ’tis true,
By force and fortune’s right he stands;

div.p: By fortune, which is in God’s hands, 35
And strength, which yet shall spring in you.
This voice did on my spirit fall,
Peschiera, when thy bridge I crost,
‘’Tis better to have fought and lost,
Than never to have fought at all.’ 40

head.label: CCXXVI
head.hi: LINES SUGGESTED BY A PICTURE OF PEELE CASTLE IN A STORM, PAINTED BY SIR GEORGE BEAUMONT.

lg.l: I was thy neighbour once, thou rugged Pile!
Four summer weeks I dwelt in sight of thee:
I saw thee every day; and all the while
Thy form was sleeping on a glassy sea.

div.p: So pure the sky, so quiet was the air! 5

lg.l: So like, so very like, was day to day!
Whene’er I looked, thy image still was there;
It trembled, but it never passed away.
How perfect was the calm! It seemed no sleep,

div.p: No mood, which season takes away, or brings: 10

lg.l: I could have fancied that the mighty Deep
Was even the gentlest of all gentle things.
Ah! then, if mine had been the painter’s hand
To express what then I saw; and add the gleam,

div.p: The light that never was, on sea or land, 15

lg.l: The consecration, and the poet’s dream,—
I would have planted thee, thou hoary Pile,
Amid a world how different from this!
Beside a sea that could not cease to smile;

div.p: On tranquil land, beneath a sky of bliss. 20

lg.l: Thou should’st have seemed a treasure-house divine
Of peaceful years, a chronicle of heaven;
Of all the sunbeams that did ever shine
The very sweetest had to thee been given.

div.p: A picture had it been of lasting ease, 25

lg.l: Elysian quiet, without toil or strife;
No motion but the moving tide, a breeze,
Or merely silent Nature’s breathing life.
Such, in the fond illusion of my heart,

div.p: Such picture would I at that time have made; 30

lg.l: And seen the soul of truth in every part,
A steadfast peace that might not be betrayed.
So once it would have been,—’tis so no more;
I have submitted to a new control:

div.p: A power is gone, which nothing can restore; 35

lg.l: A deep distress hath humanized my soul.
Not for a moment could I now behold
A smiling sea, and be what I have been:
The feeling of my loss will ne’er be old;

div.p: This, which I know, I speak with mind serene. 40

lg.l: Then, Beaumont, Friend! who would have been the friend,
If he had lived, of him whom I deplore,
This work of thine I blame not, but commend;
This sea in anger, and that dismal shore.

div.p: O ’tis a passionate work!—yet wise and well, 45

lg.l: Well chosen is the spirit that is here;
That hulk which labours in the deadly swell,
This rueful sky, this pageantry of fear!
And this huge Castle, standing here sublime,

div.p: I love to see the look with which it braves, 50
—Cased in the unfeeling armour of old time—
The lightning, the fierce wind, and trampling waves.
Farewell, farewell the heart that lives alone,
Housed in a dream, at distance from the Kind!
Such happiness, wherever it be known, 55

lg.l: Is to be pitied; for ’tis surely blind.
But welcome fortitude, and patient cheer,
And frequent sights of what is to be borne!
Such sights, or worse, as are before me here:—

div.p: Not without hope we suffer and we mourn. 60

lg.l: Thou still unravished bride of quietness!
Thou foster-child of Silence and slow Time,
Sylvan historian, who canst thus express
A flowery tale more sweetly than our rhyme:

div.p: What leaf-fringed legend haunts about thy shape 5
Of deities or mortals, or of both,
In Tempe or the dales of Arcady?
What men or gods are these? What maidens loath?
What mad pursuit? What struggle to escape?
What pipes and timbrels? What wild ecstasy? 10

lg.l: Heard melodies are sweet, but those unheard
Are sweeter; therefore, ye soft pipes, play on;
Not to the sensual ear, but, more endeared,
Pipe to the spirit ditties of no tone:

div.p: Fair youth, beneath the trees, thou canst not leave 15

lg.l: Thy song, nor ever can those trees be bare;
Bold Lover, never, never canst thou kiss,
Though winning near the goal—yet, do not grieve;
She cannot fade, though thou hast not thy bliss,

div.p: For ever wilt thou love, and she be fair! 20

lg.l: Ah, happy, happy boughs! that cannot shed
Your leaves, nor ever bid the Spring adieu;
And, happy melodist, unwearièd,
For ever piping songs for ever new;

div.p: More happy love! more happy, happy love! 25

lg.l: For ever warm and still to be enjoyed,
For ever panting and for ever young;
All breathing human passion far above,
That leaves a heart high-sorrowful and cloyed,

div.p: A burning forehead, and a parching tongue. 30

lg.l: Who are these coming to the sacrifice?
To what green altar, O mysterious priest,
Lead’st thou that heifer lowing at the skies,
And all her silken flanks with garlands drest?

div.p: What little town by river or sea-shore, 35

lg.l: Or mountain-built with peaceful citadel,
Is emptied of its folk, this pious morn?
And, little town, thy streets for evermore
Will silent be; and not a soul to tell

div.p: Why thou art desolate, can e’er return. 40

lg.l: O Attic shape! Fair attitude! with brede
Of marble men and maidens overwrought,
With forest branches and the trodden weed;
Thou, silent form! dost tease us out of thought

div.p: As doth eternity: Cold Pastoral! 45

lg.l: When old age shall this generation waste,
Thou shalt remain, in midst of other woe
Than ours, a friend to man, to whom thou say’st,
‘Beauty is truth, truth beauty,’—that is all

div.p: Ye know on earth, and all ye need to know. 50

head.label: CCXXVIII
head.hi: STANZAS WRITTEN IN DEJECTION NEAR NAPLES.

lg.l: The sun is warm, the sky is clear,
The waves are dancing fast and bright,
Blue isles and snowy mountains wear
The purple noon’s transparent light:

div.p: The breath of the moist air is light 5

lg.l: Around its unexpanded buds;
Like many a voice of one delight,
The winds, the birds, the ocean-floods,
The City’s voice itself is soft like solitude’s.

div.p: I see the Deep’s untrampled floor 10

lg.l: With green and purple sea-weeds strown;
I see the waves upon the shore,
Like light dissolved in star-showers, thrown:
I sit upon the sands alone;

div.p: The lightning of the noon-tide ocean 15

lg.l: Is flashing round me, and a tone
Arises from its measured motion—
How sweet, did any heart now share in my emotion!
Alas! I have nor hope nor health,

div.p: Nor peace within nor calm around, 20

lg.l: Nor that content surpassing wealth
The sage in meditation found,
And walked with inward glory crowned—
Nor fame, nor power, nor love, nor leisure;

div.p: Others I see whom these surround; 25

lg.l: Smiling they live, and call life pleasure;
To me that cup has been dealt in another measure.
Yet now despair itself is mild,
Even as the winds and waters are;

div.p: I could lie down like a tired child, 30

lg.l: And weep away the life of care
Which I have borne, and yet must bear,
Till death like sleep might steal on me,
And I might feel in the warm air

div.p: My cheek grow cold, and hear the sea 35

lg.l: Breathe o’er my dying brain its last monotony.
Some might lament that I were cold,
As I, when this sweet day is gone,
Which my lost heart, too soon grown old,

div.p: Insults with this untimely moan; 40

lg.l: They might lament—for I am one
Whom men love not, and yet regret;
Unlike this day, which, when the sun
Shall on its stainless glory set,

div.p: Will linger, though enjoyed, like joy in memory yet. 45

lg.l: Say not, the struggle nought availeth,
The labour and the wounds are vain,
The enemy faints not, nor faileth,
And as things have been they remain.

div.p: If hopes were dupes, fears may be liars; 5

lg.l: It may be, in yon smoke concealed,
Your comrades chase e’en now the fliers,
And, but for you, possess the field.
For while the tired waves, vainly breaking,

div.p: Seem here no painful inch to gain, 10

lg.l: Far back, through creeks and inlets making,
Comes silent, flooding in, the main.
And not by eastern windows only,
When daylight comes, comes in the light;

div.p: In front, the sun climbs slow, how slowly, 15
But westward, look, the land is bright.

lg.l: Oft in the stilly night
Ere slumber’s chain has bound me,
Fond Memory brings the light
Of other days around me:

div.p: The smiles, the tears 5

lg.l: Of boyhood’s years,
The words of love then spoken;
The eyes that shone,
Now dimmed and gone,

div.p: The cheerful hearts now broken! 10

lg.l: Thus in the stilly light
Ere slumber’s chain has bound me,
Sad Memory brings the light
Of other days around me.

div.p: When I remember all 15
The friends so linked together
I’ve seen around me fall
Like leaves in wintry weather,
I feel like one
Who treads alone 20

lg.l: Some banquet-hall deserted,
Whose lights are fled,
Whose garlands dead,
And all but he departed!

div.p: Thus in the stilly night 25

lg.l: Ere slumber’s chain has bound me,
Sad Memory brings the light
Of other days around me.
If thou wilt ease thine heart
Of love, and all its smart—
Then sleep, dear, sleep!
And not a sorrow

div.p: Hang any tear on your eyelashes; 5

lg.l: Lie still and deep,
Sad soul, until the sea-wave washes
The rim o’ the sun to-morrow
In Eastern sky.

div.p: But wilt thou cure thine heart 10
Of love, and all its smart—
Then die, dear, die!
’Tis deeper, sweeter,
Than on a rose-bank to lie dreaming
With folded eye; 15

lg.l: And then alone, amid the beaming
Of love’s stars, thou’lt meet her
In Eastern sky.

head.label: CCXXXII
head.hi: LINES WRITTEN IN MY OWN ALBUM.

lg.l: Fresh clad from heaven in robes of white,
A young probationer of light,
Thou wert, my soul, an album bright,
A spotless leaf; but thought, and care,

div.p: And friend and foe, in foul and fair, 5

lg.l: Have ‘written strange defeatures’ there;
And Time with heaviest hand of all,
Like that fierce writing on the wall,
Hath stamped sad dates—he can’t recall.

div.p: And error, gilding worst designs— 10

lg.l: Like speckled snake that strays and shines—
Betrays his path by crooked lines;
And vice hath left his ugly blot;
And good resolves, a moment hot,

div.p: Fairly began—but finished not; 15

lg.l: And fruitless, late remorse doth trace—
Like Hebrew lore a backward pace—
Her irrecoverable race.
Disjointed numbers; sense unknit;

div.p: Huge reams of folly; shreds of wit; 20
Compose the mingled mass of it.

lg.l: My scalded eyes no longer brook
Upon this ink-blurred thing to look—
Go, shut the leaves, and clasp the book.
October’s gold is dim—the forests rot,
The weary rain falls ceaseless, while the day
Is wrapt in damp. In mire of village-way
The hedgerow leaves are stampt, and, all forgot,

div.p: The broodless nest sits visible in the thorn. 5

lg.l: Autumn, among her drooping marigolds,
Weeps all her garnered fields and empty folds
And dripping orchards, plundered and forlorn.
The season is a dead one, and I die!

div.p: No more, no more for me the spring shall make 10
A resurrection in the earth, and take
The death from out her heart—O God, I die!
The cold throat-mist creeps nearer, till I breathe
Corruption. Drop, stark night, upon my death!

lg.l: Die down, O dismal day, and let me live;
And come, blue deeps, magnificently strewn
With coloured clouds—large, light, and fugitive—
By upper winds through pompous motions blown.

div.p: Now it is death in life—a vapour dense 5
Creeps round my window, till I cannot see
The far snow-shining mountains, and the glens
Shagging the mountain tops. O God! make free
This barren shackled earth, so deadly cold—
Breathe gently forth thy spring, till winter flies 10
In rude amazement, fearful and yet bold,
While she performs her customed charities.
I weigh the loaded hours till life is bare—
O God, for one clear day, a snowdrop, and sweet air!

lg.l: O Winter, wilt thou never, never, go?
O Summer, but I weary for thy coming,
Longing once more to hear the Luggie flow,
And frugal bees, laboriously humming.

div.p: Now the east wind diseases the infirm, 5

lg.l: And I must crouch in comers from rough weather;
Sometimes a winter sunset is a charm—
When the fired clouds, compacted, blaze together,
And the large sun dips red behind the hills.

div.p: I, from my window, can behold this pleasure; 10

lg.l: And the eternal moon, what time she fills
Her orb with argent, treading a soft measure,
With queenly motions of a bridal mood,
Through the white spaces of infinitude.
When my mother died I was very young,
And my father sold me while yet my tongue
Could scarcely cry, ‘’Weep! ’weep! ’weep! ’weep!’
So your chimneys I sweep, and in soot I sleep.

div.p: There’s little Tom Dacre, who cried when his head, 5

lg.l: That curled like a lamb’s back, was shaved; so I said,
‘Hush, Tom! never mind it, for when your head’s bare,
You know that the soot cannot spoil your white hair.’
And so he was quiet, and that very night,

div.p: As Tom was a-sleeping, he had such a sight; 10

lg.l: That thousands of sweepers, Dick, Joe, Ned, and Jack,
Were all of them locked up in coffins of black:
And by came an angel, who had a bright key,
And he opened the coffins, and set them all free;

div.p: Then down a green plain, leaping, laughing they run, 15

lg.l: And wash in a river, and shine in the sun.
Then naked and white, all their bags left behind,
They rise upon clouds, and sport in the wind;
And the angel told Tom, if he’d be a good boy,

div.p: He’d have God for his Father, and never want joy. 20

lg.l: And so Tom awoke, and we rose in the dark,
And got with our bags and our brushes to work;
Though the morning was cold, Tom was happy and warm:
So, if all do their duty, they need not fear harm.
Art thou pale for weariness
Of climbing heaven, and gazing on the earth,
Wandering companionless,
Among the stars that have a different birth,—

div.p: And ever changing, like a joyless eye 5
That finds no object worth its constancy?

lg.l: If I had thought thou could’st have died,
I might not weep for thee;
But I forgot, when by thy side,
That thou could’st mortal be.

div.p: It never through my mind had past 5

lg.l: That time would e’er be o’er,
And I on thee should look my last,
And thou should’st smile no more!
And still upon that face I look,

div.p: And think ’twill smile again; 10

lg.l: And still the thought I will not brook
That I must look in vain.
But when I speak thou dost not say,
What thou ne’er left’st unsaid;

div.p: And now I feel, as well I may, 15

lg.l: Sweet Mary, thou art dead!
If thou would’st stay, e’en as thou art,
All cold, and all serene—
I still might press thy silent heart,

div.p: And where thy smiles have been! 20

lg.l: While e’en thy chill, bleak corse I have,
Thou seemest still mine own;
But there—I lay thee in thy grave,
And I am now alone!

div.p: I do not think, where’er thou art, 25

lg.l: Thou hast forgotten me;
And I, perhaps, may soothe this heart,
In thinking still of thee:
Yet there was round thee such a dawn

div.p: Of light ne’er seen before, 30
As fancy never could have drawn,
And never can restore!

lg.l: Can I see another’s woe,
And not be in sorrow too?
Can I see another’s grief,
And not seek for kind relief?

div.p: Can I see a falling tear, 5

lg.l: And not feel my sorrow’s share?
Can a father see his child
Weep, nor be with sorrow filled?
Can a mother sit and hear

div.p: An infant groan, an infant fear? 10

lg.l: No, no! never can it be!
Never, never can it be!
And can He, who smiles on all,
Hear the wren, with sorrows small,

div.p: Hear the small bird’s grief and care, 15

lg.l: Hear the woes that infants bear?
And not sit beside the nest,
Pouring pity in their breast?
And not sit the cradle near,

div.p: Weeping tear on infant’s tear? 20
And not sit both night and day,
Wiping all our tears away?
Oh, no! never can it be!
Never, never can it be!
He doth give his joy to all: 25

lg.l: He becomes an infant small,
He becomes a man of woe,
He doth feel the sorrow too.
Think not thou canst sigh a sigh,

div.p: And thy Maker is not by: 30

lg.l: Think not thou canst weep a tear,
And thy Maker is not near.
Oh! He gives to us his joy,
That our griefs He may destroy:

div.p: Till our grief is fled and gone 35
He doth sit by us and moan.

lg.l: O Rose, who dares to name thee?
No longer roseate now, nor soft, nor sweet,
But pale and hard and dry as stubble wheat,—
Kept seven years in a drawer, thy titles shame thee.

div.p: The breeze that used to blow thee 5

lg.l: Between the hedgerow thorns, and take away
An odour up the lane to last all day,—
If breathing now, unsweetened would forgo thee.
The sun that used to smite thee,

div.p: And mix his glory in thy gorgeous urn, 10

lg.l: Till beam appeared to bloom, and flower to burn,—
If shining now, with not a hue would light thee.
The dew that used to wet thee,
And, white first, grow incarnadined because

div.p: It lay upon thee where the crimson was,— 15

lg.l: If dropping now, would darken where it met thee.
The fly that ’lit upon thee,
To stretch the tendrils of its tiny feet
Along thy leafs pure edges after heat,—

div.p: If ’lighting now, would coldly overrun thee. 20

lg.l: The bee that once did suck thee,
And build thy perfumed ambers up his hive,
And swoon in thee for joy, till scarce alive,—
If passing now, would blindly overlook thee.

div.p: The heart doth recognize thee, 25

lg.l: Alone, alone! the heart doth smell thee sweet,
Doth view thee fair, doth judge thee most complete,
Perceiving all those changes that disguise thee.
Yes, and the heart doth owe thee

div.p: More love, dead rose, than to’ any roses bold 30
Which Julia wears at dances smiling cold:—
Lie still upon this heart which breaks below thee!

lg.l: Although I enter not,
Yet round about the spot
Ofttimes I hover;
And near the sacred gate

div.p: With longing eyes I wait, 5

lg.l: Expectant of her.
The Minster bell tolls out
Above the city’s rout,
And noise and humming:

div.p: They’ve hushed the Minster bell: 10

lg.l: The organ ’gins to swell:
She’s coming, she’s coming!
My lady comes at last,
Timid, and stepping fast,

div.p: And hastening hither, 15

lg.l: With modest eyes downcast:
She comes—she’s here—she’s past—
May Heaven go with her!
Kneel, undisturbed, fair Saint!

div.p: Pour out your praise or plaint 20

lg.l: Meekly and duly;
I will not enter there,
To sully your pure prayer
With thoughts unruly.

div.p: But suffer me to pace 25

lg.l: Round the forbidden place,
Lingering a minute,
Like outcast spirits who wait
And see through Heaven’s gate

div.p: Angels within it. 30

head.label: CCXLII
head.hi: ON AN INFANT DYING AS SOON AS BORN.

lg.l: I saw where in the shroud did lurk
A curious frame of Nature’s work;
A floweret crushèd in the bud,
A nameless piece of Babyhood,

div.p: Was in her cradle-coffin lying; 5

lg.l: Extinct, with scarce the sense of dying:
So soon to’ exchange the imprisoning womb
For darker closets of the tomb!
She did but ope an eye, and put

div.p: A clear beam forth, then straight up shut 10

lg.l: For the long dark: ne’er more to see
Through glasses of mortality.
Riddle of destiny, who can show,
What thy short visit meant, or know

div.p: What thy errand here below? 15
Shall we say, that Nature blind
Checked her hand, and changed her mind
Just when she had exactly wrought
A finished, pattern without fault?
Could she flag, or could she tire, 20
Or lacked she the Promethean fire
(With her nine moons’ long workings sickened)
That should thy little limbs have quickened?
Limbs so firm, they seemed to’ assure
Life of health, and days mature: 25
Woman’s self in miniature!
Limbs so fair, they might supply
(Themselves now but cold imagery)
The sculptor to make Beauty by.
Or did the stern-eyed Fate descry 30

lg.l: That babe or mother, one must die;
So in mercy left the stock,
And cut the branch; to save the shock
Of young years widowed, and the pain

div.p: When Single State comes back again 35

lg.l: To the lone man who, reft of wife,
Thenceforward drags a maimèd life?
The economy of Heaven is dark,
And wisest clerks have missed the mark

div.p: Why human buds, like this, should fall 40
More brief than fly ephemeral
That has his day; while shrivelled crones
Stiffen with age to stocks and stones;
And crabbèd use the conscience sears
In sinners of an hundred years. 45
—Mother’s prattle, mother’s kiss,
Baby fond, thou ne’er wilt miss:
Rites, which custom does impose,
Silver bells, and baby clothes;
Coral redder than those lips 50

lg.l: Which pale death did late eclipse;
Music framed for infant’s glee,
Whistle never tuned for thee;
Though thou want’st not, thou shalt have them,

div.p: Loving hearts were they which gave them. 55

lg.l: Let not one be missing; nurse,
See them laid upon the hearse
Of infant slain by doom perverse.
Why should kings and nobles have

div.p: Pictured trophies to their grave, 60

lg.l: And we, churls, to thee deny
Thy pretty toys with thee to lie—
A more harmless vanity?
Child of a day, thou knowest not
The tears that overflow thine urn,
The gushing eyes that read thy lot;
Nor, if thou knewest, could’st return!

div.p: And why the wish! the pure and blest 5
Watch like thy mother o’er thy sleep:
O peaceful night! O envied rest!
Thou wilt not ever see her weep.

lg.l: Sweet Maiden, for so calm a life
Too bitter seemed thine end;
But thou hadst won thee, ere that strife,
A more than earthly Friend.

div.p: We miss thee in thy place at school, 5

lg.l: And on thine homeward way,
Where violets by the reedy pool
Peep out so shyly gay:
Where thou, a true and gentle guide,

div.p: Wouldst lead thy little band, 10

lg.l: With all an elder sister’s pride,
And rule with eye and hand.
And if we miss, oh, who may speak
What thoughts are hovering round The

div.p: pallet where thy fresh young cheek 15

lg.l: Its evening slumber found?
How many a tearful longing look
In silence seeks thee yet,
Where in its own familiar nook

div.p: Thy fireside chair is set? 20

lg.l: And oft when little voices dim
Are feeling for the note
In chanted prayer, or psalm, or hymn,
And wavering wildly float,

div.p: Comes gushing o’er a sudden thought 25

lg.l: Of her who led the strain,
How oft such music home she brought—
But ne’er shall bring again.
O say not so! the springtide air

div.p: Is fraught with whisperings sweet; 30

lg.l: Who knows but heavenly carols there
With ours may duly meet?
Who knows how near, each holy hour,
The pure and child-like dead

div.p: May linger, where in shrine or bower 35
The mourner’s prayer is said?
And He who willed thy tender frame
(O stern yet sweet decree!)
Should wear the martyr’s robe of flame,
He hath prepared for thee 40
A garland in that region bright
Where infant spirits reign, Tinged
faintly with such golden light
As crowns his martyr train.
Nay doubt it not: his tokens sure 45
Were round her death-bed shown:
The wasting pain might not endure,
’Twas calm ere life had flown,
Even as we read of Saints of yore:
Her heart and voice were free 50
To crave one quiet slumber more
Upon her mother’s knee.

p.hi: ON BEING PRESSED TO GO TO A MASQUED BALL NOT MANY MONTHS AFTER THE DEATH OF MY CHILD.

lg.l: Oh, lead me not in Pleasure’s train,
With faltering step and faded brow;
She such a votary would disdain,
And such a homage disavow.

div.p: But art thou sure the goddess leads 5

lg.l: Yon motley group that onward press?
Some gaudy phantom-shape precedes,
Arrayed in Pleasure’s borrowed dress.
When last I saw her smile serene,

div.p: And spread her soft enchantments wide, 10

lg.l: My lovely child adorned the scene,
And sported by the flowing tide.
The fairest shells for me to seek,
Intent the little wanderer strayed;

div.p: The rose that blossomed on his cheek 15

lg.l: Still deepening as the breezes played.
Exulting in his form and face,
Through the bright veil that beauty wove,
How did my heart delight to trace

div.p: A soul—all harmony and love! 20

lg.l: Fair as the dreams by fancy given,
A model of unearthly grace;
Whene’er he raised his eyes to heaven,
He seemed to seek his native place.

div.p: More lovely than the morning ray, 25

lg.l: His brilliant form of life and light
Through strange gradations of decay
In sad succession shocked my sight.
And since that agonizing hour,

div.p: That sowed the seed of mourning years, 30

lg.l: Beauty has lost its cheering power,
I see it through a mother’s tears.
Soon was my dream of bliss o’ercast,
And all the dear illusion o’er;

div.p: A few dark days of terror past, 35
And joy and Frederick bloom no more.

lg.l: We watched her breathing through the night,
Her breathing soft and low,
As in her breast the wave of life
Kept heaving to and fro.

div.p: So silently we seemed to speak, 5

lg.l: So slowly moved about,
As we had lent her half our powers,
To eke her living out.
Our very hopes belied our fears,

div.p: Our fears our hopes belied; 10

lg.l: We thought her dying when she slept,
And sleeping when she died.
For when the morn came dim and sad,
And chill with early showers,

div.p: Her quiet eyelids closed—she had 15
Another morn than ours.

head.label: CCXLVII
head.hi: LINES WRITTEN IN RICHMOND CHURCHYARD, YORKSHIRE.

lg.l: Methinks it is good to be here;
If Thou wilt, let us build—but for whom?
Nor Elias nor Moses appear,
But the shadows of eve that encompass the gloom,

div.p: The abode of the dead and the place of the tomb. 5

lg.l: Shall we build to Ambition? oh, no!
Affrighted, he shrinketh away;
For see! they would pin him below,
In a small narrow cave, and, begirt with cold clay,

div.p: To the meanest of reptiles a peer and a prey. 10

lg.l: To Beauty? ah, no!—she forgets
The charms which she wielded before—
Nor knows the foul worm that he frets
The skin which but yesterday fools could adore,

div.p: For the smoothness it held, or the tint which it wore. 15

lg.l: Shall we build to the purple of Pride—
The trappings which dizen the proud?
Alas! they are all laid aside;
And here’s neither dress nor adornment allowed,

div.p: But the long winding-sheet and the fringe of the shroud. 20

lg.l: To Riches? alas! ’tis in vain;
Who hid, in their turns have been hid:
The treasures are squandered again;
And here in the grave are all metals forbid,

div.p: But the tinsel that shone on the dark coffin-lid. 25

lg.l: To the pleasures which Mirth can afford—
The revel, the laugh, and the jeer?
Ah! here is a plentiful board!
But the guests are all mute as their pitiful cheer,

div.p: And none but the worm is a reveller here. 30

lg.l: Shall we build to Affection and Love?
Ah, no! they have withered and died,
Or fled with the spirit above;
Friends, brothers, and sisters, are laid side by side,

div.p: Yet none have saluted, and none have replied. 35

lg.l: Unto Sorrow?—The dead cannot grieve;
Not a sob, not a sigh meets mine ear,
Which compassion itself could relieve!
Ah! sweetly they slumber, nor hope, love, nor fear—

div.p: Peace, peace is the watchword, the only one here! 40

lg.l: Unto Death, to whom monarchs must bow?
Ah, no! for his empire is known,
And here there are trophies enow!
Beneath—the cold dead, and around—the dark stone,

div.p: Are the signs of a Sceptre that none may disown! 45

lg.l: The first tabernacle to Hope we will build,
And look for the sleepers around us to rise;
The second to Faith, which ensures it fulfilled;
And the third to the Lamb of the great Sacrifice,

div.p: Who bequeathed us them both when He rose to the skies. 50

lg.l: Unfathomable Sea! whose waves are years,
Ocean of Time, whose waters of deep woe
Are brackish with the salt of human tears!
Thou shoreless flood, which in thy ebb and flow

div.p: Claspest the limits of mortality! 5

lg.l: And sick of prey, yet howling on for more,
Vomitest thy wrecks on its inhospitable shore;
Treacherous in calm, and terrible in storm,
Who shall put forth on thee,

div.p: Unfathomable Sea? 10

head.label: CCXLIX
head.hi: SHE IS FAR FROM THE LAND.

lg.l: She is far from the land where her young hero sleeps,
And lovers are round her sighing;
But coldly she turns from their gaze, and weeps,
For her heart in his grave is lying.

div.p: She sings the wild songs of her dear native plains, 5

lg.l: Every note which he loved awaking;—
Ah! little they think, who delight in her strains,
How the heart of the Minstrel is breaking.
He had lived for his love, for his country he died,

div.p: They were all that to life had entwined him; 10
Nor soon shall the tears of his country be dried,
Nor long will his Love stay behind him.
Oh! make her a grave where the sunbeams rest,
When they promise a glorious morrow; 14
They’ll shine o’er her sleep, like a smile from the West,
From her own loved island of sorrow.

lg.l: All worldly shapes shall melt in gloom,
The sun himself must die,
Before this mortal shall assume
Its immortality!

div.p: I saw a vision in my sleep, 5

lg.l: That gave my spirit strength to sweep
Adown the gulf of Time!
I saw the last of human mould,
That shall Creation’s death behold,

div.p: As Adam saw her prime! 10

lg.l: The sun’s eye had a sickly glare,
The earth with age was wan,
The skeletons of nations were
Around that lonely man!

div.p: Some had expired in fight,—the brands 15

lg.l: Still rusted in their bony hands;
In plague and famine some!
Earth’s cities had no sound nor tread;
And ships were drifting with the dead

div.p: To shores where all was dumb! 20

lg.l: Yet, prophet-like, that lone one stood,
With dauntless words and high,
That shook the sere leaves from the wood,
As if a storm passed by—

div.p: Saying, We’ are twins in death, proud Sun, 25
Thy face is cold, thy race is run,
’Tis mercy bids thee go;
For thou ten thousand thousand years
Hast seen the tide of human tears,
That shall no longer flow. 30

lg.l: What though beneath thee man put forth
His pomp, his pride, his skill;
And arts that made fire, flood, and earth,
The vassals of his will;—

div.p: Yet mourn I not thy parted sway, 35

lg.l: Thou dim discrownèd king of day;
For all those trophied arts
And triumphs that beneath thee sprang,
Healed not a passion or a pang

div.p: Entailed on human hearts. 40

lg.l: Go, let oblivion’s curtain fall
Upon the stage of men,
Nor with thy rising beams recall
Life’s tragedy again.

div.p: Its piteous pageants bring not back, 45

lg.l: Nor waken flesh upon the rack
Of pain anew to writhe;
Stretched in disease’s shapes abhorred,
Or mown in battle by the sword,

div.p: Like grass beneath the scythe. 50

lg.l: Even I am weary in yon skies
To watch thy fading fire;
Test of all sumless agonies,
Behold not me expire.

div.p: My lips that speak thy dirge of death— 55

lg.l: Their rounded gasp and gurgling breath
To see thou shalt not boast.
The eclipse of nature spreads my pall,—
The majesty of darkness shall

div.p: Receive my parting ghost! 60

lg.l: This spirit shall return to Him
Who gave its heavenly spark;
Yet think not, Sun, it shall be dim,
When thou thyself art dark!

div.p: No! it shall live again, and shine, 65

lg.l: In bliss unknown to beams of thine,
By Him recalled to breath,
Who captive led captivity,
Who robbed the grave of victory,

div.p: And took the sting from death! 70

lg.l: Go, Sun, while mercy holds me up
On nature’s awful waste,
To drink this last and bitter cup
Of grief that man shall taste—

div.p: Go, tell the night that hides thy face, 75

lg.l: Thou saw’st the last of Adam’s race,
On earth’s sepulchral clod,
The darkening universe defy
To quench his immortality,

div.p: Or shake his trust in God! 80
Ah! what avails the sceptred race,
Ah! what the form divine!
What every virtue, every grace!
Rose Aylmer, all were thine.
Rose Aylmer, whom these wakeful eyes 5

lg.l: May weep, but never see,
A night of memories and of sighs
I consecrate to thee.
Gone were but the winter cold,
And gone were but the snow,
I could sleep in the wild woods
Where primroses blow.

div.p: Cold’s the snow at my head, 5

lg.l: And cold at my feet;
And the finger of death’s at my een,
Closing them to sleep.
Let none tell my father,

div.p: Or my mother so dear,— 10
I’ll meet them both in heaven
At the spring of the year.

lg.l: I thought to meet no more, so dreary seemed
Death’s interposing veil, and thou so pure,
Thy place in Paradise
Beyond where I could soar;

div.p: Friend of this worthless heart! but happier thoughts 5

lg.l: Spring like unbidden violets from the sod,
Where patiently thou tak’st
Thy sweet and sure repose.
The shadows fall more soothing, the soft air

div.p: Is full of cheering whispers like thine own; 10

lg.l: While Memory, by thy grave,
Lives o’er thy funeral day;
The deep knell dying down; the mourners’ pause,
Waiting their Saviour’s welcome at the gate;

div.p: Sure with the words of Heaven 15

lg.l: Thy spirit met us there,
And sought with us along the accustomed way
The hallowed porch, and entering in beheld
The pageant of sad joy,

div.p: So dear to Faith and Hope. 20
Oh, hadst thou brought a strain from Paradise
To cheer us, happy soul! thou hadst not touched
The sacred springs of grief
More tenderly and true,
Than those deep-warbled anthems, high and low, 25

lg.l: Low as the grave, high as the eternal Throne,
Guiding through light and gloom
Our mourning fancies wild,
